/alexandre.title: Alexandre
/alexandre.html:
A tinkerer, a handyman and a man for every situation, for him difficulties are there to be solved! No mountain too high, no descent too steep, no breakdown too big. Everything can be solved, everything can be mastered. True to the motto "let's get to it", he works out practical solutions. He loves to plan and leaves nothing, or very little, to chance. He lives by the principle: good preparation makes the job easier and reduces unpleasant surprises.

He prefers a bike tour to a meal in a restaurant or a club activity! Safety is something he takes very seriously and never loses sight of. He is not a man of big words, but of action. You can rely on him, which is important for the adventure we are planning. His wide experience in many different fields will be of great use to us.

Claudia

/ausruestung/trekkingrad.title: Touring bike
/ausruestung/trekkingrad.html:
After 23,000 kilometres through America and Asia, we decided on the Aarios "Expedition" frame. Aarios, based in Gretzenbach, designs and builds its frames in-house.

The backbone is the hand-brazed, lugged 25CrMo4 tube set frame. Chromoly steel is very strong and flexible, and hardly heavier than aluminium. This no-compromise frame is built to our needs in terms of geometry, mounting points and cable routing. A powder coating protects the surface against corrosion.

As cycling globetrotters, we want to build up our bikes ourselves. The Shimano 9-speed groupset is replaced by a Rohloff hub gear, and a suspension seatpost will soften bumpy tracks. The SON hub dynamo supplies power for the lights and a USB charging plug. The racks and any connecting parts that could corrode are replaced by stainless steel products.

/ausruestung.title: Equipment
/ausruestung.html:
We spent a long time thinking carefully about our equipment. Everything had to be robust, light, functional, practical and long-lasting. We quickly agreed that we did not want to compromise on quality. In the time ahead of us, our lives could depend on our gear in one situation or another. Saving money here would certainly be foolish and irresponsible. That you can spend hours discussing cycling jerseys and cycling shorts was a new experience for us too. The discussions are over, the bags are packed, and we are ready and excited for the experiences and encounters that lie ahead.

ADVICE AND EQUIPMENT

/berichte/argentinien.title: Argentina
/berichte/argentinien.html:
Argentina
24 June - 3 July 2009

Brazil was not planned as one of our destinations. But to visit Iguazú, the largest subtropical jungle reserve, with its cataratas (waterfalls), crossing the borders Paraguay – Brazil – Argentina is unavoidable. To keep things simple, the Brazilian cataratas are included in this Argentina travel report.

Anyone coming from the north should first see the falls on the Brazilian side from Foz do Iguaçu (32 km from the park) and then the Argentinian ones from Puerto Iguazú (18 km from the park). This order saves an extra border crossing to carry on into Argentina afterwards.

We didn't want to miss the Cataratas del Iguazú on the Río Iguazú, with their 275 waterfalls, under any circumstances! They are said to be the most beautiful in the world and are unique. That is also the reason for our choice of route, which unusually doesn't go through Chile.

The cataratas in Brazil
By public bus from Foz do Iguaçu, we reach the entrance to the 185,000-hectare Parque Nacional do Iguaçu, 32 km away, in 20 minutes. Entry costs 21 reais per person (about 11 USD), which includes the bus transfer to the various viewing platforms. The 17 points of interest (bus stops) can also be reached on well-made footpaths. In good weather you can admire the whole panorama of the saltos (waterfalls) from the Brazilian side. The fine spray usually creates a shining rainbow. Today, however, the view is unfortunately clouded by a curtain of rain coming down in sheets. The day before and the night that followed, it had poured non-stop. Only brief moments allowed photos of the whole water garden.

The geological origins of the falls go back 150 million years. The Río Iguazú flows over a high basalt plateau, which suddenly breaks off in southern Brazil, in the Parque Nacional do Iguaçu, over a total width of 2,700 metres. 800 metres are on Brazilian territory, 1,900 metres on Argentinian territory. The two banks are not connected. On average, 1,700 cubic metres of water thunder down 57 – 72 metres over 2 steps, creating a far-reaching mist. Even when, at peak times, up to 7,000 cubic metres of water move towards the edge, the riverbed stays 2 metres deep. The Brazilian cataratas have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986.

The cataratas in Argentina
The weather has improved a little. From Foz do Iguaçu (Brazil) we cross the border to Puerto Iguazú (18 km from the park), on the Argentinian side. At 60 pesos per person (about 15 USD), entry to the park was a little more expensive than on the Brazilian side. The well-made footpaths, 4 km long in total, let you get uniquely close to the "saltos" here. You should plan a whole day for the visit and a long walk through this natural spectacle. From the Argentinian side you experience these falls up close! The "Garganta del Diablo" in particular was a spectacular experience for us. You reach this U-shaped "Devil's Throat", 150 m wide and 750 m long, by narrow-gauge railway (3.6 km) and a 1,100 m walk. The path to the platform mostly runs directly over the river on a metal bridge.

Other attractions:
The Isla San Martín in the heart of the saltos, with a unique view of the San Martín falls. You are taken to the island by boat from the Paseo Inferior trail (1,400 m). The "Sendero Macuco", a 3-hour trek into the subtropical rainforest, with thousands of animal and plant species.

The Argentinian cataratas have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984.

On Ruta 12 to Bella Unión, on the border with Uruguay, there are still 700 kilometres to cover through the provinces of Misiones and Corrientes. The first 300 kilometres to Posadas run over well-built "corrugated asphalt". An endless up and down! The momentum from the descents is nowhere near enough for the next steep ramp. By now the temperatures have dropped so much that our ups and downs come with jacket on, jacket off. No fewer than 50 hills like this had to be conquered – an effort not to be underestimated. Amazingly, in Argentina, a mostly flat country, we had our biggest daily climb of the whole journey: 1,350 metres.

About 1 million people live in the small province of Misiones. The first Europeans to settle here, in the 17th century, were Jesuit missionaries. In total there are 30 reducciones (missions): 7 in Brazil, 8 in Paraguay and 15 in Argentina, 11 of which are in the province of Misiones. In San Ignacio we visit the ruins of "San Ignacio Miní". The mission of San Ignacio Miní was farmed by 4,000 people on 10 hectares. The remains of these ruins, with the church, social rooms and classrooms, dining hall, kitchen, workshops, prison and cemetery, bear witness to Guaraní baroque, a style of building also adopted by European architects. After the Jesuits were expelled in 1767, the settlement was swallowed up by the jungle. Only in 1941 did work begin on uncovering and restoring what is today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Not much is left of the impenetrable jungle today! Because of logging, the forest is only a third of the size it was 100 years ago. The clear-cut areas are being replanted with fast-growing conifers. Despite all the environmental problems, Misiones is considered one of the most varied provinces in Argentina.

The province of Corrientes, where cotton, rice and mate are grown, doesn't offer much. Ruta 12 seems endlessly long, dead straight and boring. In places there's no overtaking lane (uphill), so lorries and buses passing each other on the narrow road becomes dangerous for us. In no other country have we been harassed and pushed off the asphalt as much as here in Argentina. The long-distance lorry drivers in particular think they are on a racetrack. Speed limits are ignored, and they drive as fast as "the engine allows". On top of that come the cars, which often race along this "cross-country motorway" at 160 or more.

For us cyclists, Ruta 12 is more of a lean stretch. The towns are often more than 50 kilometres apart, and there aren't many places to stay or buy supplies. So we enjoy the hospitality of the big petrol stations, where you can not only refill your drinking water and eat, but also get a chance to shower and do your laundry. There is usually a patch of grass too, although it can be quite noisy because it's so close to the road. In the pampas, wild camping isn't easy because the grazing land is fenced. We often cycle several kilometres to a farm, where we were always offered water and a quiet place to camp.

There are still more than 800 kilometres to go to the capital, Buenos Aires. We have already left the provinces of Misiones (Puerto Iguazú to Posadas) and Corrientes (Posadas to Paso de los Libres) behind us, and we cross the Río Uruguay again. Our "zigzag course" to our destination, Montevideo in Uruguay, requires another border crossing into Brazil. The stretch from Uruguaiana to Bella Unión (Brazil), just 80 kilometres, is quickly done, and we are in our last country, Uruguay (see the Uruguay report). From Montevideo we want to take the "Buquebus" ferry to Buenos Aires.

Buenos Aires:

Buenos Aires, with about 12 million inhabitants, is made up of several districts (12). These districts each have their own unmistakable identity and were once independent communities. As they grew, however, they merged with the city. We are interested in the "barrios" of San Telmo, Puerto Madero, Centro & Retiro, and Recoleta. With our bikes we get to every attraction and don't have to worry about a parking space or a bus connection.

To really get to know Buenos Aires would probably take several days or weeks.

We limited our 5-day stay to the following sights:

The historic centre is the Plaza de Mayo, named after the May Revolution of 1810, where the 67-metre-high Obelisk stands. Here you find the presidential palace, the Casa Rosada, a striking building painted pink. The Cabildo, the former seat of the council, is right opposite – this is where independence from Spain was proclaimed – and today it houses the historical museum.

The "temple of money", the Banco de la Nación (Argentina was once one of the richest countries in the world), with its portico supported by four mighty columns. The cathedral at the political centre of the city shows the great Catholic influence in Argentina; until 1994 the office of city mayor still had to be held by a Catholic.

The Parque Colón, once a dirty harbour area. Today the new district of Puerto Madero presents itself with offices, apartments, lofts in old warehouses and lots of restaurants. In the 4 harbour basins (with pedestrian zones on both sides) there are two museum ships: the frigate "Sarmiento", the navy's former flagship, and the armoured corvette "Uruguay", which rescued an expedition from Antarctica in 1903.

The Puente de la Mujer, a futuristic-looking footbridge (it swings horizontally), which has spanned harbour basin No. 3 since 2001. The two pedestrian streets, Calle Lavalle and Calle Florida, which crosses it, and the Galería Pacífico, with lots of modern and exclusive shops – an ideal playground for keen shoppers.

The Jesuit church of San Ignacio de Loyola, consecrated in 1722, the oldest surviving church and building in the city.

The district of San Telmo was once a harbour quarter of fishermen, slaves and rich merchants. When a yellow fever epidemic broke out in 1871, only the poor and the European immigrants stayed; the rich moved to what is now the city centre. Today the big attraction is the Sunday flea market. Everything that isn't nailed down is traded, and the Plaza Dorrego and the surrounding streets become a stage. Here you'll find very good tango performances, street entertainers, and anyone who thinks they have something "out of the ordinary" to show puts it on for the public.

The district of Recoleta, built by the rich during the yellow fever epidemic, stands out for its quietly located hotels and shops with the latest displays. On the Plaza Alvear you come across dozens of the rich people's pedigree dogs on leads, taken for "walkies" by dog walkers. The cemetery with the basilica matches this exclusive district. Even after death, wealth is shamelessly put on show with oversized mausoleums and tombs in marble and precious metals.

Finding bike boxes wasn't all that easy! The few specialist shops are far outside the city or in shopping centres in the suburbs. We needed a taxi, ¾ of an hour each way, to get our packing material. By now we are well practised at taking our Kogas apart, so our luggage was quickly packed ready for the flight.


After 760 kilometres we leave Argentina with these memories:

The Cataratas del Iguazú, the largest waterfalls in the world, especially the "Garganta del Diablo"

The mission "San Ignacio Miní", a ruin from the 17th century.

Corrugated asphalt, 1,350 metres of climbing – the biggest day's effort of the whole journey

A TV interview in Santo Tomé

Ruta 12: dead straight, boring and dangerous. Long-distance lorry drivers think they are on a racetrack.

Towns up to 50 kilometres apart; places to stay and buy supplies are scarce.

A casino in (almost) every town. Gambling seems to us to be Argentina's "national sport"

The hospitality of the big petrol stations, with camping, showers and laundry facilities.

Buenos Aires:

The harbour area, the museum ships, the swing bridge "Puente de la Mujer"

The Plaza Dorrego in San Telmo, with its flea market, tango, street entertainers and artists

The first and only time we had an excellent piece of meat, at the restaurant "Piegari Vitello e Dolce"

The Recoleta cemetery: mausoleums, tombs, black marble and crumbling coffins

Active (8 days of riding)
760 kilometres
-
Total climbing
5,100 m
-
Average speed
18.5 km/h
-
Riding time in motion
41 hours

/berichte/asien.title: Asia
/berichte/asien.html:
Asia Oceania America
Turkey
1 April - 15 May 2012
After a short flight with Pegasus Airlines, we land in Istanbul at 18:00 in the evening, in stormy winds and heavy rain. Someone is waiting for us at the airport, and after a 45-minute drive we reach the Hotel Blue Tuana, booked in advance, not far from the Blue Mosque.
The rooms are extremely small, and right outside the window rattles read more

Iran
15 May - 12 June 2012
Before crossing the border from Turkey into Iran, it's time for a change of outfit. In the middle of a lorry queue about 5 kilometres long, we say goodbye to our casual cycling clothes and change into "morally appropriate" ones. Long trousers for the man; hair covered with a headscarf, a long-sleeved shirt and of course long trousers for the woman! read more

Turkmenistan
12 - 15 June 2012
At 10:00 we are standing at the Iran-Turkmenistan customs. Although there is a ramp for processing, we have to carry the bikes and luggage up 5 steps into the building. A sign directs tourists on foot to this entrance, and no exception is made for us either. The usual procedure: wait, wait, wait, and watch read more

Uzbekistan
15 June - 9 July 2012
30 kilometres after the border we look for a suitable place to sleep. This doesn't seem to be so easy here, because large areas are used for farming. Seen from the road, places to pitch the tent look suitable. Looked at a little more closely, it's a completely different picture. The "idyllic" finds are covered with thorns read more

Tajikistan
9 July - 4 August 2012
Getting through Uzbek customs took strong nerves. Endless queuing, and at the check all our bags were rummaged through! Just before 10:00 everything has finally been checked, and we get our exit stamp. The Tajik entry formalities go quickly, and half an hour later we are in our 5th country since the start of the journey. read more

Kyrgyzstan
4 - 6 August 2012
The change of country from Tajikistan to Kyrgyzstan doesn't go as usual. After the Tajik passport control at 4,220 m above sea level, there are still 2 kilometres of unpaved, bumpy track to the "Kyzyl-Art Pass" at 4,290 m. That means that after clearing customs we are already outside the country's border, but in the 22-kilometre-wide "corridor" read more

China
6 August - 14 October 2012
A promising, mysterious country! Again and again we were told that this part of Asia is difficult to travel for independent tourists who don't know China. We wanted to try it anyway. Many cycle tourists have already cycled through China, and not all of them could speak Chinese. From the Tajik border read more

Laos
14 October - 7 November 2012
The change of culture and climate from China to Laos could not be greater. A change of country in the truest sense of the word! We are pleasantly surprised. Just a few kilometres after the border we are already in the middle of the jungle of the provinces of Oudômxai and Louangphabang. Not a single square metre that isn't covered with deep green read more

Cambodia
7 - 25 November 2012
Changing countries from Laos to Cambodia at the Veun Kham border crossing was free of red tape and quick. The customs officers are friendly and speak English! Fill in a form, hand over a photo, and we get our 30-day visa. With the Angkor Wat temple complex, Cambodia is a tourist highlight. read more

Thailand
23 November - 2 January 2013
The biggest change of all was driving on the left. There was no sign when we entered to tell us "which way to go". Although the customs building was on the left side of the road, we carried on riding on the right. The Thais are very considerate drivers. No honking or head-shaking read more

Malaysia
2 - 12 January 2013 / 22 January - 4 February 2013
There are still 800 kilometres to go to the border with Singapore. We had planned our route along the better-developed west coast. Adding another country, "Borneo", at short notice brings new momentum to things. We decide on the route along the east coast through the states of read more

Singapore
12 - 22 January 2013
We have reached our planned destination! How time flies!
The huge metropolis of Singapore, at the end of the Malay Peninsula. Since the start in Istanbul 9 months ago, we have covered 12,000 kilometres and 113,000 metres of climbing in 794 hours of riding. Even the border crossing to Johor Bahru read more

Borneo
4 - 18 February 2013
At first the name Borneo was a little confusing for us. Where is this island, what links it with Malaysia, where are Sabah and the town of Lahad Datu? The explanation:
Borneo, the island in the Indonesian archipelago of South-East Asia read more

/berichte/bolivia.title: Bolivia
/berichte/bolivia.html:
Bolivia
26 September - 23 October 2015

Our plan to check in the evening before fell through, because American Airlines only accepts luggage 3 ½ hours before departure at the earliest. So back to the hotel with all our luggage, and another attempt the next day.

Surprisingly, check-in early on Saturday morning goes well and quickly, and 9 ½ hours, two hot meals and two films later we land safely in Philadelphia. We have 2 hours to collect our bike boxes and the 4 pieces of luggage holding the panniers and check them in again. 10 minutes before boarding everything is done. Another 2 ½ hours later we land in Miami.

Welcome to Miami, with a 5-hour wait for the connecting flight. Slowly getting tired, we try to sleep, which is only possible on the floor. The phone alarm is set, so nothing stands in the way of sweet dreams. 1 hour before check-in the phone wakes us, and we discover that the terminal has changed. So back via the Skytrain. We have to wait 5 minutes for the first one. Just as it pulls in and we get on, an airport official walks through and says it isn't running any more; another one will come along on the opposite side in 10 minutes. When we reach the right gate, we can already hear the announcement „last call for Naegeli/Keller“, so hurry up…. We make it, take our seats, and a little later we are in the queue of planes waiting for clearance to take off.

At last, take-off, we're in the air. After about ¾ of an hour comes the announcement that something is wrong, and about 5 minutes later that we are flying back to Miami. The cabin crew walk through the plane with tight faces, and there are repeated announcements telling us to fasten our seatbelts; the crew have strapped themselves in too. A really queasy feeling comes over us, because it isn't clear what is going on. Finally we can make out the lights of Miami. But the uneasy feeling is still there, and not without reason. On the airfield, left and right, stand masses of fire engines, police and everything that flashes and can help. So it is clear to us that something more serious must have happened on our flight.

We are taken off the plane and sent into the terminal. There we are kept quiet with meal and drink vouchers and calmed down with the news that the flight crew and the plane have to be replaced. The flight will not continue until about 6.00 in the morning, but from the same gate. Everyone settles down on the floor as best they can and gets ready for a short, uncomfortable night. 3 hours later comes the news that the gate has to be changed after all. So off on another trek through Miami airport. The planned departure is put off by another 2 hours, and then… we board after all. We take our seats and listen to the announcement that we still have to wait for oxygen for the pilots (landing in La Paz is only allowed with oxygen masks) and for flight clearance for the cabin crew. So now we have been sitting in the plane for over an hour, the air conditioning is dripping on our shoulders and we are „dog-tired“. Finally, we're ready to go. After a fairly calm flight, with only one meal, 6 ½ hours later we are rewarded with a spectacular approach into La Paz.

After 36 hours of travelling, about 20 of them in the air, the driver of our hotel bus is waiting for us and takes us to our home for the next 5 days. At 15.00 local time we fall into bed and, with short breaks, sleep until 07.30 the next morning.

The sudden change of climate took its toll on us. The difference in altitude from 400 m to 4000 m, the very dry air, and temperatures ranging from up to +30 degrees by day to almost freezing at night put a heavy strain on the body. In La Paz we had to extend our stay from 5 to 7 days because of stomach trouble and a cold. Getting into the first „cycling days“ was not easy for us.

In Oruro (225 km), Alexandre's cold turned into flu, which only antibiotics could cure. At the same time Claudia had to be treated for a viral inflammation of the lips. After 5 days of recovery in the hotel room we could swing back into the saddle and carry on towards the Lagoon Route.

We make good progress. Unexpectedly, though, on the afternoon of the second day a haze moves across the sun. An uneasy feeling creeps over us, so we decide to put up the tent at once. Just in time! For the next half hour a sandstorm rages, and we are glad to be sitting in the shelter of the tent.

As the kilometres go by it gets sandier and dustier, and 30 kilometres before Salinas the tarmac ends for good. A highlight lies ahead. The Salar de Uyuni, with its huge expanse, really snow-white, is coloured more brownish than white by the sandstorms that sweep across the country. Even so, the surface reflects the sunlight and strains the eyes. After 50 kilometres on the salar we reach Isla Incahuasi. As there are only a few tracks across the salar, and at night the jeeps drive criss-cross, some without lights, camping on the salar is not advisable. So we spend the night in the refugio with 5 other people. In the morning we leave the island and ride another 50 kilometres across the salar. Simply unbelievable, this vastness. After the salar the road gets rougher and demands more and more of us. Cycling on the unmade ground is out of the question. The track is strewn with bigger stones, shaped into corrugations by lorries, or full of deep sand. We sweat, push, and decide to ride to Ollagüe (Chile). On this route we expect less pushing than on the Lagoon Route, which we already saw 7 years ago on a guided jeep tour.

When we reach the border town of Avaroa in Bolivia, we have been on the road for 10 days since Oruro. The formalities are quickly done. Less quickly do we get through the 5-kilometre border corridor. The wind blows head-on against us with incredible strength. Cycling is impossible. A foretaste of Patagonia?

/berichte/bolivien.title: Bolivia
/berichte/bolivien.html:
Bolivia
9 May - 13 June 2009

Copacabana
In Kasani we have already crossed the border from Peru into Bolivia. The formalities were done quickly, but we were only given a 30-day permit to stay in our host country, Bolivia. The traffic has dwindled to a few vehicles of uncertain origin and age. Another 10 kilometres to the Bolivian Copacabana (not to be confused with the one in Brazil) lie ahead of us.

Copacabana, a town geared to tourism, lies at 3,800 m above sea level and has 20,000 inhabitants. This town was once an important cultural centre, and today, together with the Isla del Sol, it is an attractive destination for tourists and pilgrims. The biggest attraction is a boat trip to the Isla del Sol or the Isla de la Luna on Lake Titicaca. In a slow, heavy wooden boat with 30 other passengers, we reach the Island of the Sun, 20 kilometres away, after 3 hours (!). This island is said to be the birthplace of Inca culture, so here too there are a few terraced slopes and ruins. The 3-hour walk along the island's high ridge to the boat landing gives us one more impressive view over Lake Titicaca.

The road on towards La Paz is a scenic route at 4,300 m above sea level, with one sensational view after another of the snow-capped mountains over 6,000 metres high. This stretch is one of the most beautiful in the Andes. A narrow strait of 800 metres at Tiquina has to be crossed by ferry. Between San Pedro de Tiquina and San Pablo de Tiquina, wooden ferries with undersized outboard motors go back and forth. We have the "luck" of being taken across together with a tilting coach. This adventurous crossing cost us 10 bolivianos (CHF 1.50).

The remaining 110 kilometres to La Paz, with a pass at 4,250 metres, keep offering us impressive views of the Cordillera Real. On the way, at Huatajata, we come across the highest yacht club in the world and lots of restaurants offering "trucha" (trout) in every possible variation. What stands out is the local "architecture", which may well be the work of the one and only village architect.

Across a wide altiplano (40 km) we head dead straight towards La Paz. We notice the first signs of Bolivia's lively capital as we ride through "El Alto", the poor upper city, 8 kilometres long. This is also where the airport is, which at 4,082 m above sea level is one of the highest in the world.

La Paz
We have to cross a tangle of minibuses, wheelbarrows and hurried pedestrians before we can make out the houses of La Paz. On the 12-kilometre city motorway, which winds down into the valley basin like a worm, we find our way into the centre of this metropolis of a million people. As in most big cities in South America, looking for somewhere to stay in the evening traffic becomes a nerve-racking test of patience.

A stroll around the city the next day shows us a hectic, noisy business city with a strong Indigenous character. Remarkably little tourism, lots of fast-food corners along the main street, and again and again steep side streets and stairways leading up to the next parallel street.

We explore:

The "Witches' Market", where herbs are sold against evil spirits and illnesses, and for happiness and a long life.

The market, where you can buy everything from textiles, sausages and meat and vegetables to stolen goods.

The most beautiful car-free cobbled street in La Paz, Calle Jaén, with its old 18th-century house fronts.

The "Plaza Murillo", where the freedom fighter Murillo was hanged by the royalists in 1810, the parliament building, and the presidential palace, "heavily guarded" by the palace guard.

Almost everything your heart desires is traded here. There is pushing and shoving, you come across quarrelling dogs, and buses packed to bursting squeeze through the streets, honking.

Carretera de la Muerte
What interests us most, though, is the "Carretera de la Muerte". An experience of a special kind! We are going to ride the most dangerous road in the world, also called the "Death Road", on downhill bikes. The company "Madness" offers the tour for a maximum of seven riders with a professional guide. At 07:00 in the morning the participants are kitted out with full-face helmets, reflective vests, gloves, goggles, nylon trousers and a full-suspension Rocky Mountain downhill bike. With all the bikes on the roof, a support vehicle takes us up to the pass "La Cumbre" (4,655 m above sea level) in the Cordillera Real, where we start.

Over a distance of 64 kilometres we drop 3,345 metres down to Yolosa, which lies at 1,295 m above sea level. This spectacular downhill takes us through banks of fog, waterfalls and subtropical jungle and along sheer rock faces. On this unsecured gravel track, 4 - 6 metres wide, traffic keeps to the left side of the road, both uphill and downhill, as an exception. During this 4-hour ride we are supplied with snacks and drinks from the support vehicle. Before the transport back to La Paz there is a chance to shower, a swimming pool, a buffet lunch, and a Madness T-shirt as a certificate. After this perfectly organised tour, led with the greatest possible safety, we reach our hotel at 19:00.

An experience we can highly recommend under "Downhill Madness".

Route info: La Paz – Uyuni – Potosí
From La Paz via Oruro to Huari, the 350 kilometres of paved road could be ridden without much effort. From Huari onwards, however, the road conditions are disastrous. The remaining 180-kilometre stretch, in an extremely remote area, runs through a vast desert. A sandpit as far as the eye can see! The wheel tracks are partly filled with fine sandy dust. Where they aren't, the corrugated surface provides variety, like being in a cocktail shaker. The road crosses dry and water-filled fords several times, forcing even motor vehicles down to walking pace. The terrain has changed too. Steep descents and equally steep climbs make progress even harder.

To say it straight away: from Uyuni to Potosí the same miserable conditions currently apply. With few exceptions, the 210-kilometre sandy track winds through an "inhospitable" region, with 2 passes (4,200 m above sea level) thrown in. There are few places to buy supplies, and water is correspondingly hard to come by! Along the whole route, heavy construction machinery is currently widening the road. Here and there, rocky obstacles have to be blasted away and laboriously carted off. The Uyuni – Potosí stretch is supposed to be paved by the end of 2010.

Because of the extremely bad road conditions, we decide to cover the 2 sections in a "comfortable" coach. From La Paz to Uyuni, we board the "first-class coach" at 22:00, to reach Uyuni at 08:00 the next morning. A hot meal is served, we watch the film "Indiana Jones" to the end, and the bumpy track begins. The passengers are asked to move all sensitive items under their seats. Pillows against the "shaking" and blankets against the cold (down to -10 degrees is possible) are handed out. Even the comfortable reclining seat can't rock us to sleep. The night becomes a 10-hour ordeal through dark, unlit desert to Uyuni.

Salar de Uyuni and the lagoon route
As soon as we arrive in Uyuni, we go into one of the many "tour offices" to book a 3-day classic tour by 4x4 jeep. Organised trips around Uyuni, led by the driver, are on offer. The price of 140 USD per person includes a Toyota 4WD jeep, food, simple accommodation and (in our case) excellent guiding by the driver. Everything is already loaded onto the roof of the jeep, covered with a tarpaulin (against the dust) and strapped down. We, 4 other guests and the driver set off on the 800-kilometre adventure at 10:30.

We would rather tell the story of our experiences with photos than with text. Even so, below we try to pass on these unique natural scenes in a few key words.

Day 1
The Cementerio de Trenes (train cemetery)

Table salt production in Colchani (houses made of salt blocks)

The Salar de Uyuni: at 2,000 km², the largest salt flat in the world. The salt crust is up to 28 m thick. 60% of the world's salt needs. Mineral salt was washed down from the surrounding mountains over more than 1,000 years. Impassable during the rainy season from November – April.

A unique salt hotel, where you sleep on llama skins

Incahuasi (Isla Pescado), 100 kilometres from Uyuni. Cacti up to 1,200 years old, growing 8 – 12 metres high.

Dinner and a night in San Juan: 400 inhabitants and 2 football pitches. Simple accommodation (no heating, but a hot shower).

Day 2
The active and dangerous Ollagüe volcano (5,980 m above sea level). Severe earthquakes on the Chilean side.

4 small lagoons and wild vicuñas (the domesticated ones wear ribbons in their ears)

The Siloli desert with the Árbol de Piedra (stone trees). Snow cover of up to 10 cm is possible in June. Sand and dust everywhere, even in the jeep.

Laguna Cañapa, rich in minerals and still partly covered by a sheet of ice from the night.

Laguna Colorada (4,274 m above sea level), a 60 km² lake whose colour changes depending on the wind and the sunlight. The lagoon consists of fresh water, minerals, algae and white islands of borax. 3 different kinds of flamingo breed here. At night the thermometer drops as low as -20 degrees.

Dinner and a night in a simple dormitory

Day 3
Getting up at 05:00 at -20 degrees! It's freezing cold (there's no heating or hot water here)

Sol de Mañana, a geyser basin at 4,850 m above sea level, and the Termas de Chalviri with water at 30 degrees (you can bathe).

Breakfast at 08:00, back at the Laguna Colorada.

The Salvador Dalí desert, with volcanic rocks thrown out by an eruption. Surreal!

The Laguna Verde at the foot of the Licancabur and Juriques volcanoes, 17 km² in size and at 4,850 m above sea level, with high levels of lead, calcium and sulphur. No life is possible here.

The Salar de Chiguana (borax mining)

The Laguna Blanca (white lagoon)

The Chilean border (a fellow traveller is dropped off and takes a bus to San Pedro de Atacama)

The active Uturuncu volcano (6,010 m above sea level). A road goes up to 4,000 metres, and you can hike to the crater lake at 6,000 metres.

Lunch, brought along in the jeep and prepared on the spot by the driver.

Dancing rocks

From afar, the 5th-largest silver mine in the world, San Cristóbal, can be seen.

Excellently led and without a single breakdown, the tour ended at 19:00 in front of our accommodation, the Hostal Tonito. The natural variety of south-western Bolivia thrilled us. An experience we could never have imagined in South America.

Note:
The accommodation is very "basic" and run by locals. Electricity and light from a generator are only available after dark. Dormitories and shared bathrooms. Dinner and breakfast depend on the tour operator and on what the driver has been given to bring. And…. as soon as the last rays of sun disappear below the horizon, it gets bitterly cold. Even inside the accommodation, the thermometer drops to a bitter -20 degrees because of single glazing and gaps. A good sleeping bag is priceless. And….. don't forget, you are always between 4,000 – 5,000 metres above sea level, so breathing can become laboured at the slightest effort (lack of acclimatisation). It can get quite dusty inside the vehicle. You have to reckon with about 20 hours of driving for 800 kilometres, and you need a good backside.

Potosí
Because of the miserable road to Potosí (already described above), we decide on another "transfer". In a packed 48-seat regional bus, we leave the unpaved, dusty streets of Uyuni.

This day's journey of 200 kilometres should only have taken 6 hours (!). Shortly after leaving at 10:00 there is an unplanned stop. A flat tyre! A rear wheel is losing pressure. No fuss: the passengers watch in amazement as the 2 "mechanics" who travel with the driver do the repair. During a general check of the tyres, they find that the tread on a front wheel is coming away and the valve seems to be leaking. So a 2nd wheel change is carried out. After an hour the journey can continue, to our astonishment without a single stop (5 hours), so the lost time can be made up. We leave it to your imagination how you go to the toilet on a moving bus. At 18:00, by which time we no longer knew which "cheek" to sit on, we reach the city of Potosí, with 170,000 inhabitants.

At 4,067 m above sea level, this city is the highest in the world. Thanks to its mining (underground mines), in the 16th century Potosí was the richest city in the world, bigger and more important than Madrid, Paris or Rome, and once the treasury of the Americas. To this day, almost 50,000 tonnes of silver have been taken out of the "Cerro Rico" mountain. The veins have since been exhausted, and now mainly tin and zinc are mined. The inhuman working conditions (altitude, mercury poisoning, black lung, etc.) had claimed 8 million lives by the 18th century! Currently the world market price of the minerals is at a record low, and hardly anything about the situation has changed to this day.

It's hard to imagine that such exploitation of human labour still exists today. To get 1 kilogram of ore, many tonnes of rock first have to be mined. According to the information we were given, the Potosí ores are exported, not processed into silver bars as they once were in 1850. All that remains of the city's former wealth are 36 churches (some of them in ruins). The historic centre was declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO. Silver mining once gave this city great importance through the making and minting of coins and medals. A visit to the museum "Casa Real de la Moneda" gives an interesting insight into the art of coin making.

Many agencies offer guided tours of a mine (10 USD). This attraction is considered the highlight of a stay in Potosí. As a group of 2 with an English-speaking guide, we are picked up to collect overalls, boots, helmets and headlamps. In our mining gear we buy presents at the "Calvario miners' market" to hand out to the workers on site. For 35 bolivianos (5 USD) we get a bag of coca leaves, 2 dl of 96% sugar cane alcohol, cigarettes, mineral water, banana concentrate and dynamite for the road. A minibus takes us to a viewpoint overlooking the city and the mining area. Then comes a dynamite-nitroglycerine blast with a fuse, demonstrated by a tour guide.

On the way to the mine entrance we meet women smashing rocks by hand and sorting them by quality. A 79-year-old woman (photo) works 16 hours a week and, depending on the yield, gets 500 bolivianos (70 USD) a month, and a handful of coca leaves from us.

A "miner's" wife, who is usually already a widow, works and sorts 7 tonnes of rock in 3 months. They are all "trapped" by the family tradition of having to work as miners. Mine tunnels are passed down over generations. Around Potosí there are still 180 active mines, currently worked by 5,000 miners; 3 years ago there were still 8,000. Because the mineral content is poor today, family earnings are poor too. 12-year-old children are made to work outside the mines, go to school at night, and earn 30 bolivianos a day. At 14-15 the hard work begins inside the tunnels, as labourers earning 50 bolivianos a day. Promotion to machine operator, where one is needed in that tunnel, brings in 140 bolivianos a day. As a mine owner (who pays rent to the state), the miner works at the dangerous rock face and, depending on the quality of the ore, earns 200 - 300 bolivianos a day.

A miner's life expectancy is 40 – 50 years. The cause of death is usually asbestosis or black lung, collapse from excessive alcohol and pill consumption, or premature ageing. The working conditions are extremely hard. All the workers, women and men, chew coca leaves non-stop, taking them from the wad they keep in their cheeks. Coca leaves suppress hunger and keep exhaustion and pain at bay. For a mine to be profitable, 1 tonne a day has to be dug out by hand, or 20 tonnes with the help of machines. Profitability depends on the quality of the mineral content. A working day lasts 8 hours, with no food and no breaks. Depending on the job, the work consists of pushing carts weighing 1 tonne, driving blast holes into the rock with a hammer and chisel, moving and sorting chunks of rock, and…. chewing coca leaves all day.

By now we have handed out our presents, left the mine and said goodbye with a "Gracias por la visita". We will remember the faces of these workers for a long time.

Potosí to Puerto Suárez
Delighted by the fully paved main road, we set off from Potosí to Sucre. The road runs through a fertile valley, and it gets noticeably warmer with every kilometre. As we have come to expect, there are a few hills in between. The first 35 kilometres after Potosí are given to us free, as a fast descent. But over the whole 160-kilometre route there are 2,000 metres of climbing in total, which should not be underestimated. The last part in particular takes it out of us. You think: yes, there's our destination up ahead, but no, there's one last hard climb to Sucre.

Sucre, the capital of Bolivia but not the seat of government (that is in La Paz), looks very well kept, and we feel at home straight away. Sucre (just under 300,000 inhabitants) is celebrating its 200th birthday this year, and the 50th anniversary of its motor race. Yes! An annual race like the one in Monaco, where the track runs right through the streets of the old town. No side street is closed off, there are no barriers, and the spectators follow the action from the pavement. When a "racing car" approaches at up to 170 km/h, the police blow their whistles so people get off the road. The most dangerous bends around the "Plaza 25 de Mayo" are made safer with sandbags filled by women. To our amazement, a few "old bangers" don't make it round the corners and thunder straight into the sandbags. Incredibly dangerous! Surely this only happens here in Bolivia, but apparently there has never been a serious accident. Most of the racing cars look to us as if they have been cobbled together from surplus car parts and sent onto the track without silencers.

Because of the race, all the surrounding roads are closed, so we couldn't visit the famous Sunday market in Tarabuco. This market, 65 kilometres from Sucre, is said to be one of the most beautiful in Bolivia. The city of Sucre is named after "General José de Sucre", who began the fight for independence here in 1809, hence the 200th anniversary. In 1992 Sucre was declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO.

Alexandre's toothache forces us to stay for several days. The tooth, already badly treated in Cusco, is causing big problems again, so a crown had to be made. Successfully, as it turns out! We spend the time between the "dentista" and strolling around town at the "Hostal de Su Merced" www.desumerced.com , an address we highly recommend. A hotel in the middle of the city, in a quiet spot, with a friendly atmosphere and a lovely breakfast buffet. The owner invites us to the Espectáculo Origen, a 2-hour show of Bolivian Indigenous dances and traditional costumes. At first we were a little sceptical about shows like this. We had already seen something similar, not very imaginative, in Cusco. But we really enjoyed this attraction here in Sucre.

With our teeth back in working order, we leave Sucre heading for Santa Cruz. A tough 600-kilometre stretch lies ahead of us. Bolivia showing cyclists its most extreme side. After Sucre, first 300 metres of hard climbing, followed by countless bends downhill to about 2,000 m above sea level. At Puente Arce, 97 kilometres beyond Sucre, the fun stops! The finest asphalt turns into a stony, dusty mountain road. The remaining 67 kilometres to Aiquile are exhausting! In places we push our narrow tyres (excellent on asphalt) through sand and dust. The route runs through bleak, dry mountains, with some steep climbs and bends. As a precaution, in the last village after Puente Arce we filled our 5 bottles and the 2 water bags (20 litres), so we have enough to drink. In Aiquile, a rather inhospitable place where the north-south and east-west roads cross, we find somewhere to stay with a shower. A "caliente" (hot) shower here means cold water pushed through an electric instantaneous shower head. With a lot of delicate fiddling you find the right flow rate, so that you get the feeling of warm water. They aren't too fussy about electrical installations here. If the earth wire isn't connected properly, your caliente shower comes with a tingling feeling.

There are still 450 kilometres to Santa Cruz. The information from locals about the state of the road ranges from "todo plano" (all flat) and "todo asfalto" (all paved) to "empedrado" (stone-paved). The well-meant motto is: better to give wrong information than none at all. That's why route descriptions are often useless to us. Empedrado roads are made of rough fieldstones joined together with cement to form a surface. Highways like this are one of the worst things there are for bicycles, cyclists and panniers! We feel the vibrations through the chattering of our upper and lower jaws, so speeds of more than 5 km/h are unthinkable.

Supposedly the whole stage from Aiquile to Epizana (90 kilometres) is paved like this. That is why, after 8 kilometres, we leave the "empedrado experience" and want to ride across the mountains to the highland road (near San Isidro), to carry on from there to Santa Cruz. The highland route Cochabamba – Santa Cruz is generally considered more varied than the newly built, less spectacular lowland route over the Sacaba pass at 3,660 m above sea level. At first still enthusiastic about our short cut, we soon lose the desire to push our bikes through the sand and dust yet again. We don't want to turn back to the empedrado route. At the dusty roadside we wait for a lift that meets our "requirements".

In fact the road from Aiquile to San Isidro is used by very few vehicles, but... as if we had ordered it, a powerful lorry comes towards us. It's easy to see it's a ride: several Indigenous people's hats are already poking up over the sides of the trailer. Load everything on! Great: the 70-boliviano ticket (10 USD) for over 400 kilometres to Santa Cruz is sorted. We make ourselves comfortable on about 400 bags of cement and chat with the others, who don't quite understand all our gear. They all have sacks of onions, potatoes or vegetables with them, bought at the market in Sucre. The long-distance drivers earn a welcome extra income from carrying passengers like this. People hop on and off along the way with "stop on request". Babies, children and the elderly, everyone can benefit from this cheap way of travelling. The men stand stiffly at the sides, the women lie in woollen blankets sleeping or breastfeeding their babies, and the children play on the loading platform.

The heavy load and the wide tyres of the 5-axle vehicle push the fine sand, several centimetres deep, out of the wheel tracks. We marvel at the barren, mountainous, dry landscape and are relieved to have chosen this way of getting around. With passengers getting on and off, there are regular chances to stretch our legs, go to the toilet behind a bush or visit a kiosk by the road. By now we have already spent 12 hours on the loading platform, and at 22:00 we reach Mataral. Because it starts to rain, the delicate cargo (cement bags and passengers) is covered and protected with a tarpaulin. The driver says goodbye and disappears into the bunk in his cab for the next 7 hours. An unusual situation for us. Nobody can get in, nobody can get out. For the locals it's no problem; they lie snoring in the blankets they brought along. On our "Therm-a-Rest" mats, covered with a dusty lorry tarpaulin, we try to keep the cold at bay.

5 o'clock! Engine noise, the smell of diesel and squeaking wheels: our journey continues. The last of the biscuits and a bottle of Coca-Cola calm our rumbling stomachs for now. Rain all night long has turned the dust and fine sand on the road into a sticky mass. For the remaining 6 hours we have to sit tight on cement bags without seeing anything of what's going on, and after a total of 28 hours we reach the outskirts of Santa Cruz.

Santa Cruz (2,100,000 inhabitants) lies at 420 m above sea level in the lowlands of Bolivia. A tropical climate lets the vegetation flourish right into the city centre. During the winter (the dry season) from May to August it gets quite cool at night, but it stays frost-free. With the building of the road to Cochabamba, Santa Cruz became more and more important, and today it is Bolivia's most important city after La Paz. Soya and maize growing and cattle farming are practised intensively, making Santa Cruz Bolivia's economic capital. Santa Cruz also has a reputation as the hub of the cocaine trade and is therefore also called the country's drug capital. For us this big city had nothing out of the ordinary to offer. The townscape and the outskirts are often full of rubbish, and the houses look neglected to us. So after 2 days it's easy for us to head for the border with Paraguay soon.

Already while planning the trip, we realised that with bicycles it would be easier to enter Bolivia from Peru than to leave it towards Paraguay. The "Ruta Trans-Chaco" (Paraguay) runs from Sucre via Boyuibe (border control) to Mariscal Estigarribia. The road is unpaved and very muddy. By now the section from Espinola to Mariscal Estigarribia (100 kilometres) should have been completed. The 530 kilometres to Asunción are paved. The long sandy stretches are difficult, and there are hardly any places to stock up on food and water. As far as we know, the only option left is to reach Asunción by boat on the Río Paraguay.

The road from Santa Cruz to Puerto Suárez (660 kilometres) should by now be paved. The surroundings are pure wilderness, endless dust and sand, and there are few places to buy supplies. We take the chance to travel on the "Expreso Oriental" from Santa Cruz to Puerto Suárez (on the Brazilian border). For this adventurous night journey we pay 15 USD per person, 2 bicycle supplements of 4 USD, and an extra tip of 4 USD to have our gear treated with care. Departure 16:00, arrival at 08:00 the next morning. We are looking forward to the comfortable reclining seats, the food service and the films to while away the 14-hour train ride.

The train, pulled by a diesel locomotive, slowly leaves the safety of the station. We soon realise that the tracks and the railway bed could do with an overhaul. The carriages sway, and you can't miss the gaps between the rails. Are we on a roller coaster? You quickly get used to your new surroundings: the 2 films have finished, the lights are dimmed, and the train rattles on, swaying through the night. The heating in the air conditioning has broken down, and the longer we travel, the cooler it gets in our compartment. Once again we don't have the blankets we need. The locals are used to breakdowns like this and have brought their pillows and blankets as a precaution. Necessity is the mother of invention, so we help ourselves to the covers of unused seats and use them as "sleeping bags". Arriving on time in Puerto Suárez, we collect all our luggage and the bikes unharmed. The tip was worth it!

We decide on option 2 (the boat) and spend the rest of the day dealing with the border formalities for Paraguay. We take a taxi to the Bolivian border, 11 kilometres away, and have our exit stamp entered for the following day. A Brazilian driver takes us to the bus terminal in Corumbá, 7 kilometres away, where we get our entry stamp for Brazil. It all sounds very long-winded and complicated, but it's necessary if we want to cross the "green border" into Paraguay.

Nothing turns out the way you plan it! As we leave the terminal, we notice a map of Brazil stuck to the wall. Following the course of the Río Paraguay, which forms the border between Bolivia, Brazil and Paraguay, we spot a Porto Esperança (Brazil) and a Puerto Esperanza (Paraguay). Very confusing! As everyone confirmed that the place in question was in Brazil, we spontaneously decided to head for Porto Esperança in Brazil.

And firstly, things turn out differently, and secondly, not the way you think.

More about that in the next travel report, from Paraguay.

After 670 kilometres we leave Bolivia with these memories:

Lots seen, lots experienced, and not much cycling

Crossing on a ferry with a tilting coach

The Carretera de la Muerte, a spectacular downhill from 4,465 m to 1,295 m above sea level

The train cemetery, the Salar de Uyuni and the salt hotel, Fish Island and the cacti

The Laguna Colorada, Verde, Blanca and Cañapa

Alpacas, vicuñas and flamingos

Geysers, hot springs, stone trees and dancing rocks

Sucre, the capital, reachable only by dirt roads

Road conditions mostly unsuitable for cyclists

Empedrado roads, surfaced with rough fieldstones

Potosí, the highest city in the world, at 4,100 metres

Miners, dynamite and coca leaves

The night train from Santa Cruz to Puerto Suárez

The coach journey La Paz – Uyuni – Potosí

28 hours on bags of cement

Dust, fine sand and dried-up riverbeds

Wild, barren landscapes with savanna, steppe and lush vegetation

Tropical, temperate and subpolar climates

Temperatures from -20 to +30 degrees

Biker info for the route

-
Active (11 days of riding)
550 kilometres
-
Transfer (bus, car, train)
1,900 kilometres
-
Total climbing
5,200 m
-
Average speed
18.3 km/h

/berichte/borneo.title: Borneo
/berichte/borneo.html:
Borneo
4 - 18 February 2013

At first the name Borneo was a little confusing for us. Where is this island, what links it with Malaysia, where are Sabah and the town of Lahad Datu? The explanation:
Borneo, the island in the Indonesian archipelago of South-East Asia, is divided between three countries: Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei. The Malaysian part is called Borneo, the Indonesian part Kalimantan. With an area of 751,936 km², it is the third-largest island in the world after Greenland and New Guinea, and 18 times bigger than Switzerland. Sabah in the east and Sarawak in the west are the two Malaysian provinces. Lahad Datu is our starting point and lies in the south-east.

At Lahad Datu airport we land on a runway surrounded by palms and lots of greenery. The passengers walk to the spartan check-in/out building. There's no shuttle bus. Not far from the airfield is the home of our friends Tisha and Simon, who are building their future here. Their company, bikeandtours, has existed for a year and offers accommodation, meals, bike hire and guided tours. Over the next 2 weeks we will get to experience Borneo's wildlife up close. By mountain bike, with a four-wheel-drive support vehicle, Simon will show us Borneo's natural treats.

Already well used to the climate, we cycled to Tumunong Hallu Beach the same day. It was hot and sticky, and alternating sun and rain showers showed us the reality of South-East Asia. On light mountain bikes, we roll quickly along an unpaved road with deep ruts washed out by the rain down to the bay. On the beach of the "Telukan Sea", Tisha surprised us with a packed lunch. We ended the day at a local seafood restaurant over shrimps, squid, deer, fried noodles and steamed rice, talking shop about our trip through Asia and Simon's adventures in Africa.

The newly delivered "Polygon" mountain bikes still need a few adjustments to get them ready. After that, something cultural couldn't be missing. Today we ride on good asphalt to Agop Batu Tulug. "Agop" means cave, "batu" is the Malay word for rock, and "tulug" translates as sleep. It's an archaeological burial site in the Kinabatangan district. 500 to 900 years ago, the steep limestone rock was chosen as a burial place. Some of the 125 carved wooden coffins are still laid out in these caves today and can be visited freely.

Now wildlife is on the tour plan: the project "Species protection in south-eastern Sabah" was launched in 2006 by the BCT (Borneo Conservation Trust). Around the Kinabatangan and Segama rivers, a corridor has been created for wild animals such as orangutans, elephants and rhinos. This reserve covers an area of about 1.3 million hectares, which is 17% of Sabah. The conservation efforts focus on the Kinabatangan, Segama and Kalabakan areas, where we will spend the next few days.

The support vehicle is loaded with equipment, food, spare parts and personal things, so we can reach our night's lodging comfortably. By mountain bike we follow the dirt road through the vastness of the jungle to the Barefoot Lodge in Sukau. The welcome drink on the terrace by the river can't do anything about the oppressive heat and the 90% humidity. Two hours before dusk we board the boat (max. 15 people) for the afternoon safari – hopefully without rain showers.

The Kinabatangan River and its wetlands are one of the richest ecosystems in the world. On the water, we first want to look out for proboscis monkeys. Nothing is promised, but maybe we'll also come across elephants, crocodiles and other wild animals. The boat glides quietly into a side river. It smells of damp rainforest, and the banks are lined with mangroves and rampant thicket. We noticed a long cable stretched across the river between two tall trees. The answer to the question "why" and "what for" came straight away. Acrobatically dancing proboscis monkeys (see the film) moved back and forth on the ropes between the tree trunks. Because monkeys are afraid of water, rope bridges were built to link their territories. The big animals stayed hidden for now.

After dark we board the boat again for the night safari. Everything is pitch black, nothing can be made out. Only the gentle lapping of the water and little points of light in the distance give away the course of the river. The handheld spotlight searches the thicket for nocturnal wildlife. In the dark we make out birds on the branches, monkeys sleeping in the treetops, and now and then a pair of mysterious glowing dots. Sadly, the pachyderms stayed hidden behind the scenes. The ranger: "There was more going on last week."

Only 80 kilometres away is the Sepilok Orang Utan Rehabilitation Centre, set up in 1964. Here orphaned baby orangutans are rehabilitated and then released back into the wild. In the middle of the lush 4,300-hectare Kabili-Sepilok forest, we can watch the orangutans in their natural habitat. A wooden boardwalk led us to a platform where we could watch the feeding (10:00 and 15:00). The apes are given fruit, vegetables and milk. The animals enjoy the treats and say thank you with acrobatics on the long ropes.

Imbak Canyon Conservation Area
A unique journey to one of the most remote places in Malaysia awaits us. The Imbak Canyon reserve, a still relatively untouched wilderness on this earth, lies 300 kilometres south-east of Kota Kinabalu. The protected area covers a total of 30,000 hectares.

We say goodbye to the orangutans and drive 80 kilometres towards Telupid in the pleasantly air-conditioned support vehicle. The bikes and cool boxes are strapped down on the back of the four-wheel drive. A plastic sheet printed with "AWAS Cyclist ahead" signals "Caution, cyclists ahead". After another 70 kilometres to Imbak town, we leave the asphalt and switch to the dirt road that leads to the Tampoi base camp. The sun is at its highest, and the shade of the jungle forest doesn't reach beyond the edge of the road. It's hot and humid. The track is dusty and full of chunks of rock. The washed-out ruts and ridges, and the "ups and downs", tell us this won't be a weekend outing. After 40 kilometres we reached the gateway to exploring Imbak Canyon. At the Tampoi base camp, ranger Chris welcomes us with the words: you are the first cyclists to have strayed this far. We're happy to hear that, of course.

It's the thrill, that certain something, of moving through completely new surroundings. Cycling in the rainforest, on a road lined left and right by huge trees and impenetrable thicket. The near and far-off calls of birds, monkeys and other creatures show that we haven't gone entirely unnoticed. Drinks are handed to us from the support vehicle, so you get the feeling you haven't reached the end of civilisation.

Entering the "Canyon Conservation Area" requires a permit, which has to be obtained in advance. When it rains, the road can become an impassable mud track, and the simple bridges are in danger of collapsing. An off-road four-wheel-drive vehicle is essential. In the 25 km long gorge, the Imbak River flows through dense forests with 300-year-old trees reaching up to 60 metres high. A "green canyon" where you can also find 1,000-year-old giants. It is home to more than 80 species of mammals, such as the rare Sumatran rhino, the endangered Asian elephant, proboscis monkeys and orangutans, and a wide variety of amphibians and reptiles. In the rich flora of this protected area, more than 1,800 plant species have been identified so far.

At the Tampoi base camp we move into adequately furnished rooms with a private toilet. The light and the ceiling fan stop working at 22:00, because the generator is switched off. For smaller budgets, open-air bunk beds are also available. In the rented camp kitchen, Simon from Bike and Tours cooked a delicious dinner. He had brought the food he needed in the support vehicle.

Sweating, we trek through the rainforest for 2 hours. It's very hot, and the smell of damp, rotting ground goes with us! Along the jungle path we discover termite mounds a metre high and insect nests. White cotton socks pulled up to below the knee protect us from the jumbo tiger leeches. The 1-2 cm long "hungry" leeches look like worms and cling to leaves and branches. They can live off one blood meal for up to 5 years, so they have plenty of time to wait for fresh meat. Unbelievable! With perfect timing and aim, these creatures drop onto our clothes and bare skin.

Halfway! A rumbling sound gives away that we're close to the Imbak River and one of the most important waterfalls in Malaysia. After dry days, crystal-clear water rushes along the rock faces and through the riverbed. Last night's heavy rain has turned the river cloudy brown. But that didn't stop us from jumping into the cooling water, over 20 degrees (!) warm. At the Kangkawat suspension bridge, Simon can show off his cooking skills again. Chinese noodle stew from the petrol stove, with coffee and cake for dessert.

The trip from hell! The heavy rain during the night has softened the road and turned it into a mud track. One look at the road makes us suspect the drive back will be an adventure. Can the four-wheel drive cope with this? Does it have enough ground clearance and power to plough through the mud? We give the driver advice on how best to tackle the obstacles: slowly, fast, 2-wheel or 4-wheel drive, the choice mostly leads to the same fiasco. Slithering and sliding, we scrape past collapsed slopes. Driving over the undermined bridges becomes target practice. A bit of luck was needed to get back to solid asphalt without being forced to spend the night in the jungle. As a reward, we treat ourselves and Simon to a "Happy Meal" at McDonald's. After 11 hours, the 280 kilometres to Lahad Datu are behind us. By now the fine-grained sand has hardened like brick in every crack of the vehicle and is "baked on". Cleaning the car inside, outside and underneath took 3 hours of hard graft.

Palm oil plantation and factory
What the orangutans and proboscis monkeys were for Claudia, a visit to a "palm oil factory" is for Alexandre today. It took several phone calls to get access to an oil palm plantation and its processing. Companies guard the production process like a secret. Through our contact with the Borneo Paradise Eco-Farm Resort in Kunak, we were given a guided tour of a plantation and factory.

By jeep to the plantations
At the site manager's we are given shoes, helmets and safety instructions. This was followed by a detailed explanation of palm oil. The oil palm, up to 30 metres tall, produces bunches weighing 15 to 50 kilograms. 3 years after planting it begins to bear fruit, and at 28 years old it is felled because the yield is too low. A palm carries 3,000 to 6,000 fruits, which are black when unripe and later orange-red when ready for harvest. A long pole with a razor-sharp sickle on the end cuts the fruit bunches from the trunk. A worker showed us how to handle the blade. Alexandre couldn't manage to cut a fruit bunch off the palm. The foreman laughed: "It takes practice and know-how to harvest 200 bunches a day."

The factory
The fruit spoils quickly and has to be processed immediately after harvesting. The fruit bunches, pre-treated with steam, are pressed in the oil mill and the kernels separated, the hard shell cracked and the seeds dried. The orange, carotene-rich flesh of the fruit gives palm oil, and the seed gives palm kernel oil. To Alexandre's pointed questions, the engineer is reserved with his explanations. The processing remains a secret. Every photo first needed the approval of the guide before it could be taken. Still, the few pictures give an impression of the processing, up to the loading of the lorry. We will remember the taste in the air and the layers of sticky oil film on the chequer plates and handrails.

Palm oil, one of the most important raw materials in the world
Malaysia's main exports are electronic products at 33%, palm oil at 8%, followed by petroleum refining at 7%. With their annual production (2012), Malaysia (18 million tonnes) and Indonesia (25 million t) dominate the palm oil market. Most of the world's production is used for food, 71% (margarine, cooking fat), and 21% to make cleaning products and cosmetics. A comparatively small share, 5%, of palm oil is used for energy and to make biofuels (biodiesel), and as fuel in combined heat and power plants. The oil palm is now the most important supplier of vegetable oil.

International criticism
The creation of new oil palm plantations and the way they are farmed face international criticism. Large areas of rainforest are cleared to create more plantations. Oil palms grow especially well in tropical regions, which is exactly where rainforests are. Palm oil cultivation is now the main cause of deforestation in Malaysia and Indonesia, and slash-and-burn clearance releases immense amounts of CO2. The heavy use of pesticides and artificial fertiliser poisons the groundwater, the rivers and, indirectly, the local population. On top of that, drinking and service water resources are badly affected by the enormous water consumption of the plantations. The vast oil palm monocultures threaten the habitat of the orangutans and the biodiversity of the rainforests.

The bike tours and treks described can be booked with bikeandtours . Simon and Tisha are happy to give information about what they offer. An individual day tour, or a trek of several days to suit your wishes, is possible.
