/berichte/costa-rica.title: Costa Rica
/berichte/costa-rica.html:
Costa Rica
7 - 27 November 2008

Costa Rica - the Switzerland of Central America

Costa Rica, with its prosperity, efficiency and cleanliness, is something special in Central America. Tropical rainforests, exciting beaches, active volcanoes, jungle rivers and many national parks make Costa Rica a cycling adventure full of variety.

Almost 30% of the country is protected, and ecotourism is a big deal. Especially worth mentioning: Costa Rica has no army, it is neutral, and the money this frees up is used for environmental and social purposes. A true paradise, the third-smallest country in Central America, covering 51,000 square kilometres between the Atlantic and the Pacific, which are only 3 hours apart by car.

The average temperature is 32 degrees on the coasts and 17 degrees inland. The rainy season lasts from May to November; the rest of the year there is hardly any rain. Every cycling enthusiast soon understands why Costa Rica is called the "Switzerland of Central America". Costa Rica, with the colón as its currency, is unfortunately, along with Panama, the most expensive country in Central America.

Our experiences from 7 to 27 November were varied, many-sided, exciting and full of surprises, and should give you a picture of how we got on over a total of 752 kilometres (a daily average of about 52 kilometres).

Getting through the various border offices without a "tourist guide" would have taken us several hours. Leaving Nicaragua is bureaucratic and expensive (20 dollars). Costa Rica charges no entry fees. The border crossing at "Peñas Blancas", with 5 cm of fine dust and lots of lorries, is a disaster. The striking jump in civilisation compared to the countries we had already cycled through really struck us.

From the border to La Cruz (20 kilometres) there are more "ups" than "downs". The road leads through dense wild growth of trees, palms and other exotic plants. Falling branches alert us to monkeys living in the wild. In La Cruz we get the last free hotel room, "all inclusive": no window, a fan with a cut power cable, missing slats in the bed frame and a few cockroaches. A power cut from 23:00 made the musty air even hotter. Now our Therm-a-Rest mats come in handy again, and we swap the beds for the sun loungers by the pool and spend the night "open-air".

After 65 km of asphalt with nowhere to buy food, we reach Liberia. From Liberia to Brasilito (72 km), only just under 20 km are paved. We take a wrong turn and lose a whole hour. After 5 hours of riding with 20% climbs and descents on the "Monkey Trail", we reach the little village of Brasilito after dark. Playa Brasilito and Playa Conchal, 500 m away, are among the most beautiful beaches in Costa Rica.

We move from Brasilito to Tamarindo, just 20 km away. Here too, only 5 km are paved. Tamarindo, spoilt by tourism, is very expensive, with lots of surf shops, souvenir shops and a beach that is nothing special. You can skip this place with a clear conscience. The exception: the "Parque Nacional Marino Las Baulas", where we take a boat through a maze of shallow waterways and see lots of birds, crocodiles, monkeys and mangroves.

Tamarindo – Manzanillo: 42 km! Very exhausting: one stream crossing, 5 hours of riding, an average of 10 km/h, very dusty, big climbs. We spend the night at the "La Joya" resort (near the village of Lagarto); we could not have gone any further. We light a campfire on the beach and cook our own dinner. In our bungalow (we are the only hotel guests) we feel like Robinson Crusoe.

Manzanillo – Sámara: 60 km! Extremely exhausting: 3 river crossings, the last one 20 metres wide and 80 cm deep. 3 suspension bridges, and the roads are unpaved and full of potholes. Our average speed is "just" 8 km/h.

On the whole stretch from Liberia to Sámara, you have to reckon with an average speed of 10 km/h, not counting river crossings. Splitting the route into three daily stages is the minimum; there are places to stay about every 10 kilometres. A river crossing takes about 30 minutes (carrying 2 bikes and every bag through the water one by one). Some stretches mean pushing uphill and downhill (dusty, dry and slippery).

It's worth checking carefully and thinking about whether you want to ride these 150 km of unpaved road from Sardinal to Sámara, or take the alternative of 110 km on asphalt via Santa Cruz and Nicoya to Sámara.

We like Sámara better than Tamarindo, but it is very touristy.

Sámara – Corozalito: We had actually wanted to reach "Playa Coyote", 60 km away, in one day. But how wrong we were! The first river crossing, 10 km after Sámara, took 1 hour. A river about 20 metres wide and 80 cm deep really "eats up time". On top of that came 3 hills under the motto "steep, steeper, steepest". More than 1,000 metres of climbing! Most of the time it took both of us to push each loaded bike. The descents turned into a braking exercise, with some "pushing downhill" (riding on the gravel was no longer possible). And so, after 33 kilometres and 6 hours of sweaty work, we reached the little village of "Corozalito", where we got a cabina with meals (dinner and breakfast). There was no restaurant or supermarket to be found here.

Corozalito – Puntarenas: At 08:00 in the morning we were already on our way to conquer the last 2 hills and gravel roads with gradients of up to 20%. Not quite as high as the day before, but we had planned 60 km to "Jicaral". Nothing but gravel tracks, our hands always on the brake levers, our forearms aching. We are lucky: a coconut farmer gives us a lift for 12 kilometres, so we reach the ferry to Puntarenas just in time (17:30). The crossing over the Gulf of Nicoya takes a little more than 1 hour. In a hotel just 200 metres from the port (more of a dive than a hotel) we get an apartment with a kitchen. Everything's fine, so we don't have to worry about dinner as well.

Puntarenas - Jacó: 78 km in a hot, sticky climate, with several climbs (the last steep ramp just before the finish). Jacó, a tourist town, offers everything your heart desires. We treat ourselves to a room in a Best Western hotel. The beach and bay are nothing special. Here we decide to leave our bikes at the hotel and take the public bus to Puerto Limón. The 2 x 3-hour journey, changing buses in San José (by taxi to the bus station for the Caribbean side), is hectic and chaotic. In San José there are strong winds, and the weather gets worse by the minute. In Puerto Limón we can't find a hotel, so we spend the night outside the city at the Hotel Maribu Resort. A few days earlier, a small oil tanker had run aground on the coast at Puerto Limón in a storm. It rains like a hurricane all day. We drop our visit to Tortuguero National Park, because a tour (only possible with a guide) cannot go ahead and there is no sign of the weather improving. We decide to go back to Jacó the next day without having achieved anything, collect our bikes from the hotel and carry on with our journey.

Jacó – Quepos: We ride through kilometres of oil palm plantations, where the harvest is in full swing. The rainy season isn't over yet. Again and again we have to look for a dry place to shelter.

Quepos: We want to visit Manuel Antonio National Park, 7 kilometres away and advertised as a "don't miss". Entry costs 10 dollars per person. A guided tour with a "Swarovski telescope" magnifying up to 60 times, so you can see the small animals and insects, is recommended. The extra cost depends on the number of guests and is quite expensive. We go without a guide and search the treetops and bushes ourselves with our Leitz binoculars. To still our hunger, we crack open one of the many coconuts lying around. Not bad, if you know how to get at the vitamin-rich white inside.

Quepos – Uvita: Our journey continues on a 50 km bone-shaking track to Dominical. We are 1 year too early: the whole stretch is being turned into a highway more than 20 metres wide. The surface consists of countless potholes, round stones the size of a fist, and gravel. Our average speed is just 10 km/h. On this stretch without any climbs, we get 5 hours of non-stop blows to our wrists in 41 degrees of heat, and finally rain, which quickly turns the dusty road into a mud track. On the next 20 kilometres to Uvita we recover on the asphalt we have been longing for.

In Uvita we spend the night in a cabina (2 kilometres off-road from the main road) at Playa Ballenas. The next morning, before high tide, we walk out to a reef that is flooded at every spring tide, and enjoy the impressive sight of the waves meeting. The link from the reef to the beach floods more and more. Within a few minutes the water rises so much that you can already feel the current pulling back. By 11 o'clock it is no longer possible to reach the reef safely. The photos give an impression of this unique spectacle in Marino Ballena National Park, which costs 6 dollars per person during the day. At night, entry is free. Because of the crocodiles in the river just 30 metres away, which don't sleep, great care is needed. At 12:00 we set off in drizzle for Palmar Norte, 45 km away. The drizzle turns into unusually heavy rain for this time of year. We spend the unplanned stop in a "welcome" shopping centre and wait, wait, wait. As the rain doesn't let up, we have to struggle into our uncomfortably tight and already damp rain gear anyway, to reach our night's lodging before dark.

Palmar Norte - Ciudad Neily: A relatively flat 79 km. Cloudbursts keep surprising us and force us into unplanned stops. We are never sure whether it's "just" a short "disturbance" or whether it's about to pour down in buckets. You can guess the right decision (rain gear or not, or head for the next shelter and wait) from the speed of the windscreen wipers on the oncoming cars. Ciudad Neily, 20 kilometres from the border with Panama, offers plenty of places to stay and is a pleasant little town.

Ciudad Neily - Paso Canoas: The route is unspectacular, with a slow-rolling surface and lots of potholes, some of them repaired unprofessionally.

Our recommendation for cycling globetrotters:

When visiting Manuel Antonio National Park: leave the bikes at your accommodation (in Quepos) and take the public bus to the national park; the fare is 210 colones per person each way. The road (7 kilometres) winds over the hill like a corkscrew, and by bike it takes at least an hour each way, which isn't worth it.

After 752 kilometres we leave Costa Rica with these memories:

An un-planned night by the swimming pool

The Nicoya Peninsula: the toughest stretches so far; steep, unpaved dirt roads

Dreamlike, lonely Pacific beaches at Brasilito and Playa Conchal

Campfire romance as the only hotel guests at Playa Manzanillo

Hot, sticky, humid, dusty

River crossings: carrying the bikes and gear through the water

A coconut farmer carrying the bikes, the gear and the Zentralbiker on his "load"

National parks:
Marino Las Baulas with crocodiles and water birds. Manuel Antonio with monkeys, insects and beautiful beaches. Marino Ballena with its reef and the "play of the waves" at low and high tide

The most wild animals we have seen so far.

Chaotic San José: 340,000 people, and bus terminals 3 kilometres apart

/berichte/ecuador.title: Ecuador
/berichte/ecuador.html:
Ecuador
3 - 24 March 2009

Quito to Alausí
After 26 hours of travelling, Zurich – London – Miami – Quito, we reach the capital of Ecuador in the province of Pichincha. After a spectacular approach to an extremely short runway, with a view into the local residents' bedrooms, we land at "Mariscal Sucre". The customs and immigration formalities are straightforward and quick. The driver from the Hotel Sandmelis is already waiting for us, and we are driven to our accommodation just 10 minutes away.

A proper acclimatisation period of 3 days is a good idea. The 6-hour time difference, though, will bother us for longer.

We spend the first day putting our bikes back together and taking a taxi trip to the "Mariscal" district. A taxi ride costs about 2-3 USD, and the distance within the city makes no difference. For safety reasons, it is recommended to take a taxi rather than walk or take a public bus.

On the second day we decide to take a guided tour of the city centre by taxi. We visit the "Virgin of Quito", the city's patron saint, on the "Panecillo", the "Museo de la Ciudad", wander through the historic quarter and see the Plaza San Francisco, the Basilica and the Independence monument on the Plaza de la Independencia.

Quito's old town, with its colonial look, has been declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO; the city has 13 million inhabitants and lies at 2,850 metres.

Day three: the hotel's taxi driver takes us to the nearby "Pululahua" volcanic crater. The farmed hollow is enclosed by a crater rim about 5 kilometres across (our estimate). Because of "racing hearts", we decide not to join a 45-minute hike from the car park down into the hollow. We prefer to linger at the equator monument "Mitad del Mundo" and take the obligatory photos. The monument is not on the equator line! The museum with its exhibition of Indigenous culture, not far away (about 1,000 m), is on the real equator, which was calculated by GPS. There is also a hands-on, educational tour about the Coriolis force and gravity, the position of the sun in the 4 seasons, and magnetism.

Day four: with a queasy feeling, we leave the Hotel Sandmelis heading south. Thanks to the good directions, including a sketch, from the hotel owner, we reach the expressway and conquer our first 1,000 metres of climbing on the way to Machachi.

At the Hostería Chiguac, a starting point for climbers heading to the surrounding volcanoes, we find welcoming accommodation. Now comes the first hurdle. The way to Lasso, on the "Avenue of the Volcanoes", leads over a pass at 3,500 metres in Cotopaxi National Park. Following in the footsteps of Alexander von Humboldt, we spend the night at the "Hacienda La Ciénega". Built in 1580, the hacienda is one of the oldest in South America. The rooms of today's country estate are furnished with 19th-century furniture.

Via Latacunga, which lies at an altitude of 2,850 metres (like Quito) and has an average temperature of 12 degrees, the Pan-American Highway takes us to Ambato. The Hotel Ambato seems to us the best place to spend the night and the starting point for a stroll around town. The Monday market on the Río Ambato is uniquely set between the volcanoes Chimborazo (6,310 m), Carihuairazo (5,020 m) and Tungurahua (5,016 m). At the widely praised pizzeria "La Fornace", run by an Ecuadorian who learned his trade from Sicilians, we eat superbly. Well rested and after breakfast, we set off for Riobamba. Within 3½ hours and 34 kilometres, we are once again at the top of a pass at 3,600 metres. Literally: 30 kilometres up, followed by 30 kilometres down, and we reach the Hostería "El Troje" in Riobamba, where we spend the night.

We break off the day's stage to Guamote after 35 kilometres in Cajabamba, because of 35 degrees of heat and exhausting ups and downs. A small lorry then takes us through the winding, foggy mountains (visibility less than 30 metres) to Alausí.

Our decision to take the "pickup ride" works out perfectly, so nothing stands in the way of a train ride to the Devil's Nose, "Nariz del Diablo", on Thursday. The breathtaking railway ride from Alausí (2,347 m) down into the valley (1,800 m), dropping 500 metres, is the steepest railway descent in the world. Today the line is used only for tourists, and the steam locomotives have been replaced by Mercedes-Benz lorry chassis with bus bodies.

An uninvited roommate, who ate the biscuits off our bedside table in the night, disturbs our well-earned sleep at midnight. We soon found the mouse hole in the skirting board and blocked it with soap and toilet paper, so we could sleep peacefully for the remaining hours until dawn. Only changing hotels guaranteed us undisturbed nights for the rest of our stay in Alausí.

Alausí to Cuenca
Alausí, just a tourist starting point for the "Nariz del Diablo" and a car park for coaches, has nothing else to offer. The town does not have many hotels or restaurants. Still, you can always find an acceptable place to stay and something to eat somewhere. Especially at the restaurant at the station, where we had a very good, reasonably priced lunch together with a tour group. The way to Chunchi is peppered with three passes (the highest at 2,700 m). In total there are 750 metres of climbing over 39 kilometres. The effort is rewarded with sensational views of the surrounding mountains (all over 4,000 m) and varied vegetation.
The stretch Alausí – Chunchi should have been completely paved by the end of 2008, but 2 kilometres are still missing. We assume the gap of bumpy track will be finished by the end of 2009.

Addendum:
From Quito to Ambato there is heavy traffic, especially lorries with their smoking exhausts. From Ambato heading south, the traffic drops noticeably. The heavy traffic is reduced to rolling fuel tankers supplying the petrol stations. The cars mostly belong to people from the communities along the Pan-American Highway. The roads are very well built, paved and have a hard shoulder.

Chunchi, smaller than Alausí, immediately seems much better kept and friendlier to us. At the Hotel Chunchi we find comfortable, clean accommodation for 20 USD, including breakfast. Gradually the landscape and the climate of the Sierra change. The "Avenue of the Volcanoes" ends, and the fertile valley of Cañar begins. The extreme mountains and valleys become more and more even. The Pan-American Highway now runs into the geologically calmer part of Ecuador's Sierra.

It's supposed to get drier and warmer? Not for us today! On the extremely exhausting way from Chunchi to Zhud (45 kilometres, 960 metres of climbing), from 2,800 m we are surprised by fog and drizzle. Our photo "above the clouds" didn't last long; the fog line rose steadily with us to 3,000 metres.

There was nowhere to stay in Zhud. It was cold and wet, and everything was grey on grey. In situations like this we are usually lucky! A pickup driver advises us to load the bikes onto his truck and come along with him to Cañar. Besides, he says, the road on the next stretch is partly unpaved and full of potholes. We don't miss the chance to reach Cañar, just 27 kilometres away, the "easy" way.

We cover the remaining 70 kilometres of downhill to Cuenca easily the next day. At the Hotel El Dorado we spend 3 nights recovering and strolling through the "Ciudad Histórica". The next daily stages, a total of 8,000 metres of climbing over 400 kilometres to Macará, through partly remote mountains with nowhere to stay, now have to be carefully planned.

Cuenca lies at 2,530 m in a high mountain basin and, with 300,000 inhabitants, is Ecuador's third-largest city. Cuenca, also called the "Athens of Ecuador", is shaped by republican-era houses, small shops and cobbled streets from colonial times. To learn more about the cultural and historical background of this interesting city (the Inca of the 15th century and the Spanish occupation in 1557), it's worth taking a look at www.ecuadorexplorer.com/html/cuenca.html

Cuenca to Macará
We liked Cuenca extraordinarily well. Nice, obliging and helpful people. The city has a high standard of living, is well kept and clean, and is really worth a visit.
We have to move on! Ahead of us lie about 4,000 more metres of climbing and over 300 kilometres. From Cuenca there is first a pass of 3,500 metres to conquer, the Altiplano de Tinajillas. There is nowhere to stay, so we look for an outdoor "campsite" out of sight of the road. It's going to be cold; a starry sky gives it away. Our newly bought sleeping bags are great and live up to their promise. In the morning, with everything packed up again, one of the longest descents begins! For 40 kilometres we "wipe out" 1,600 metres of altitude, with a few short climbs in between. Because of the terrain, there is "almost" a rule of thumb: 10 kilometres of climbing followed by 20 kilometres of descent. Nothing comes for free. Just when you think "that's it up there", you are surprised by another 400 metres of climbing to Oña. At the Hotel Buenos Aires (photo with the crystal chandelier on the veranda), the only "hotel" in the village, we find a bed, a room door with a padlock, light, a cold-water shower and somewhere to cook. Otherwise there is no reason to stay here any longer. Still a bit worn out from the previous day's efforts, it's straight back to work. Out of the hotel door, and immediately there is a climb to 3,100 metres.

In Saraguro we meet Peter from Aargau, who is travelling on his off-road BMW. Months ago he had shipped himself and his motorbike to Buenos Aires on a freighter (a 5-week crossing for 4,000 CHF). He tells us about the hardships he too had to cope with on his motorbike. Patagonia in particular had taken its toll on him. Now he is on his way through Central America and Mexico to Canada. From somewhere he will fly back to Switzerland. The village of Saraguro lies 140 kilometres south of Cuenca and is home to the Saraguro people. The Saraguros originally came from Lake Titicaca and were brought here from there to work the land.

Most Saraguros wear their traditional dress even on working days. Men and women wear a black poncho; the women in particular also wear a white straw hat and a black skirt. The men wear a black hat, with their long plaited braid showing beneath it, and knee-length black or dark trousers. Between Saraguro and Loja we are surprised by rain for the first time, and so get the "pleasure" of testing whether our rain gear is really waterproof. The rain has hardly stopped before the sun is beating mercilessly down on the asphalt again, and the annoying "sandflies" start to keep us busy. Disgusting creatures! You only notice their bite when it's already too late, and at night you soon scratch yourself bloody because of the unbearable itching. Every village, however small, even one above 3,000 metres, has its own village square with a statue on a pedestal in the middle, and of course a church. Without a square, a statue and a church, a group of houses cannot call itself a "village". Loja is one of the oldest cities in Ecuador; it lies at an altitude of 2,100 metres and has 130,000 inhabitants. Even Alexander von Humboldt was impressed by the wealth of plants in this area and called Loja the "Garden of Ecuador". It is worth mentioning that Loja won an international prize for urban ecology. Here too, the townscape is dominated by colonial-style houses, cathedrals and statues. By the way, we ate exceptionally well in Loja and spent the night at the 4-star hotel "Libertador".

Because of the extremely bad weather forecast, with constant heavy rain for the next 3 days, we decide to take a transfer to Macará. At 13:00 our bikes are loaded into the rear luggage hold of an international coach. At 13:30, in sunshine, our adventurous 5½-hour journey to Macará begins; we are supposed to arrive at 19:00. The fare for this 175-kilometre stretch is 6 USD per person, and the bicycles travel free. At first everything went as you would imagine. Gradually, the higher we "climb" towards the mountain pass at 2,800 metres, the foggier it gets; the rain starts and becomes heavier and heavier. Visibility is only a few metres, the coach drives slower and slower, and you can see how carefully the driver is steering. A sudden stop! Several people are standing in the road, waving and pointing at the road buried under rubble. Nothing is moving! All the passengers have to get out. A second coach has been sent to wait beyond the landslide. It is pouring with rain, and the 20-metre-wide landslide is still moving. Chunks of rock keep rolling onto the road. Two men are posted as lookouts, and by shouting they tell the passengers one by one when to cross the rubble. While we take our bikes out of the luggage hold and load them up, it is raining "cats and dogs". In our cycling clothes (by now the thermometer has dropped by 20 degrees) we push and carry our belongings to the waiting bus on the other side. With everything loaded again and wrapped in woollen blankets, we continue the coach journey. After another 10 kilometres, in Sozoranga, once again nothing is moving: the road to Macará is buried by big boulders and mud. We are trapped! There is no going back to Loja, no going forward to Macará, and apart from a bar there are no hotels in Sozoranga! We soon realised that a night on the coach was on the cards. We leave it to your imagination how you can squeeze yourself "comfortably" into a seat until dawn. "Where there's a bike, there's a way"! With this motto we head downhill the next morning towards the buried road. Wow, not bad! What a landslide! For over 80 metres there is no way through. Boulders up to 4 metres across block the way. The slope has been washed out, and more stones keep rolling onto the road. We have to get through here! A local watches the movements, and we carry the bags and the bikes piece by piece to the other side. Made it! On we go downhill. We'll soon reach Macará. Only 10 kilometres to go. This stretch became the most exhausting of all Ecuador for us. There followed a second landslide just as big, and 2 mud tracks where we had to trudge ankle-deep through a sticky brew. In no time the temperature rose from 15 to 38 degrees. There was no sign of "todo plano" (all flat); instead there were several climbs that really wore us out in this heat. Completely exhausted, after 6 hours for just 25 kilometres of descent and 10 kilometres "straight on", we reach the border town of Macará.

Macará lies at 450 metres; the mercury often reaches the 40-degree mark here, which makes it the hottest town in Ecuador. After a well-earned rest day spent writing our travel report, we will cross the border into Peru on 25 March 2009. While we are writing this text, we are served broccoli soup with popcorn in it. Really tasty! It makes a change from "pollo con arroz" (chicken with rice).

After 700 kilometres we leave Ecuador with these memories:

Clean, well kept, and extremely good roads, some with concrete surfaces.

A good quality of life. "Supposedly nobody has ever starved in Ecuador."

The Ecuadorians of the "Sierra" are cheerful, friendly and helpful.

The Sierra route is extremely exhausting, but worth it (the views).

Thin air, passes of 3,650 metres: acclimatisation is a "must".

The capital, Quito, with 13 million inhabitants. Very few tall buildings. Wide, sprawling residential areas, with the airport in the middle of the city.

Handicrafts, wool spinning, knitting, and the hats of the Saraguro people.

Good accommodation, hotels and restaurants in the towns geared to tourism.

We were pleasantly surprised and recommend a trip through Ecuador to everyone.



Biker info for the mountain route (Sierra route)

- Active (13 days of riding) 700 kilometres
- Transfer (bus, car) 260 kilometres
- Total climbing 10,300 m
- Average speed 11.6 km/h
- Riding time in motion 60 hours

/berichte/florida.title: Florida
/berichte/florida.html:
Florida
11 December 2008 - 13 January 2009

So much experienced – seen – pedalled – sweated – carried – pushed

Because we flew over Mexico, we reached Panama 2 months too early. The rainy season in Ecuador and Peru does not end until March. During this period the roads are often impassable, and there is no going forwards or backwards. That is why we decide to spend the holidays in Florida and fly from Panama to Miami. With the bikes packed in boxes again and our gear in a kitbag, a shuttle bus takes us to our hotel in Miami Beach.

The number 1 hobbies: mowing huge lawns, or putting out as many fishing rods as you have bait. What the strimmer is to the Panamanian, the fishing rod is to the American. Those are our first impressions of the change of country from Panama to Florida.

Motorhomes the size of a coach or an articulated lorry, made up of a towing vehicle and a trailer the size of a holiday apartment, are steered through the streets. It is not unusual for a private car to be hitched to these vehicles on a tow bar, with a four-seater all-terrain vehicle loaded piggyback on top. Boats with outboard motors of up to 400 horsepower are also towed behind the motorhomes. The campsites are perfectly equipped for vehicles like these: water and sewage connections, electricity and TV hook-ups, and a level concrete pad. All of this is surrounded by lots of lawn, so there is still enough room for the veranda, the BBQ, the boat trailer, the Harley-Davidson and the Christmas lights.

Endless roads, all dead straight, no hills, and only the main roads, at 90° angles, are marked on the tourist maps (the road atlas is more detailed). It's hard to judge distances from the maps. There are usually several more side streets in between, so we had to work our way from 184th to 344th Street to find the road to the Keys. Again and again, about every 500 metres, an annoying traffic light makes us stop, press the button and wait for green before we can carry on. That means: brake, get back on and accelerate from zero to 20 km/h with all our luggage, over and over again, at more than 40 junctions in total.

Bike paths are rare, and are mostly found only on residential streets, or next to bus lanes, where they are pointless. Supposedly there are plans to run these "bicycle paths" through the city centres too. Basically, as a cyclist in Florida you are only tolerated. You are more likely to get a pitying look, or be told through an open car window to leave the multi-lane road and ride on the pavement. The number of cyclists you meet reflects that.

During our stay in Miami we only saw 20 bicycles.

The car rules life! Public transport is poor and badly connected, or not attractive enough for American distances (roads up to 3 lanes wide through the city). A bus ride with 2 changes, an elevated railway, a train and a shuttle bus to the airport took more than 3 hours. By car you can do the trip in ¾ of an hour. Correspondingly far away, "not far, only a few blocks", is our next campground, 2 hours from Miami city.

Florida, also called the state with 365 days of sunshine and a thousand bridges, made us curious too. We want to visit the Keys, Fort Lauderdale, Miami Beach and the Everglades. Many bridges in and around downtown Miami let boats pass through the many navigable canals. When a ship passes through, the sections of the multi-lane road are raised, and the traffic is stopped for 15 minutes.

"Number 1" (the first road) runs along the east coast from the north, right through Miami to Key West, the southernmost point of the USA. The word "Key" comes from the Spanish word "cayo". The original name for Key West was Cayo Hueso, which means "little bone island". Key West, once the longest town in Florida, is strategically placed in the Straits of Florida and has the highest income per head in the USA. The warm Gulf Stream brings an abundance of fish, sponges and lobsters.

Key West was once the country's biggest cigar producer and supplier of natural sponges, and it has always attracted famous visitors such as John James Audubon, Ernest Hemingway, Harry Truman, Tennessee Williams, Robert Frost, and also us "Zentralbikers".

We set off for the "Keys", made up of 5 sections stretching over a total of 105 miles.

Key Largo known for its offshore reefs in John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park and the Key Largo "National Marine Sanctuary"
Islamorada the "Purple Isles" and a magnet for deep-sea sport fishing
Marathon the heart of the Keys, because it lies at the centre of the chain of coral islands
Lower Keys the longest and most recently developed part of the island chain. Deer and wildlife have their home here. People looking for peace and quiet, and the elderly, come here to retreat.
Key West the little island town that has something to offer around the clock. In an hour you drive from Miami through the "Gateway to the Keys" with the Everglades, top of the list of attractions. The following 105 miles (175 kilometres) to Key West are said to take 2½ hours by car. On the Kogas we needed a little more than 8 hours for this stretch.

Henry Flagler, an engineer, made it possible to build a railway. On 22 January 1912 this "miracle of technology" reached Key West over several viaducts, which changed the island town dramatically.

There are only a handful of campsites on the Keys. They are usually booked up to 12 months in advance. Surprisingly, a tent pitch costs the same per night as a motorhome pitch, whatever its size. The flat rate for a caravan pitch includes water, electricity and sewage connections. Tent pitches are often not allowed at RV campgrounds because there are no toilets or washing facilities. These necessities can be found in every motorhome! That is why we spend 2 nights in Key West at the Radisson hotel, only a little more expensive than a 10 m² campsite pitch.

For the 175 kilometres back to Key Largo, by which time we had eaten our last power gels and bars, we only needed 8 hours. We want to spend the holidays at the "Larry and Penny Thompson" campground, not far from the "Metro Zoo". Our disappointment is great: the cosy Christmas BBQ in front of the tent is not to be. Within a period of 30 days we had already been guests for 7 days, so after 2 days we are asked to take down our tent and leave. With this rule, the ranger wants to prevent "homeless people" or "strangers" from settling on campsites.

Baffled and annoyed, we set off to find somewhere else to grill our "Christmas turkey". "Only" 90 kilometres away, near Fort Lauderdale, we find the nearest tent pitch, for 40 USD. After a sleepless night, disturbed by the constant roar of the nearby freeway and the horn of the AMTRAK freight train, we prefer to move into a 70 USD motel.

We are constantly accompanied by fast-food chains like McDonald's, KFC, Subway, Taco Bell, Burger King, Pizza Hut and co. Every petrol station has a "Food Mart" sign too, and on TV there is a 24-hour "food channel". Everything revolves around food, beauty, cars and plastic money. To pay for a 3 USD train ticket, we were first sent to a restaurant to change a 20-dollar note.

During our stay in Miami until our flight back, we visited, explored and experienced Fort Lauderdale, Port Everglades, Dania Beach, the Hollywood Broadwalk, the A1A highway, Key Biscayne, Coral Gables, Metro Zoo, the Port of Miami and downtown Miami by bike.

After 1,200 kilometres we leave Miami with these memories:

We especially liked the beaches along the "A1A" and "Crandon Park" with its beach on "Key Biscayne". We found the many "drawbridges" and the size of the multi-lane roads built over the straits and waterways interesting and impressive. We were also amazed by the traffic flowing without jams despite the enormous number of private cars (and very few lorries). Driving through the Keys and the Everglades in a rental car is surely the greatest attraction.

After California, Miami was the most expensive part of the journey. But you have to remember that, because there are so few campsites, hotel nights make up the biggest share of the costs.

Thanks to wrong information and a lack of signs, we will remember our wrong turn onto the 5-lane expressway in Miami for a long time!

Distances:

Lauderdale by the Sea South Beach 50 kilometres
South Beach Key Biscayne 35 kilometres
Miami International Airport Miami Beach 20 kilometres
Downtown Miami Key West 288 kilometres

Note:

A tent pitch per night, for a limited number of people, without water or electricity, usually costs 40 USD. The length of stay may be limited.

A motorhome of any size, on a pitch with water, electricity and sewage connections, costs 40 – 50 USD. Mostly there is no limit on the length of stay.

The journey continues on 3 March 2009 in Quito, Ecuador

/berichte/guatemala.title: Guatemala
/berichte/guatemala.html:
Guatemala
3 - 24 October 2008

After a bumpy landing in Guatemala City, we were delighted to collect all our luggage in perfect condition. Passport control and customs took just 35 minutes. A bus transfer to a nearby mid-range hotel (50 US dollars) suited us very well, and our fears of spending the night at the airport were quickly forgotten.

At breakfast, behind a safe pane of glass, we realised what was waiting for us on the ride to Antigua. Monday at 09:00, the best time to leave the city after the rush hour, seemed right to us. The 45 kilometres to Antigua were all smog, exhaust fumes, sooty, smoking buses, noise and "Wild West" traffic. There are (almost) no rules about right of way: the "faster" one goes first, and there is very little room left for bicycles. After five hours and a few "ups and downs", we reach Antigua at 1,500 metres above sea level.

Antigua, known for its more than 80 language schools and for tourism, shows us a completely different side of Guatemala. The contrast between the tin shacks by the roadside and the restored buildings could not be greater. Antigua, once the capital, was destroyed by an earthquake and has now been rebuilt. The streets of the whole town are paved with natural cobblestones, so we had to push our bikes to the hotel.

There are no places to camp, but simple accommodation can be found from 25 US dollars. At first we only wanted to spend two days in Antigua. But our Spanish left a lot to be desired, so we did not want to miss the chance of an intensive course. A private teacher, 1 exercise book and 1 ballpoint pen, a wooden chair, bring your own toilet paper: our first day of lessons had begun. Cost: 510 US dollars for 2 people, including board and lodging with a local host family. Other countries, other customs: after the first night we had already moved back into a hotel.

With 5 hours of intensive lessons from 08:00 to 13:00, we still had enough time for trips to "Lake Atitlán" and the active volcano "Pacaya". Tourists are taken to the distant starting points by shuttle bus (max. 13 people). On the pot-holed roads, a trip takes up to 3 hours (one way). If the shock absorbers, brakes, gears and lights all work properly, you have picked the right tour agency.

Shaped by tourism, Antigua has a special place in Guatemala. The poverty and low incomes of the people are not obvious at first sight. One night with a middle-class host family showed us the gap between "having nothing" and "the bare necessities" you need to live.

With our Spanish improved, we are ready to head for the border with Honduras, 400 kilometres away. From Antigua (1,500 metres above sea level), one good push on the pedals and it's 45 kilometres downhill, and we are at 560 metres above sea level.

We are escorted by the police through the noisy, smog-filled town of Escuintla. Our helpful escorts say a friendly goodbye and give us directions so we can safely reach the plain of "Santa Rosa". More than 30 degrees of heat and extremely high humidity weigh heavily on us. Dripping with sweat, pedalling becomes hard and exhausting. The long, heavy rain showers before Chiquimulilla bring the refreshment we have been longing for. And so, soaked to the skin, after more than 100 kilometres, we reach the place where we will spend the night.

From Antigua onwards, the hotels get worse and worse and less and less clean. The rooms are damp, mouldy, dark and cramped, and shared with uninvited vermin. Our sleeping bags are a great help again, even if only as "fitted sheets" in the hot, sticky rooms. The nights are filled with barking dogs, crowing roosters, vehicles without silencers, mosquitoes and TVs turned up far too loud. Under these conditions we found ourselves wishing we were back at a campground next to the squeaking "Pacific Coast train".

To get to Honduras as quickly as possible, we divide the remaining 250 kilometres into 5 daily stages. A mistake we will pay dearly for straight away. On the "easy" stretch of "only" 37 kilometres from Chiquimulilla to Cuilapa, we have to give up, completely exhausted, after 11 kilometres. We get up the endless climbs of up to 15 percent over 5 kilometres by pushing. After 4 hours, the 3 litres of water that are normally enough for us are already gone. The remaining 6 kilometres to the top of the pass at 1,400 metres above sea level, and the rest of the way to Jutiapa, we conquer on the loading ramp of a tow truck.

We will certainly remember how exhausted we were on this unusual day. Our decision not to give up is rewarded with a varied ride without any draining ups and downs. The vegetation looks greener and more lush, and the cows, pigs and chickens wander right up to the edge of the road. The houses look better kept, and the roads are well paved, without potholes and free of rubbish. We are looking forward to Honduras.

The border crossing went smoothly. The people are curious and interested in our adventure. We are happy to tell them about our travel experiences, our equipment, and that "Suiza" is in Europe.

After 402 kilometres we leave Guatemala with these memories:

Climbing the active Pacaya volcano and seeing liquid lava at dusk

The market in Antigua, where almost everything is sold, used or new

Roosters crowing from 3 in the morning, dogs barking all night

Language schools competing for every student

Poverty, mobile phones, TV, traffic, smog

Black clouds of exhaust from the chicken buses (old US school buses)

Motorbikes loaded with 4 people (the whole family)

The 11 most exhausting kilometres on the way to Cuilapa

Restaurants?

Cold showers take some getting used to

Biker info Guatemala

Maps:

www.reise-know-how.de
Maps and travel guides for Latin America

Food:

Carry enough for 2 days. Snacks can be bought on the way

Water:

ONLY mineral water is safe (buy PET bottles)
Top up your fluids whenever you can!

Stages:

Find out about the elevation profile, distances, road conditions and places to stay.
Don't underestimate the time needed.

Bike path:

Locals get their driving licence in 2 hours! Hence the "Wild West" behaviour on the roads. On the Pan-American Highway a rear-view mirror is a must. Lorries and buses create a strong suction! Potholes, ruts, missing drain covers, and old and new asphalt that don't match

Transport:

Bicycles are carried on the roof of public buses (old US school buses). It's a good idea to have your own straps (4 x 50 cm) ready and to tie the bikes down yourself. A tip is good motivation.

Climate:

Very varied climate depending on altitude. Hot, sticky and very humid. Sun protection! In the mountains, local rain and fog are possible.

Hotels:

Hotels are cheap. Bed linen and hygiene are not up to European standards.
Laundry is mostly washed in cold water.

Camping:

In our opinion, basically not possible.
There are no safe campsites. "Wild" camping is not recommended. Most land is fenced with barbed wire and guarded by dogs.

Internet:

Internet cafés, laundries, hotel lobbies. PCs with "Skype" and a camera are available. Wi-Fi access is rather rare (slow or broken)

/berichte/honduras.title: Honduras
/berichte/honduras.html:
Honduras
24 - 31 October 2008

10 kilometres after the Guatemalan border, we made our first stop in Copán Ruinas, famous for its Maya ruins. This unique World Heritage Site, protected by UNESCO, is said to be the greatest sight in Honduras. We spend half a day on a guided tour to learn more about the background and history of the Maya. At the "Espresso Americano" we enjoy a really good cappuccino for the first time in ages. Because the beans are exported, good coffee cannot be taken for granted. Copán Ruinas, firmly in the hands of tourism, stands out for its many restaurants, souvenir shops and cobbled streets.

In drizzle and under an overcast sky, which is nothing unusual here, we leave this well-kept provincial town. On the way towards "La Entrada" we come across herds of cattle, women at the river, pigs being transported, and muddy roads buried by landslides. Because of the constant rain and washouts, many stretches of road have turned into soggy clay tracks. After 50 metres the wheels and brakes jam, and the mud gets into the chain, cassette and cranks. This forces us to clean our bikes several times. With "water jets" from PET bottles, we have to get the parts moving again, an extremely time-consuming business. Just before La Entrada, Alexandre gets his fourth flat tyre. Well practised at patching by now, we fix this mishap quickly.

On the way to Santa Rosa there are again many "ups and downs", and 500 metres of climbing at an 11% gradient. We reach Gracias after dark and look for a hotel. At "La Posada Don Juan", the best hotel in town, we spend the night for just 25 US dollars. When we ask about the road ahead to "La Esperanza", we learn that it is officially closed. The dirt road has been badly damaged by the constant rain, and the clean-up work is still going on. Only "going back" with a long detour via San Salvador would get us on to Nicaragua. We set off to find a four-wheel-drive vehicle with a driver to take us from Gracias to La Esperanza.

As we pass heavy construction machinery, we realise that under normal conditions this stretch would take at least 3 days by bike. After a 3-hour drive on a bone-shaking track, with 5 other passengers squeezed in between the luggage and the bikes, and 3,000 lempira (150 US dollars) lighter, we reach La Esperanza after 80 kilometres. Thanks to the Lenca people, whose code of honour stands for honesty, this town is considered the safest in Honduras.

In rain showers we leave La Esperanza on unpaved, pot-holed and waterlogged roads. An "insider tip" from a local takes us over the mountains to Marcala on the old pass road. Far from civilisation, we enjoy 30 kilometres of car-free dirt road leading us through vast mountain forests. At these altitudes, fog, drizzle and changing temperatures with sunny spells are nothing unusual, so we have to put our rain gear on and take it off again several times. This stretch would make an excellent mountain bike route with long downhills. After 5 hours we are back on solid asphalt, which takes us to Marcala.

For just 9 US dollars including drinks, we eat plenty and well in a Honduran-Chinese restaurant. This town stands out for its well-kept appearance, shops with neatly arranged displays, and good hotel accommodation. In the local café we sketch the distance and elevation profile for the next stage on a paper napkin. Helpful information from a lorry driver helps us master the 700 metres of climbing ahead to La Paz. Good preparation spares us the extra strain of riding into the unknown. And so we reach our destination just in time, before the short dusk sets in.

The road from La Paz to Tegucigalpa, the capital of Honduras, has some obstacles that should not be underestimated. 70 kilometres in one day, more than 1,000 metres of climbing, nowhere to spend the night and not much food on the way do not seem doable to us. According to information at the bus terminal, there is thick fog with poor visibility in this mountain region, it rains again and again, and it is dangerous (we don't know exactly why).

We decide to continue by "chicken bus" to Tegucigalpa. We strap the Kogas onto the roof of the bus with the 5 straps we brought with us (2 cm wide, 1 m long, with a buckle). To avoid damage to the bikes, it's a good idea to tie them down yourself. An extra tip for the driver motivates him to steer around the potholes. After 2 hours we arrive in hectic, noisy Tegucigalpa, and are greeted by rubbish, smog, foul smells and traffic grinding to a standstill. We had actually wanted to spend a night in the capital of Honduras. Our first impressions of Tegucigalpa made us decide to carry on to Danlí and get there before dark (on the advice of a fellow passenger). Around midday, changing buses at the terminal 1 kilometre away becomes a real test and needs strong nerves. Every bus has its own stop, and this in a part of town you would never walk through by choice.

After an adventurous 3½-hour (85-kilometre) bus ride to Danlí, we are relieved to have survived it without any spectacular incidents. As we already knew only too well, we passed collapsed stretches of road, a lorry being pulled out of the mud, and construction workers with picks and shovels, surrounded by onlookers waiting for the road to reopen. With just two wheel-widths to spare, we drive past a 20-metre stretch where half the road has broken away. Below the damaged lane, several houses have been buried by the broken-off chunks and the mud. Because it is a main road with two-way traffic, the vehicles keep rolling over the unsecured stretch of road. Worrying and extremely dangerous! In comparison, the "rowdy ride" with our private driver was more harmless than this "20-metre stretch".

Before crossing the border into Nicaragua: one last visit to the lavandería to have our laundry washed, and a trip to the supermarket for the food and drinks we need, so we can set off for "Las Manos" (the Honduras/Nicaragua border) at 07:00 the next morning. In the evening, after 51 kilometres, we want to reach the town of Ocotal in our 4th country.

After 290 kilometres we leave Honduras with these memories:

All in all, we liked Honduras better than Guatemala. The country feels more cultivated, the hotels are better kept, and we enjoyed the food more. In Honduras the roads are not yet paved everywhere. Where they are, the surface is excellent and free of potholes. The central highlands are mountainous, wooded and green. The people seem more open to us, and most of them live in houses rather than wooden shacks. In our view, the standard of living is clearly higher than in Guatemala. We always felt comfortable and never in any way threatened or unsafe. Except at night, when it's better not to ride at all, you can get around safely on the roads.

What does it cost?
Chicken bus ride, 80 kilometres, 2 people, 2 bicycles
CHF 10.--
A night in the "best in town" hotel, double room with shower
CHF 30.--
1 hour repairing the 150 mm steel bolt of the Koga handlebar
CHF 10.--
Dinner incl. drinks, 2 people, on average
CHF 15.--
1 banana from the market (2 lempira)
12 centimes

/berichte/iran.title: Iran
/berichte/iran.html:
Iran
15 May - 12 June 2012

Before crossing the border from Turkey into Iran, it's time for a change of outfit. In the middle of a lorry queue about 5 kilometres long, we say goodbye to our casual cycling clothes and change into "morally appropriate" ones. Long trousers for the man; hair covered with a headscarf, a long-sleeved shirt and of course long trousers for the woman! The border check is quick and straightforward, and our 30-day visa starts now. As at most border crossings, the "street money-changers" soon spot us. Each one offers the best rate and says it's impossible to change foreign currency on the other side of the border. By now we have become a little wiser and only change money outside the customs area, on Iranian soil. For 164 Turkish lira we are handed 1,300,000 Iranian rial (CHF 100.00). Outside the customs area, on Iranian soil, you get twice as much, which means our next accommodation costs only "half". Our piggy bank is happy, and we race downhill to Maku, 22 kilometres away. At the best hotel in town, the Tourist Inn, only the suite is still free. As "rial millionaires" we can afford it, and we spend the night in this oversized suite with 2 rooms and 2 bathrooms.

While stopping under a shady tree, we get talking to a lorry driver. After some initial problems understanding each other, and with the help of the "German - Farsi" phrasebook from "Reise Know-How", it turns out that we are all heading for Tabriz. After tea and biscuits we continue our journey in his lorry. It's already 19:00 when we are dropped off on the edge of Tabriz. Time to look for a hotel. As dusk falls, at 21:00, thanks to a police escort, we find one. The hotel is fully booked! After long discussions at reception we get a room after all. In front of the hotel we meet Frieda and Norbert, a German couple cycling from Shiraz (Iran) to Trabzon (Turkey). We swap experiences, rest for a day, go sightseeing in Tabriz, and then carry on towards Miyaneh. After more than 1,000 metres of climbing, and while looking for drinking water, we come across a station of the Red Crescent paramedics. We know that this organisation also offers free places to sleep, and sure enough we are invited to spend the night at the camp. We quickly set up our mobile beds on the carpeted floor and are welcomed with the obligatory çay. Our next stop is Miyaneh, where we have a tailor alter Claudia's clothes once again. The search for the ideal Iranian cycling clothes – a topic that will keep us busy for quite a while yet! With the help of an Iranian woman and the experienced tailor, the fitting already shows the first signs of success. Claudia now feels visibly relieved and better "ventilated". A group photo with everyone involved, and of course, afterwards there is çay, melon, nuts, and a "Farsi-English" textbook, which we are given as a present when we say goodbye.

The temperatures keep rising, the midday sun is burning, and the road surface reflects the heat. We take it easy and wait at the roadside until the next lorry driver gives us another lift. Once in Takestan, we top up our supplies and set off to look for a suitable place to camp. As usual, not so easy: our "nice to have" list of requirements calls for shelter from the wind, shade, no risk of flooding, as level as possible and without stones, no thorns that could pierce the tent floor, and above all the promise of a quiet night. And if possible no stray dogs, crowing roosters or diesel generators starting up unexpectedly – the list could go on! Only at 20:45 do we find the "right" spot for our tent. The first attempt, in the middle of a plantation, doesn't work out. With everything set up and furnished, a diesel generator with a groundwater pump is started. We already know all about sleepless nights, so we prefer to take everything down, pack up and move on. The second attempt succeeds. A quick introduction to the farmer, with a handshake and a "merci", and our well-earned rest is secured.

On to Hamadan. The temperature in the sun climbs to an unbearable 49 degrees, simply too hot for us. We soon find a solution: at the edge of town we "flag down" a lift. This time it isn't free. For a fare of 200,000 rial (12 euros), we and our bikes are taken to Hamadan in an air-conditioned "VIP coach". At no extra cost we get a snack and hot tea. Another 175 kilometres covered, we cycle a short 8 kilometres into the town centre, where we will visit the sights of Hamadan the next morning.

In the cities we mostly get around on foot, and we don't go unnoticed. The astonished faces and smiles of the locals don't go unnoticed by us either. Tourists are unusual here, and in our strikingly "adapted" clothing we look exotic. As will turn out later, we had already been spotted as we rode into the city and were registered at precisely 16:47.......story to follow.

We are greeted with unmissable calls of "hello" and "where are you from". Our answers: "no Farsi" and "Switzerland". To our surprise: the "Rolling Stones" are just as unknown as "Switzerland", but "Dolce & Gabbana" is a name everyone knows.
While looking for something to photograph, we are approached by a man with dual US-Persian citizenship. He has noticed our aimlessness – and we notice his English mixed with a parallel mobile phone conversation in "Farsi". He spontaneously invites us on a "sightseeing tour" in his slightly battered Peugeot. In this travel report we will call our new companion "Israf".........story to follow.

A sightseeing drive through Hamadan or Esfahan is an adventure that can't be beaten. Pure adrenaline! It outdoes everything we have ever seen! It's not the temperament of the driver, but the "lawlessness" that decides how the traffic flows. Even the police have to bow to the "local customs". Two-wheelers are barely tolerated, pedestrians are an obstacle. You find elderly people neither behind the wheel nor crossing the road. One hand on the wheel, the other on the horn, and the mobile phone wedged between ear and shoulder. Although we didn't see a single accident in the cities, the statistics are frightening. In 2006 there were reportedly 28,000 road deaths and 270,000 injuries, with 74 million inhabitants.

By now our acquaintance with "Israf" has grown into a friendship. He handles his "original Peugeot" (not an Iranian copy) superbly, so in no time at all we know every sight and the few traffic lights. We gladly accept his invitation to dinner and to stay the night, and he picks us up in front of the hotel in his "original Peugeot with Iranian number plates".

At his family's home, sitting comfortably over tea and dates, the phone rings: "Are the 2 cycle tourists who arrived in Hamadan yesterday at 16:47 with you? – YES – Come to headquarters, all of you, with the passports." After our passports have been checked, 2 hours follow: us on folding chairs in the anteroom, our friend "Israf" in the interrogation room. The accusation of breaking the law: "A tourist is not permitted to accept a private Iranian invitation without the consent of the police." A report is written by hand, our passports are copied, and "Israf" receives a warning. The invitation is forbidden under threat of punishment, and we are given 2 options: "Go back to the hotel, or leave the city, stating your destination." Contrary to every travel report we had read, we, like those involved, knew nothing about this rule. We prefer to set off immediately for Esfahan.

An unusually strong headwind stops us from making quick progress. This time we are offered a "cosy" little spot for the tent. Not a bad idea: spending a quiet night sheltered by the neighbouring woods. The wind has turned 180 degrees, storm gusts shake the outer tent and the guy ropes vibrate. Woken from his sleep, Alex has to secure the tent against "taking off" with extra pegs and stones. Our Hilleberg holds firm, and we can retreat into our sleeping bags. Meanwhile the temperatures have moderated too: 3 days ago it was 49 in the sun, and now it's only 23 degrees. We get up early and battle our way to Arak into a headwind (we already know all about those from Turkey). For our lunch break we eat in a small lokanta and are surprised by a typical, delicious Iranian dish (photo Iran No. 33). Further on, at the halfway point, we meet a fellow cyclist from Poland. We quickly swap website addresses, and then the good news: now it's the remaining 65 kilometres smoothly and steadily downhill. The result was a new daily record, Gonbad to Arak, 156 kilometres.

Evenings at the hotel: 18:30 "check-in", a freshly made bed; shower and wash the dusty clothes at the same time, write the report, get the photos ready, update the internet, charge the batteries, make coffee on the MSR stove in the bathroom (ideally under the extractor fan), top up our supplies, 23:00 sleep.
Mornings at the hotel: 06:30 get up, 7:00 breakfast, taking whatever we like from the buffet, snacks for the road included, pack the bags, "check-out" at 08:30, off we go.

The remaining 320 kilometres still mean 2 more nights in the tent. We only just manage to reach the goals we have set ourselves, because fierce headwinds or crosswinds take a lot of strength and nerve. In Esfahan we are already expected at the beautifully restored, 400-year-old "Dibai House", near the bazaar and the Harounieh Mosque. We have planned 3 days off to recover and a trip to Shiraz.

To our surprise, "Israf" has decided at short notice to follow us 500 kilometres from Hamadan on the night bus. He has relatives here in Esfahan, a chance to get hold of another "original Peugeot" for sightseeing. Our friend's driving skills can't be beaten here either. The "highlights" are soon captured on camera, the Iranian ice cream speciality tested – it really tastes good – and evening has come. In the meantime his uncle has organised a picnic in the park with us and his family. Even though the headscarf and the Islamic rules and customs are always there, we spend a spontaneous, relaxed evening full of laughter.

We are allowed to leave our bikes and luggage at the guesthouse. With only the bare essentials in 2 small backpacks, we take the "VIP bus" to Shiraz, a 6-hour journey. A 485-kilometre route, dead straight, bleak and boring. The bus is air-conditioned, generously laid out with only 3 x 15 seats, and has plenty of legroom and space to recline. Listening to music and writing our travel report, we "shorten" the time and reach Shiraz in the evening. By bike, the journey would have taken a week.

The fastest and most comfortable way to see a city in Iran is by taxi. Above all, you aren't constantly exposed to the heat. Through a recommendation we find an English-speaking tour guide who, for a flat day rate of only 60 euros, takes us to all the ancient buildings worth seeing (guide, driver, air-conditioned car and all entrance fees included). In the morning we visit the inner part of Shiraz, and in the afternoon we drive to Naqsh-e Rostam, the necropolis, and to Persepolis, where we learn a lot about the history of Persia and its kings. Back at the hotel at 21:00 – the next day at 13:00 back to Esfahan by coach, to the "Dibai House". That leaves us one more day to do the laundry and plan the rest of our journey.

The east of Iran seems unsuitable for cyclists to us. Already in May the thermometer climbs to 40 degrees around midday. The heat takes a lot of energy, and you need twice as much to drink. The 300 kilometres from Esfahan to Yazd gave us a first impression of what cycling through a desert-like dry region feels like. Incredibly hot, bleak, dead straight, little vegetation, boring, and long stretches without a hard shoulder. The infrastructure "thins out", and the places to buy supplies get further and further apart. Once again there are 800 metres of climbing, and our routes are often at 2,300 metres above sea level. After 100 km we spend the first night in "Kuhpayeh" in the tent, bedded on sand. Another 125 km without any climbs, then the second night, on a carpet at someone's invitation. The rest from "Aqda", 115 km to go, "head down, eyes on infinity", and we reach the "Silk Road Hotel" in Yazd. Once, and never again!

For the next day, the "Silk Road Tour" is planned. It's the most popular excursion around Yazd, through the desert and the pre-Islamic town of Meybod. From 08:00 to 15:00, for a flat price of 1,000,000 rial (CHF 60.00), with a guide, there's plenty to see:

Mud brick village
Shaking Minaret
4000 years old citadel of kharanagh
Zaprastrian's holy temple
Narin castle
Caravanserai
Ice house

We still have 2 hours left to walk the 5-kilometre "City Walkway" through the old town. It's best not to leave the well-signposted route. If you haven't got lost, you should come across the following ancient buildings:

  • Jameh Mosque
    Alexander Prison

One more sight you shouldn't miss: the free tour of the "Fahadan Hotel" (ask at reception), not far from "Alexander Prison".

Yazd, one of the oldest historic cities in Iran, lies between the Dasht-e Kavir and Dasht-e Lut deserts. The city was founded at an oasis and, according to historical records, has existed since the third millennium BC. Its architecture is unique in history. Many fire temples (atashkadeh) can still be found here today. When it was founded, the city is said to have been on the shore of a large inland lake. To this day, water channels and pipes, some of them built in ancient times, are used for the water supply.
Yazd is one of the oldest cities (in the world) and lies in the middle of the provinces of Fars, Isfahan, Kerman and Khorasan. On the route of the Silk Road, in ancient times Yazd was an important crossroads for many travellers and merchants.
According to UNESCO, Yazd is the second-largest city built with fired clay bricks. The old part is fortified by a high mud-brick wall dating back to the 5th century. The Narin fort (the largest mud-brick caravanserai) and the Jameh Mosque, whose origins go back more than 1,000 years, are masterpieces of Islamic architecture.
Yazd's wind towers, the natural cooling systems for houses and public buildings, remain a wonder of architectural planning.

900 kilometres to Mashhad? No thank you! About 400 kilometres of it run through the "Dasht-e Lut" desert. Following the good advice of the locals, who know what they are talking about, we buy two tickets north for 300,000 rial including bikes (CHF 15.00). At 20:00 we leave Yazd to arrive in Mashhad on the night bus after a 12-hour journey.

16 hours by bus, this time not VIP, which showed in the service and the late departure. On top of that, while one bike was being unloaded, the rear-view mirror came off the handlebars. Annoying: a repair in unfamiliar surroundings always takes a lot of time.

The Holy Shrine! Taking photos is not allowed, either inside or outside. As non-Muslims, access to the inner area is closed to us. Believer or not, anyone who wants to be inside the barriers must wear a chador. Claudia has the option of renting one to get in. But neither of us will get to see the Holy Shrine. We do without that fortune and look at its magic in the photographic masterpieces instead. In countless photo studios, "digital artists" create souvenirs and family keepsakes. Proof of the pilgrimage can be bought for anything from 60,000 rial to "the sky's the limit". The crush in the streets and on the pavements is correspondingly great. After one day we leave Mashhad with relief, heading for Sarakhs.

Mashhad is the second-largest city in Iran and is considered one of the seven holy places of Shia Islam. Because of the holy Goharshad Mosque, the city became a religious centre. Every year more than 100,000 Shia pilgrims visit this place of pilgrimage. Mashhad's special religious importance for Iran comes from the fact that the remains of the (eighth) Imam Reza are buried here. Mashhad benefited from its location on the Silk Road and was a trading point on the way between West and East.

Getting out of Mashhad, no problem for us? But the Iranian driving style and the heavy traffic block our way too. "Stop and go", honking, pushing, phoning and waving through the window at the same time – unbelievable, and yet it works.

The road from Mashhad to Sarakhs, as it presented itself to us, can be described in just one word: "headwind" – head-on! Again and again this hot, relentless north wind. At a snail's pace of 12 - 14 km/h into the wind, we didn't even notice the 600 metres of climbing – and that was only by pedalling hard! We have never experienced anything like it! The glaring sun, which pushes temperatures up to 49 degrees, dries us out. We drink about 10 litres of water a day and are grateful that passing drivers keep handing us bottles of water.

We wanted to reach Sarakhs, the border town with Turkmenistan, in 2 days. The daily stages couldn't be kept to, and we were still 30 kilometres short of the border. Because we never ride after dark, another night in the tent was unavoidable. Camping on the way is no problem as long as you carry enough water. We had too little! The solution: collect the empty PET bottles at the roadside and wave at the approaching vehicles. A water tanker stops, and from an oversized outlet valve 8 litres of water were quickly filled, leaving the road and my shoes soaking wet.

We spend one more day recovering in Sarakhs, to collect the required visa the next day and cross the border into Turkmenistan.

Iran for beginners:
Anyone who wants to travel in Iran should first get properly acquainted with the rules and customs!

Dress code:
Long trousers for men and women. Women: a head covering (choose a silk scarf or an airy cotton scarf, never synthetic), and long-sleeved tops reaching over the bottom. Travelling by bike can become an ordeal! A woman must be aware that she will be out in almost 50 degrees in the sun in "dress code". This rule must be followed without fail.

Money, currency and exchange rate (inflation is 25%!)
Bring enough cash (preferably) in euros or US dollars. It's impossible to use a credit card in Iran or to get money in any form. The many cash machines only accept Iranian cards. Money by airmail or bank transfer is simply impossible. If you lose your money, your only option is to go to the consulate!
The national currency is the rial; but prices are mostly given in toman. 10,000 rial equals 1,000 toman; it's the same banknote. Careful: make sure you know which one you're talking about!
Money is best changed, for example, in Tabriz at "Daraie Amirno", or with a "money-changer" on foot; ask around, with caution.
Changing money at a bank or in a hotel? Unfortunately you only get half for each unit of currency!
Exchange rate in May 2012 in Tabriz:
1 euro = 11,000 to 22,000 rial
1 US$ = 8,000 to 16,000 rial

Language:
National = Persian, local = Turkish, 6 languages across the country.
In English, anything is possible, from no knowledge at all to perfect.

Shopping:
You can buy everything, almost everything, but there is no money for tourists. Under the women's chadors hide lingerie, brand-name goods and copies. The products (even those you wouldn't dare think about) are displayed in the shops and can be bought freely, but they may only be tried on behind closed doors.
3 kinds of flatbread, it doesn't get any cheaper."

Other things:
No restaurants as we know them, more like lokandas with 6 - 10 tables
Salad or vegetables are the exception, stews and fast food the rule
Mostly squat toilets, only occasionally sit-down ones, sometimes with paper and a flush
Only a few hotels; for example: in Hamadan, 7 hotels for 500,000 inhabitants
The largest cities are Tehran, Esfahan, Tabriz, Shiraz, Yazd and Mashhad
Iran has 74 million inhabitants
You can't miss the countless boxes of tissues, but you'll look in vain for packets of paper handkerchiefs
Alcohol, physical contact before marriage and homosexuality are forbidden
Women are not allowed to ride bicycles; dress code for girls from the age of 9
Pets that have to be taken for walks are not allowed
At 2,000 metres above sea level, Hamadan is the 2nd-highest city in Iran
Equal rights are a foreign concept
If a woman dies, the insurance pays her surviving family only half the pension
A man may marry several women, but a woman only one man

We leave Iran with these memories:
Seen a lot, and a little
Mosques covered with mosaics, and historic buildings
Friendly, helpful people
Islam bound up with the state
"Wild West" traffic conditions
Dry, hot, dusty, sand, little vegetation
Storm gusts from every direction, no rain
Sweaty clothing
Tea, tea, tea – you'll look in vain for coffee as a ready-made drink
Most of our routes were at an average of 2,000 metres above sea level
