/berichte/kalifornien.title: California
/berichte/kalifornien.html:
California
1 September - 3 October 2008
The first photo of our journey was taken at Lucerne railway station by Sandro, who snapped us with all our luggage. The "evening-before check-in" of our 4 pieces of luggage, weighing more than 100 kilograms in total, went smoothly, and nothing stood in the way of the start of our Central America bike tour.

Unexpectedly, our planned flight on 1 September was cancelled because of bad weather, which meant we could only take the second connecting flight to San Francisco three hours later. We were a little surprised when we had to open our bags at the check-in desk. They checked the two empty MSR fuel bottles. One bottle was fine; the second still gave off a few fumes and was confiscated.

At London Heathrow, British Airways boarding staff at first would not let us onto the plane, saying: "No flight to San Francisco without a valid return ticket and without a US visa." Some explaining, and calling in someone who knew what they were doing, finally got us through.

The plane left Heathrow another hour late, so we only landed in SF at 18:00 instead of 14:00. At baggage reclaim we heard: "Mrs. Naegeli and Mr. Keller, please present at the information desk". We were greeted with a friendly "hello". Our assumption that, as "Zentralbiker VIPs", we would be whisked through customs faster soon turned out to be wrong. Three pieces of luggage had stayed behind in London, including, of course, our bikes and a bag with four panniers. The report was quickly filled in, and we were compensated with a 100-dollar Visa card. A shuttle bus took us to the "Bay Landing" hotel in Burlingame, San Francisco.

We used the next day as a "sightseeing day" to explore SF on foot. Downtown, Fisherman's Wharf, the Cable Car Museum, Pier 39, the "crooked street" and Chinatown were on the programme.

Back at the hotel, what a surprise! Two completely shredded bike boxes, soaked with water and standing upside down, were waiting for us. The cardboard was so wet that taking them back to the airport to report the damage became a balancing act. 1½ hours at the airport, from "desk to desk" and "floor to floor", and not a single person responsible from British Airways to be found. With no report, and totally exhausted by the ordeal, we went back to the hotel.

Day 3 was all about: a second attempt at reporting the damage, finding the missing parts and getting the bikes back into working order. No problem, we thought, it'll all be done by lunchtime. How wrong we were! Despite BART (Bay Area Rapid Transit), which always got us around quickly, our search for spare parts in SF and the surrounding area was unsuccessful. One shop ordered a part we needed from Ventura, 650 km away. A cheap temporary solution will have to last until mid-September. Totally discouraged and fed up, we went back to the hotel. The result was one more night in a hotel.

Now we can finally get going! With "BART" and our bikes straight into downtown San Francisco, a test ride along SF Bay over the Golden Gate Bridge, on to Sausalito and Tiburon, and a trip on the high-speed catamaran give us back our confidence.

At midday, at 35 degrees, we leave Burlingame heading for Half Moon Bay. In the evening, with the thermometer showing only 15 degrees, which is normal for this region, we reach Half Moon Bay. The place is described as "beautiful", but apart from souvenir shops, honeymoon suites and weddings it doesn't offer very much. In the village, a wedding party has taken almost all the hotel rooms, so we pay USD 150 for a room and a place at the wedding buffet. We were then allowed to spend two more nights with a local, camping in their garden and enjoying a BBQ. Here we also got rid of 20 kg of excess luggage, which was sent back to Lucerne by UPS.

Greetings to our friends at Half Moon Bay: Thank you for your help, Bike storage, the Campground and the beautiful BBQ-Dinner. See you soon in Switzerland.

On the recommendation of Jack and Vicky, a "tandem cycling couple", and for a better overview, we have two bike maps sent to Carmel. The road maps we had "stuck together" from a road atlas turned out to be completely useless! Without the Bicycle and Touring Map of the Pacific Coast, sections 4 and 5, you get absolutely nowhere.

The following example gives a first impression of distances in the USA: shopping at the nearby centre takes "only 20 minutes", or it might be: "after 2 miles take a right, then 4 blocks down the street, at the left". That is roughly how Americans give directions and distances. And so, in the evening, after 35 miles (56 km) and two new lightweight outdoor backpacks, we reached our campsite. Another rest day gone!

Fog and drizzle without any sun, everything grey on grey, accompany us on the way to "Pigeon Point", where we want to spend the night in a "dorm" (a 6-bed room). Standing on a cliff 50 km south of San Francisco, the 16-metre-high "Pigeon Point Lighthouse" is one of the tallest lighthouses in America. Its first lens, weighing 8,000 kilograms, with a diameter of 6 metres, a 1,008-prism Fresnel lens and a five-wick lard oil lamp, was lit for the first time in 1872. Today the modernised lighthouse is still an active part of the US Coast Guard.

In Monterey we visit the aquarium, ride the 17-Mile Drive, photograph the world-famous cypress and scan the Pacific for whales with our binoculars. Apart from seals and pelicans we haven't spotted anything exciting yet. The weather is cool and foggy. Sleeping bags, tent and clothes stay wet and damp. Further south it is supposed to get better. That is encouraging, and our search for the sun has already taken us 200 miles.

From Monterey onwards, California shows us a completely different face. Sunny, pleasant temperatures, and changing vegetation, from well-kept greenery to sparse grazing land. Pismo Beach, Lompoc and the coastal towns that follow are all about surfing. After football and basketball, surfing is probably the third most popular sport. Wherever there are Pacific waves, there are plenty of surfers in their black wetsuits. The "Californians" always have time for a chat and are interested in our plans. They are helpful and happy to tell us about the USA, the coming elections, and to give us travel tips. Coffee breaks, swapping email addresses, meeting kindred spirits and collecting travel advice have often left us short of time. Like at El Capitán State Beach, where we arrived at 18:00 without any food - no shop - no dinner. Hoping to get something warm in our stomachs after all, we ask our camping neighbour for some pasta and salsa. He spontaneously invites us to his family reunion with a BBQ. All perfect, and as a result, dinner at a birthday party the next day is already taken care of too.

Many thanks to all SCIARONIS for this wonderful evening and BBQ at the Campground. We liked your Beans and Birthday Cake.

Carmel is very expensive! A night in a 2- or 3-star hotel without a sea view costs between USD 250 and 300. We prefer to track down the "cheap" 40-dollar campsite, 7 miles off Highway 1. Because of roaming mountain lions, we were advised not to go hiking away from the camp! By now we have pedalled 270 miles and reached the Pfeiffer Big Sur Campground. The sun is back, and so are the ever-present souvenir shops of the tourist centres. Just 35 miles from Carmel, the price of a campsite has already dropped to 6 dollars. We are curious to see how these "hard ground prices" develop all the way to San Diego.

Big Sur, with its rugged rocky coastline, is a landscape full of variety, curvy and hilly. These miles are really worth it. On this stretch we also spotted our first whales. By now we only need 2 hours for breakfast, showering, taking down the tent and loading the bikes. Every move is now in tune, and the spare tyres have finally found a secure place to be strapped on. Equipped with the bike maps, planning the daily stages is "a piece of cake"; only the question of "what's where" in our panniers still hasn't been fully settled. Even so, we have got used to our new everyday life, and we have successfully finished adjusting the position of the grips, the gear shifter, the saddle height and the saddle angle.

Cambria, a small town in "Wild West style", lies roughly halfway between San Francisco and Los Angeles. In the pretty "Bridge Street Inn" hostel we take two rest days and treat ourselves to a fine meal in a restaurant. What stands out is that Cambria has one main street lined with lots of little shops and restaurants. Not overrun by tourists, this little town invites you to stroll and linger in its street cafés. The climate has changed too, and the sun shines at 25 to 30 degrees from 10:00 until 19:00. But there is a steady wind, and at night the temperature drops below 15 degrees.

Already 21 September? Already 20 days in California?

We leave Carpinteria, heading for Los Angeles. On the way to Point Mugu we spend the night at a Pacific campground close to the beach. Dusk has already fallen, and while we are putting up the tent we are attacked by an invasion of mosquitoes. Too late, we notice the wetland just a few steps away. Cooking outside the tent was out of the question, so dinner had to be made inside the tent. In the morning it was the same scene all over again, so we left this unpleasant campsite without breakfast. We have never packed up so fast!

One last hill before Santa Monica, Purisima Hill (900 feet high), still had to be conquered. Now the skyline of LA came into view. From Malibu, a well-kept bike path takes us along "Pacific Beach" to "Venice Beach". We skip a Los Angeles sightseeing tour and devote ourselves all the more to the bizarre goings-on at Venice Beach, with its many free spirits selling anything that brings in dollars, and the Muscle Beach cage, "forever young and fit", kickboards, skateboards, rollerblades and everything that rolls, hops or jumps on muscle power.

After 2 nights in an extremely unsatisfactory hostel, we leave LA to tackle our longest daily stage so far: 130 kilometres. Somewhat exhausted, we reach the Capistrano Beach campground at 20:00. Even with our well-practised routine, putting up the tent and cooking dinner by headlamp takes at least an hour.

The stretch from Los Angeles to San Diego is described as not very attractive. We were pleasantly surprised by the bike paths and the varied beaches, with the islands and towns off the coast. We quickly found "Campland on the Beach" on a peninsula in San Diego. With 2 pools, 2 jacuzzis, the best facilities and none of the Pacific Coast roar, this is the most expensive, but also the most beautiful, campsite so far (44 dollars a day).

We wanted to spend a few restful days in San Diego before continuing to Mexico. The trip to Tijuana (the Mexican border town next to the USA) became a real test. Despite plenty of advice and all our caution, we did not escape a theft. The idea of taking the bus from Tijuana via Mexico City (changing buses) to Tapachula was quickly dropped. Tapachula lies on the Pacific coast, 18 kilometres from the border with Guatemala. The vague prices, the complicated transport of the bikes and the 4-day, 4,000-kilometre bus journey to the Guatemalan border were too risky for us.

We decide to rent a pickup, drive back to LA with our luggage and then fly to Guatemala City with "Continental Airlines". The 5 days in San Diego were anything but restful. During that time we rode 150 miles by bike to replace the stolen sunglasses, organised bike boxes, repaired a flat rear tyre twice, packed the bikes, and replaced our lost coffee mugs at the "REI" outdoor shop!

The 3-hour drive to LA went smoothly despite the rush hour, and we quickly reached the motel for the night. The preparations for the next day's flight to Guatemala were done. We had plenty of time left for a relaxed dinner to round off Alexandre's birthday.

Our flight to Guatemala was pure stress!

The 4 hours we had allowed before departure turned out not to be enough. Up at 7:30, return the rental car, queue at check-in, and problems checking in the bike boxes, which counted as excess weight. As a result, we missed our feeder flight to Houston. Luckily there was a second way to catch the connecting flight from Houston to Guatemala City. Queuing, special screenings, passport control, and again and again "stand in the queue". 10 minutes before departure we reach the gate, which is already closed. Boarding had to be reopened especially for us. After a 3-hour flight we reach Houston at 17:00 (time difference +2 h).

The onward flight to Guatemala at 19:10 left us only a little time for a coffee break.

After 1,390 kilometres we leave California with these memories:

Riding our bikes over the Golden Gate Bridge to Sausalito

A BBQ party with friends in Half Moon Bay

Raccoons in the rubbish bin and in our tent

Cycling on the freeway

US drivers and motorhome drivers who treated us with consideration

The Pacific Coast Highway, almost 90% of it with a bike lane, in places up to 3 metres wide

The mosquito invasion at the campground after Point Mugu

Venice Beach with its bizarre houses, many free spirits and the Muscle Beach cage

Camp Pendleton, the US military base with 14 kilometres of coastline

The invitation to the "Sciaroni" family party at El Capitán State Beach

In Monterey: the aquarium, the seals and the 17-Mile Drive

The border town of Tijuana in Mexico, and the decision to fly over Baja California

Biker info California

Test ride:

At home, with all your gear. 300 metres of climbing!

Food:

Carry enough for 2 days
Snacks can be bought on the way

Water:

Not always safe to drink in state parks

Stages:

Elevation profile, distances and time needed: don't underestimate them.

Bike path:

Use the bike lane. Highways can turn into freeways, which bikes are usually not allowed on. There are exceptions, though.

Transport:

Bicycles are carried free of charge on public buses (max. 2) and on the rail network (metro).

Climate:

Temperature differences of 10-25 degrees are possible, damp and foggy, headwinds. Important: sun protection

Hotels:

Hotel rooms are usually twice as expensive on Fridays and Saturdays. (Weekend = campground)

Internet:

Without your own laptop: in public libraries.
Wi-Fi access in Starbucks cafés (buy a card)

/berichte/kambodscha.title: Cambodia
/berichte/kambodscha.html:
Cambodia
7 - 25 November 2013

Changing countries from Laos to Cambodia at the Veun Kham border crossing was free of red tape and quick. The customs officers are friendly and speak English! Fill in a form, hand over a photo, and we get our 30-day visa. With the Angkor Wat temple complex, Cambodia offers a tourist highlight.

As we already know from other borders, the difference in vegetation surprises us again as we cross. 60% of Cambodia is covered by jungle. Above 700 metres grows evergreen mountain forest; below it, tropical rainforest with trees that often reach 40-50 metres. The exhausting mountain climbs are now definitely over. We cycle easily along flat roads – the highest mountain, Phnom Aural, 1,810 metres high, is far from our route. In the countryside, places to stay have become a rarity.

Longer stages are needed to find somewhere with air conditioning. We tried it: a room with only a ceiling fan didn't let us sleep. At night the temperature doesn't drop below 20 degrees – much too sticky and warm for us. To find "temperature-controlled" accommodation, we have to choose our daily goals so that we reach a town by evening. Distances of 100 to 140 kilometres a day are therefore not unusual. To avoid the heat and still make progress, the alarm goes off at 4:30.

In just 5 days of riding we reach Phnom Penh, the capital of Cambodia.
Here we visit the Killing Fields, a little outside Phnom Penh. We learn a lot about the reign of terror of Pol Pot and the genocide, in which more than a third of the Cambodian population died. We saw an oppressive testimony to history, one that must not be forgotten. For anyone who wants to find out more: Khmer Rouge

The royal palace, another sight in Phnom Penh, was closed to the public. Norodom Sihanouk died in China on 15.10.2012 after a long illness. During the official state mourning, the "Father of the Nation" lies in state in the palace. On the front of the building, by the entrance gate, the funeral ceremonies are shown on a large projection screen. According to Buddhist tradition, the body must be cremated and laid to rest in a golden urn in the grounds of the royal palace in Phnom Penh.

A holiday mood without bikes! From Phnom Penh, by coach, we reach the "tourist mecca" of Sihanoukville in just 4 hours. The finest sandy beach, sun and swimming in the turquoise Gulf of Thailand await us. On offer: a "3-island tour" to the nearby islands. That sounds good: breakfast "on the beach" and a boat trip with snorkelling, a BBQ under the palms and a walk along an island trail. The last part seemed too exhausting to us, so we "swapped" the walk for lazing in a deckchair.

In the meantime our visas for Thailand have been issued. For a stay of more than 30 days, a visa is required. We had given the job to one of the many travel agencies in Phnom Penh. Cost per person, including the processing fee: 50 USD. Sadly there was no time left to visit the "Tuol Sleng Museum". The former Khmer Rouge prison "S-21" is a reminder of the crimes committed there against hundreds of thousands of Cambodians, who died from abuse, malnutrition and disease. Skulls, instruments of torture, photos of executions and hundreds of portraits make the museum a chamber of horrors.

Overland there are still 250 kilometres to go to Siem Reap. Cycling or river cruising? We are told there's a ferry that runs if there are enough passengers. We were lucky! After 130 kilometres on the shallow "Tonlé Sap", we pass the fishing village of "Kampong Chhnang". The many houseboats are tied together as a village community and linked to the bank. Then come another 100 kilometres through "Lake Tonlé Sap", which, at 25,000 square kilometres, is the largest lake in South-East Asia and one of the richest inland waters for fish on earth. After only a few groundings, we reach the ferry landing at 14:00. There are only 15 kilometres left to Siem Reap by muscle power.

The highlight of any trip to Cambodia: the world-famous temple complex of Angkor Wat. We decide on the 30-kilometre "small circuit". With a 20 USD day pass and our bikes, our cultural journey through Angkor Wat begins. These gigantic structures were built between 900 and 1200 AD. An area ruled by the Khmer kings stretched from the Mekong Delta to Burma, and over large parts of Vietnam and Thailand. The Khmer kings were outstanding architects and engineers. Over 600 years they built more than 100 temples and palaces, until the state coffers ran dry. In 1430 the Thais conquered Angkor, and the rule of the Khmer empire broke apart. In 1860 the temples were discovered in the thick of the jungle by a Mekong expedition, and 47 years later Thailand returned them to Cambodia. More at this link: Angkor Wat

Our goal, Singapore, is getting closer and closer. 11,000 kilometres and more than 100,000 metres of climbing are behind us. The mountains are behind us. Now come white sandy beaches, palms, turquoise sea, seafood, pineapples and everything we have had to do without in the last few months.

First we have to earn what we're looking forward to. Poipet, a small, ugly border town between Cambodia and Thailand, put our patience to the test. Leaving the country took 2 hours of queuing. This border crossing is always crowded. Before weekends, waits of 3-4 hours to enter are not unusual. By paying a VIP supplement, you can cut the queuing considerably.

To reach the next town by bike before dark, we pay the extra fee. After 1 more hour of waiting, the stamp was pressed into our passports – now nothing stood in the way of beach life and cracking coconuts.

30 years of war and the reign of terror of the Khmer Rouge:
After Thailand and Vietnam had conquered Cambodia, the country was a French protectorate from 1863 to 1953. In 1973, under the leadership of Pol Pot, a bitter civil war began, which ended in April 1975 with the capture of Phnom Penh. Pol Pot's 4-year rule that followed claimed a total of 2 million Cambodian lives in the genocide, about a third of the population. Cambodia was to become a communist agrarian state without private property, religion or science. Anyone who had studied, spoke a foreign language or wore glasses was considered an enemy of the state and sent to a labour camp or killed immediately. In concentration camps, children, women and men were imprisoned, interrogated and tortured. Across the country, a total of about 400 killing fields were created, where the condemned were brutally murdered.

On 7 January 1979, Vietnamese troops freed Cambodia from its tormentors and murderers. They found a starving country, set back by years. Rapid international aid saved the surviving population from starvation. Cambodia remained occupied by the Vietnamese until 1991, and a "relaxed" form of communism was introduced. Only in 1993 did the first free elections take place. A democratic system and a new constitution were to give Cambodia a new future.

/berichte/kirgistan.title: Kyrgyzstan
/berichte/kirgistan.html:
Kyrgyzstan
4 - 6 August 2012

The change of country from Tajikistan to Kyrgyzstan doesn't go as usual.

There are still 2 kilometres of unpaved, bumpy track to the "Kyzyl-Art Pass" (4,290 m). To be precise: after clearing customs we are already outside the country's border, but in the 22-kilometre-wide "corridor" between Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan. We don't know which territory this "no-man's-land" belongs to.

We have reached the top of the "Kyzyl-Art" pass and are looking forward to a relaxing descent and a "Snickers" from the next kiosk. The stretch to the Kyrgyz border took great concentration and strength. The headwind was still there, and it wasn't getting any warmer either. Once again, nothing came of the "easy" descent. The 12-kilometre unpaved road was peppered with countless potholes and with stretches of road that had broken away or were missing altogether. The Kyrgyz border, 800 metres lower down (3,490 m), took more than two hours to reach. Smaller streams washing over the road can still be judged when crossing by bike. In murky water it's hard to tell how deep it is or what the bottom is like. Reaching the other bank with dry feet becomes a balancing act.

What? Swiss citizens don't need a visa for Kyrgyzstan? No, the customs officer explains. The visa requirement was lifted a week ago for 45 countries worldwide. The stamp was pressed into our passports straight away, no annoying luggage check, no incomprehensible declaration form to fill in, and on we go towards Sary-Tash.

On a large pasture with a handful of yurts, we find a cosy place to camp. Nothing goes unnoticed! First the cows and goats come closer, and soon children bring bread, butter and kefir. People marvel curiously at the bikes and our futuristic-looking "yurt". We noticed the shaggy young yaks, which grunt like pigs.

Off we go: the wind is still blowing at full strength. The approaching storm front moved a little faster than expected and caught up with us in the evening, 25 kilometres after Sary-Tash. There was no time to find a "cosy" spot for the night. With a quick decision and a well-practised routine, we hope to pitch the tent in record time, stow the panniers in the vestibule and close the zip. Made it! We are in the dry while it pours down outside.

The next morning: everything around us is wet and damp, and the view soon ends in fog. There is still no improvement in the weather. An hour of "pedalling" in rain gear with a view of "infinity" sends our motivation to rock bottom. We prefer to cover the remaining 40 kilometres to Irkeshtam in a heated lorry cab. We have reached the Chinese border.

From the barrier at the Kyrgyz border to the Chinese customs area there are still 6 kilometres to go. A road completely destroyed by lorries and turned into a corrugated track rattles our nerves. Halfway along we meet two walking backpacks, carried by 2 tourists who have already been on foot for three-quarters of an hour. The passing lorries are not allowed to pick up people in the customs corridor, there's no taxi service or shuttle bus, so all that's left is to walk, as the old German song says: "wandering is the miller's joy".

/berichte/laos.title: Laos
/berichte/laos.html:
Laos
14 October - 7 November 2012

The change of culture and climate from China to Laos could not be greater. We are pleasantly surprised.

Just a few kilometres after the border we are already in the middle of the jungle of the provinces of Oudômxai and Louangphabang. Not a single square metre that isn't covered with deep green plants, and a road that squeezes its way through the undergrowth. At 35 degrees and over 85% humidity, the sweat pours out of our pores. Our shirts and shorts have long been dripping wet, and the Brooks leather saddle has changed colour from light brown to deep black.

Again and again a cheerful "Sabaidee" reaches us, from little huts, from the roadside or from somewhere in the thicket. These are spontaneous calls from Lao people with shining eyes and warm laughter. The children jump towards us and slap our hands for a "give me 5". We feel welcome. People use what nature provides, and the "huts" are built and furnished accordingly simply: 4 posts, a few wooden slats, woven walls and anything that will make a roof. Running water is fetched from the village well. A washing line turns out to be a live power cable, and the satellite dish gives away that there's a TV. The people seem happy and content.

In Laos there are lots of places to stay, and they are extremely cheap, so we do without camping in rice fields and banana and rubber plantations. Besides, wild camping is forbidden in Laos and not advisable anyway because of wild animals you'd better avoid (poisonous snakes and scorpions). In Oudômxai, a place where you would certainly not expect a "multi-star hotel", Laos shows its best side. In a newly built hotel we were surprised with a room that lacked nothing. As a "welcome" there was a free massage instead of beer or wine, and for breakfast bread, butter, jam and coffee like at an Italian's. The hostess thanked us for our visit and handed us the bill for 400,000 kip. Expensive? No! 1,000 kip = CHF 0.12

Good to know:
06:00, the day breaks. The sun rises quickly above the horizon. By 8:00 the thermometer is already over 25 degrees, and 2 hours later over 30. At these latitudes (Oct./Nov.) we reckon with 12 hours of sunshine and a dusk of 30 minutes. At 17:00 the sun is still so high that you'd like to ride on. But careful! By 18:00 it's already dark, and street lighting is sparse or doesn't work. When time gets short, we are always relieved to reach the "guest house" in time, without needing our headlamps.

Rested, massaged and well fed, we set off at 08:00 into mountains unknown to us. The 82 kilometres and 2 "hills" ahead are normally nothing unusual for us and should be easy to manage. What we didn't reckon with: the mountains reach 1,400 metres, and the valleys lie 1,000 metres lower. On top of that we were surprised by two "cloudbursts", which meant waiting for a while under our rain capes. Heavy downpours are refreshing, but they don't last long. After half an hour the sun comes out again, the water evaporates within a few minutes, and the temperature is back where it was before the rain.

Just before dark we reach "Pak Mong". With 2,600 metres of climbing in 9 hours (moving time), Laos has given us a new record. In a country where we would never have expected it, we achieved our biggest climb in a single day. Tajikistan and China, which had seemed impossible to "top", were now outdone in the jungle mountains. Unbelievable!

Luang Prabang: the infrastructure, lots of hotels, and restaurants with an astonishing choice of menus remind us of Europe. From our hotel room with a balcony, we enjoy a holiday mood and the view of the "Nam Khan River". In flip-flops, shorts and T-shirts, we stroll through the streets of Luang Prabang, watch the calm at the market and visit various temples. The sights in the town centre are well visited by tourists, but not so overrun that there's nothing left to discover. The rather unspectacular temples a little further out have often turned out to be a "highlight". As so often, we skip a guided tourist excursion and set off to explore by bike.

In "Vang Vieng", 130 kilometres before Vientiane, there's a lot going on. A magnet for travellers who like backpacks and public transport. Among the many places to stay and eat, it's easy to find something for every budget. For the first time since the start of our journey, something like a holiday feeling sets in. We have breakfast on the veranda of our bungalow and even have time to do "nothing". Countless billboards with package deals from travel agencies line the streets. The signs plastered with photos are impossible to miss and made us curious too. Why not let someone else organise our day for once? With "tubing/caving/kayaking", TCK Adventures.laos.com is our favourite. Float through stalactite caves on a lorry inner tube, and paddle 7 kilometres by kayak through small rapids back to the starting point. With only 5 participants, we were offered professional guiding, a relaxed atmosphere and a tasty lunch. This restful holiday day gave us a lot of fun. Laos was the right choice of route for us to cycle from China to Cambodia (without Vietnam!).

We leave the mountains heading for Vientiane. Hilly at first, then flatter and flatter, we reach the capital of Laos after 2 days. By now we've seen lots of temples and their shrines. The Buddha Park is a sight we don't want to miss. In 1958 the mystic Luang Pu Bunleua Sulilat created a large number of huge concrete sculptures of Buddhist and Hindu deities. In the afternoon there's still time to visit That Luang, the landmark of Vientiane. We meet Clare and Moritz, who are covering part of their round-the-world trip on "recumbent bikes". We arrange to meet for dinner and swap travel experiences. From the wide choice of restaurants, the decision is quickly made: the Korean is to surprise us with his specialities. We were served an excellent meal. After an entertaining German-Swiss evening, we once again say goodbye to international cycling friends. The next day takes the two of them towards Thailand, and us towards "Thakhek".

Having already achieved our biggest daily climb, now comes the 166-kilometre "mammoth stage" to Paksmong. Only 320 kilometres to go to the border with Cambodia. By now the alarm goes off at 04:30. In bearable temperatures, we want to cover 100 kilometres each day from sunrise to midday. Claudia has caught a bad cold with fever. We suspect air conditioning and ceiling fans are to blame. So in Pakse, rest and recovery in a suitably air-conditioned hotel room are more important than pedalling on. As a change from a boring stay in the hotel room, a trip to the "Bolaven Plateau" was to provide some variety.

A "day off" in the green:
The scooter – the workhorse. Locals use it to carry all kinds of loads, tourists to reach the sights. For one day we swap our "iron horse" for a 100 cc "moped" to explore hidden caves and the surrounding rivers. With a rented scooter, we wanted to visit the waterfalls and a coffee plantation. The rental man pressed a sketch map, photocopied several times over, into our hands for the road. With a full tank, we rolled off in the direction the map showed. After 60 kilometres we reached "water" but no "fall". It was immediately clear: wrong turning! Turn the map 180 degrees, now east is where west used to be, and back to the junction. Here! A signpost that roughly matches the sketch. Now nothing can go wrong. By now we've done 120 kilometres, and the tank needs filling. A Coke for us, petrol for the "Laomoto".......

30 kilometres on, a bang, the rear tyre has burst! Far from Pakse city, somewhere in the middle of nowhere, no mobile phone, now what? Together, Claudia and I push the two-wheeler back to the main road. The Lao people are very helpful and usually have a mobile with them. The rental man promises us a mechanic with "tyre repair patches" in 30 minutes. That's bound to be a long half-hour. It might well have been the pizza baker from next door who brings us a replacement scooter after 2 hours.
Conclusion: the "pizza mechanic" waits for hours more with the broken scooter for the lorry that's supposed to collect him, we have covered 220 kilometres like in "Easy Rider", and the "Bolaven Plateau" stays in our memory just as it looks on the advertising flyer.

From Pakse (N13), over the Mekong bridge and the "New Road", we reach the town of Champasak and the temple complex of "Wat Phou", a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Wat Phou is an ideal stopover for us before we have to cover 100 kilometres the next day to "Khong Island". The province of Champasak lies right on the Mekong, and Wat Phou is close by at the foot of Mount Lingaparvata. The historic remains include the former royal city, and this is also where the road to Angkor Wat begins.

From Champasak we get ourselves taken to the other bank of the Mekong. The barge ferry consists of two narrow hulls held together by a few planks. This spartan float has room for 2 bikes, 2 people and 1 captain. Like a food mixer, the craft is driven through the water by a 3-metre drive shaft and a propeller. This way of getting around is chosen because of the many shallows and sandbanks.

These small boats are the only way for us to cross from one bank to the other. The privately run ferries don't have to keep to a timetable, and the price can be negotiated. A detour we don't want to miss: "Don Khong", the largest river island in the Mekong. In a barge that can float 14 people, we got to the "beach". A change of clothes behind the bushes, followed by a bold leap into the water. So you don't get caught in the dangerous current of the Mekong, the beach is secured with a 15-metre rope. The river water just a few metres away pulls as hard as a counter-current system in a swimming pool. Pure nature – getting our tired legs going again.

It's only 30 km to the Cambodian border at "Veun Kham". We leave Laos with memories of a natural, varied country and our encounter with one of the greatest rivers in the world.

Now we're looking forward to Cambodia.

/berichte/malaysia.title: Malaysia
/berichte/malaysia.html:
Malaysia
2 - 12 January + 22 January - 3 February 2013

2 – 12 January 2013 (part 1)

One hard push on the pedals, and the chain on Alexandre's Koga has snapped for the 4th time. While Claudia deals with the entry formalities, Alexandre is busy behind the immigration hut fitting new chain links.
Entry stamp for Malaysia received, repair finished, keep cycling!

There are still 800 kilometres to go to the Singapore border. We had planned our route along the better-developed west coast. The last-minute decision to extend our travel adventure to "Borneo" (Kalimantan) brings new momentum to things. So we cycle along the east coast through the states of Kuala Terengganu, Pahang and Kuantan. They are among the most varied regions of Malaysia. The heavy monsoon rains are responsible for flooded roads and closed resorts. Do they still exist, the long palm-fringed sandy beaches that haven't yet been overrun by mass tourism?

The "Perhentian Islands" are surely among the most beautiful islands. With our bikes, though, getting across is awkward. During the monsoon season there are fewer ferries, which could mean an unexpectedly long stay on the island. We stay on the mainland and let ourselves be surprised by Kuantan and Cherating to the south and the beach of Tanjung Jara further north. But first, our short cut of several kilometres at "Pak Bai" from Thailand to Malaysia had to be crossed by ferry.

We're spared nothing: the remaining 30 kilometres to Kota Bharu are dominated by monsoon storms. Even our rain capes were no match for the heavy rain, so we reached the hotel soaked to the skin. In our air-conditioned room we deal with outstanding office work, like writing the travel report, choosing photos and updating the website, while it rains non-stop outside.

Everything has to be "earned": the distances we covered each day were over 100 kilometres and took a lot of strength. From Mersing to the border there was an endless corrugated stretch to cover. 135 kilometres of up and down, countless hills adding up to 1,400 metres of climbing, reminded us of Argentina (South America 2009). From our hotel room in Johor Bahru we can already see our "destination port". Now there are only 30 kilometres left to the bustling centre where life happens. Singapore is within reach.

After a week in Singapore (see the travel report) we ride back to Malaysia. According to one report, the western border crossing, Tuas – Gelang Patah, is closed to bicycles. So that we aren't turned back at customs, we choose the longer way via Kota Bharu, to then reach Melaka on the west coast.

22 January – 3 February 2013 (part 2)
In just 2 days we reach Melaka, the oldest coastal town in Malaysia. It lies about 200 kilometres north-west of Singapore on the Strait of Malacca and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Protected from storms by a ring of small islands, this port was once a thriving trading place for ships sailing from India to China. Because the water isn't deep enough, Melaka has lost its importance for ocean-going ships today, and is now only suitable for coastal shipping.

Strolling along the Melaka River and climbing St Paul's Hill soon gave us a first impression of this historic town. We noticed the colonial-era buildings, so untypical of the country. The ruins of the "Porta de Santiago" from Portuguese rule (1511–1641), the gabled roofs and "Christ Church" from Dutch rule (1641–1824), and other sights from British rule (1824–1957). Until independence in 1957, the town and the Malay Peninsula belonged to the British colonial empire. Of course "St Paul's Church", the "Red Square", "Queen Victoria's Fountain" and the "Stadthuys" didn't escape our camera either.

The last kilometres to the capital, Kuala Lumpur, were a bit awkward. The road layout, disrupted by several construction sites, caused quite a lot of confusion for us and the GPS. Finding our way around "KL", as the Malays call Kuala Lumpur, wasn't easy. Probably someone slept through the road planning. The name Kuala Lumpur means "muddy confluence" of two rivers. The name comes from the rivers Klang and Gombak and was given by the Chinese when they founded the city in 1857.

At the Swiss Garden Residence we found suitable accommodation for the next 5 days. A spacious kitchen, a "living and sleeping room", and enough space to pack the bikes into boxes. As usual, we had a few kilos too much again, which had to be sent home by post. Until our onward flight to Sabah (Borneo), we passed the time feasting on sushi and sightseeing. There isn't much to see in Kuala Lumpur, and yet there was a lot going on. Chinese New Year celebrations were just around the corner. Coloured lanterns, magic trees and, once again, deafening firecrackers weren't missing.

In this metropolis of 1.5 million people you meet the most diverse cultures and religions. You see Christian church towers, the minarets of mosques, Chinese pagodas and Indian temples. Alongside the houses of the historic past, more and more new buildings shape Kuala Lumpur's progress.

By now our equipment is packed and ready for the flight, and there's still plenty of time to walk to the best-known sights. First we want to get a 360-degree view over Kuala Lumpur from the 421-metre-high Menara TV tower. At 276 metres there's a platform that is the highest viewpoint in the city. In just a few seconds, one of the 4 lifts takes us up to the dizzying observation deck, with a view of the twin skyscrapers of the oil company Petronas. 7 metres higher there's also a revolving restaurant.

On foot again, 2 kilometres away, we come to the gigantic Petronas Towers. At 452 metres, they are the tallest twin towers in the world. The golden triangle around the complex, the centre of the city, also offers a lively nightlife. All 1,200 visitor tickets, a limited daily allocation, are already sold out. The price of 80 ringgit seems rather too expensive to us compared with the Menara, at 47 ringgit and with a better view. We skip this high flight and go one floor down into "Suria KLCC", one of the largest shopping centres in Malaysia. A shopping mall of superlatives at the foot of the Petronas Towers! There's nothing you can't find here. Everything your heart desires, on several floors. Goods in every price range, from sinfully expensive designer brands to postcards.

At the Pavilion, another multi-storey mall, we come across a sticky speciality. The unique sweet Sticky is probably one of the sweetest temptations of Australian origin. In front of this production stand, lots of onlookers gather, cameras in hand, to capture the work of the highly skilled confectioners. Before the eyes of the watchers, the most beautiful and delicious Sticky candies are made for almost every occasion. There seem to be no limits to the variations in colour, shape and flavour. At the time, the Chinese New Year designs were the attraction. We couldn't resist this sweet either, and helped ourselves generously from the tasting bowl.

At "Sushi Tei", which by now we have chosen as our favourite place to eat and meet, Tisha and Simon are waiting for us for a week of mountain biking in Borneo. In the rainforest, with bikeandtours, we want to track down proboscis monkeys and orangutans.
