/berichte/panama.title: Panama
/berichte/panama.html:
Panama
27 November - 10 December 2008

Panama lies at the narrowest point of Central America and, through the 80-kilometre-long Panama Canal, links the Pacific with the Atlantic. Panama City owes its present-day prosperity to the canal, built in 1903 with the help of the USA. Liberal tax and banking laws have favoured its rise to an international financial centre.

One in five sailing yachts in the world sails under the Panamanian flag. Tourism has not spread as much in Panama as in other Central American countries. The climate is hot and humid, and there is a lot of rain. In Colón, on the Caribbean side, there are rain showers almost every day. We spend a few days in Panama City to see some of the sights, like the "Puente de las Américas", the "Miraflores" locks, Panama's "Ciudad Vieja" (old town) and much more.

Happily, unlike the border between Nicaragua and Costa Rica, the border crossing from Costa Rica into Panama takes place on asphalt. Crossing is free of charge. However, the "Salida" (exit) and "Entrada" (entry) are 100 metres apart. We spotted the counters right away because of the long queues of people crossing the border. With the help of an official, we are allowed to jump the queue as "cycling globetrotters" and get all the formalities done straight away. Our bike clothes, and the excuse that we wanted to reach a hotel before the rain, got us processed quickly and sent off with a friendly "buen viaje". In the border area of "Paso Canoas" there is a duty-free zone. You can buy almost anything, but at first we can't find a supermarket or minimarket to top up our water supply. People are hectic, and life seems chaotic to us. After searching for a long time, we finally come across a shelf with the PET bottles we are after.

Paso Canoas – David:
After a short descent, it's 30 kilometres not steeply, but steadily, uphill. On a boring dual carriageway made of concrete, we reach the "top of the pass" after 2.5 hours. There are another 25 kilometres to David, mostly downhill with a few short climbs. In pouring rain, wearing flip-flops, a sleeveless T-shirt and short cycling shorts, and pushed by a tailwind to speeds of up to 40 km/h, we soon reach the town of David. Soaked to the skin (even inside the waterproof Ortlieb front panniers, water had collected), we find the hotel "Gran Nacional". Our 2 tyres leave a brownish trail of water through the hotel lobby. At reception we are handed warm towels straight away. We spend 2 nights "drying out" and cleaning our equipment in a not-so-cheap double room.

Several times a day, long, heavy downpours pelt down and leave whole streets under water. We use this stay to prepare for the bad weather and the onward journey to Panama City.

David - Santiago:
This stretch seems especially worth mentioning because there are so few places to buy food or spend the night. This extremely exhausting route of over 200 kilometres has to be split into at least 2 – 3 daily stages.

"Hardcore" bike-toreros manage the distance David – Tolé (105 km) and Tolé – Santiago (95 km) in 2 days.

Cyclists "with good stamina" prefer David – San Félix (85 km), San Félix – top of the Tolé pass (25 km) and top of the Tolé pass – Santiago (90 km), in 3 days.

Because of the downpours, which had been going on for days and made visibility so poor that lorry drivers could overlook us, we hire a taxi for 45 US dollars to drive us from San Félix to Santiago.

Route description:

From David to San Lorenzo there is almost nowhere to buy food, nowhere to spend the night, and some climbs that should not be underestimated. The vegetation is nothing special, it is hot and sticky, and there is no shade.

San Lorenzo – San Félix:
200 metres after the "Terpel" petrol station, at the "Centro Comercial Oriente", you reach San Félix. Turn left, 2 kilometres to just past the hospital, then 100 metres to the left: at the hotel "Cholo" (no sign!) you'll find an acceptable place to stay for 10 US dollars, and a supermarket.
10 kilometres after San Félix we noticed the newly built, more comfortable "Cabinas La Isleta".

San Félix – Tolé:
Tolé lies about 2 kilometres before the top of the pass, a little off (2 km) the Pan-American Highway. There are supposed to be private rooms here, or a place to stay at the mission. At the top of the pass there is a petrol station and a small restaurant. Then comes a winding descent with several short climbs. These hurdles are exhausting and monotonous! A constant up and down for 100 kilometres. About 5 kilometres before Santiago you can sense civilisation again, because the "sodas" (small restaurants) become more frequent.

In general, after the Panamanian border there are fewer places to buy supplies than we were used to. Many towns on the Pan-American Highway lie a little away from the main road. This stretch (David – Santiago) is generally considered a "lean stretch" for bike globetrotters.

In Santiago, a rather inhospitable town, we set off again early in the morning after a night at the hotel "Gran David".

In Penonomé, at the hotel "La Pradera", which we are happy to recommend, we meet Malinka, a development worker in agriculture. She spontaneously lent us her laptop, and her invitation to a tour of the town was very welcome. Malinka knows Central America extremely well and gives us lots of good tips for the way to Gorgona.

Happily with sunshine again, we come across several exhausting "up and down" stretches. At Playa Gorgona we want to spend a few restful days and relax. Nobody was expecting us! The hotels were closed, run down, or in a state you might call "renovation". The thought of camping was also soon forgotten, because there are no suitable places for it. Many plots are locked up with a "se vende" (for sale) sign. We assume this has to do with the Americans leaving 9 years ago. A little tired, and riding aimlessly through the streets, we meet Inés, an elderly Panamanian lady, who immediately realised we were looking for somewhere to stay. Shortly afterwards, for 40 USD a night, we get a well-kept house with a garden, a children's paddling pool and everything we need. Delighted with this stroke of luck, for 4 days we feel like Panamanian homeowners.

On the hard shoulder on the way to Panama City we are often surprised by big holes more than a metre across. These are cast concrete covers, frames and all, that have been ripped out and stolen. Extremely dangerous for bicycles, and a profitable sideline for thieves. Falling into one of these holes, several metres deep, with a bike would be a disaster! One more reason not to be out at night, because holes like these are also found in the pavements.

Riding into the city by bike is said to be anything from adventurous to dangerous. Already a few kilometres before the "Puente de las Américas", the lanes of the Pan-American Highway get narrower and narrower, and there is no hard shoulder at all. It gets tight! That is why we want to take a hotel room in Arraiján, the last larger town before Panama City, and take a taxi into the heart of this metropolis of 3 million people. Arraiján only has an "hourly hotel", which doesn't appeal to us. While we are standing on a street corner looking for the way, Glen invites us into his house. His explanation that it is far too dangerous out here in the "red zone" because of youth gangs makes us think. Glen's suggestion to drive us in his pickup straight to a hotel in the city was the welcome solution for us. We get all the advice we need for our safety and are immediately equipped with pepper spray. No joke! Some districts of Panama City are off-limits for tourists! And you shouldn't be out on the streets at night either. The list of violent crimes, both in number and in variety, is worrying. In December especially, attacks are very frequent. Even so, we enjoy a safe tour of the city with Glen, who picks us up from the hotel and brings us back several times.

Many thanks to Glen for the sight seeing tour through Panama-City and your frendly help.

A "highlight" was the Panama Canal (completed in 1913), where we could watch everything happening around the Miraflores locks. Other sights: Panama City's Ciudad Vieja, the Puente de las Américas, the church "Natá de los Caballeros" built in 1522, the Puente Centenario made by Germany, and a visit to Glen's brother, a well-known builder of dugout canoes. These 4-seater boats of fine hardwood are made for a 3-day international "Ocean to Ocean Race" through the Panama Canal. All handmade! Glen's whole family are keen canoeists and have already won several prizes and titles. After 5 days in Panama City and almost 4,000 kilometres through Central America, we decide to spend Christmas in Florida.

Our recommendation for cycling globetrotters:
The Ortlieb front pannier, folded 3 times with the closure at the top, is not watertight in extreme downpours. Pull the closure down tight with the carrying strap, or cover the bags with rubbish sacks.

A rain poncho is useless! The Central American climate is too hot and too humid. Because you sweat, the plastic gets just as wet inside as outside in no time. Careful: heat build-up can make you feel sick.

"Flip-flops" make the ideal substitute for shoes. Changing into them early saves using up lots of toilet paper to dry your shoes (one roll per shoe).


After 520 kilometres we leave Panama with these memories:

Glen: a friend who showed us Panama City and its sights

Playa Gorgona: a restful week in our rented "Panamanian home"

A transit country: from Costa Rica to Colombia, not very attractive for cyclists

Rain showers: constant and heavy! Reached the hotel soaked to the skin, in "flip-flops"

The Miraflores locks: the link from the Pacific to the Atlantic

Panama's Ciudad Vieja: a "don't miss", but to be enjoyed with caution

The Pan-American Highway: boring, monotonous, countless exhausting "ups and downs"

David - Santiago: a 200-kilometre lean stretch with nowhere to buy supplies

Lanes and pavements: dangerous holes left by stolen cast covers

The canoe builder and his hardwood boats, each made from a single tree trunk

/berichte/paraguay.title: Paraguay
/berichte/paraguay.html:
Paraguay
13 - 24 June 2009

From Puerto Suárez (Bolivia), via Corumbá (Brazil), after 100 kilometres we reach Puente Morinho (Brazil) and take a boat to Porto Esperança (Brazil). Assuming we would board our ship to Asunción there, we enjoy the ride in a river taxi on the Río Paraguay. You can quickly tell how fast the river is flowing from the "water lilies" that have been torn loose. In places these drifting plants cover large areas of the waterway. Our boatman has to choose his route carefully ahead of time so he can get through the gaps in time. A stop at the railway viaduct gives us a fantastic view out over the Río Paraguay.

After 40 minutes we reach Porto Esperança. What a shock! Where is the port? It seems that apart from us and the mosquitoes, nobody ever strays out here. Yes, yes, the boatman proudly confirms, this is Porto Esperança in Brazil. Dusk has already fallen, and the question is where we will spend the night. Miguel sees our dismay and takes us to his friend, who lives on the riverbank. Once again we are delighted by South American helpfulness. The whole family helps unload and carries our bags into a 4-bed room made ready at short notice. 2 beds are made up with fresh sheets for us. The boys have carried the mattresses from the other 2 beds into the next room. In the kitchen, Mama is already cooking, so our hunger will soon be over too.

Even the best planning can literally "fall into the water". We are on the wrong riverbank. The ship we were expecting leaves from Puerto Esperanza in Paraguay, which is about 200 kilometres further downstream and can only be reached from here by water. What's more, it only sails to Asunción once a week, on Fridays at 07:00, so not for another 5 days. Our host would take us further downstream to the port in the morning. A 5-hour boat trip: 140 litres of petrol plus 100 USD is what the fun would cost us. There is only one sensible solution! Back to Puente Morinho, where there are also just a few lonely huts, the petrol station and the bridge.

Where there's a "petrol pump", there's bound to be a lorry going to the next bus terminal. A lift soon comes along, and we are taken to Miranda, 160 kilometres away. We don't understand Portuguese, and speaking it is even more out of the question. Sign language and the help of a Spanish-speaking local soon get us onto a coach for another 270 kilometres to Campo Grande. At the big bus terminal, where most of Brazil's routes meet, we have to change to get to Asunción, 1,000 kilometres away. At 06:00 in the morning, after a 14-hour night journey, before dawn has broken, we cycle into the city centre, 8 kilometres away.

Asunción, the capital of Paraguay, with 600,000 inhabitants, didn't offer us much apart from lots of dangerous potholes in the asphalt. On our walk around town, the "Panteón de los Héroes" with its 2 guards caught our eye. This magnificent domed building was turned into a war memorial after it was completed in 1936. Impossible to miss are the government palace and the slums right in front of it. The slums stretch down to the banks of the Río Paraguay and are watched over by the Policía Nacional. The contrast could not be more extreme! The people in government enjoy a sensational view, and those on the margins can't even afford windows for their wooden shacks.

The old railway station, which in 1856 was one of the first on the South American continent, also stands abandoned and derelict. Just one street away is the "Plaza Uruguaya". A shocking picture of misery, rubbish and plastic-sheet tents. We can't understand how such a place of misery in the middle of Paraguay's capital can be called "Uruguaya". This patch of ground, the size of a football pitch, is home to 50 – 100 shelters, their families and a handful of toilet huts. This misery, too, is guarded all round by the police, as a precaution so that no tourist can wander in. Two days in Asunción were enough for us; we move on to Ciudad del Este, 360 kilometres to the east.

The "Ruta Internacional" leads out of the city as a dual carriageway at first, but it soon becomes a single lane each way. Everything, absolutely everything, is moved across the country on this main road. The volume of traffic is enormous. Even on the other side of the road there is traffic coming towards you. Wherever there is a hard shoulder, which is the case on almost the whole highway, "microsleep bumps" have been built in. These ridges of asphalt laid across the direction of travel are so unpleasant for us cyclists that we have to stop before riding over them. So we are always caught between fast traffic, an asphalt bump, or oncoming vehicles squeezing through to get to their house.

All along the route from Asunción to Ciudad del Este there are enough places to buy supplies, and at the neighbouring farms, the "estancias", you can usually find a spot for the tent too. After 4 days, with more frustration than pleasure, we reach Ciudad del Este, the fastest-growing city in the country. The "Puente de la Amistad" (Friendship Bridge) across the Río Paraná and the building of the hydroelectric power station brought the city its boom. By now 300,000 people live here, in a smugglers' town where anything that makes money can be bought and sold. Electronic goods, spirits, perfumes, clothes and copies of brand-name goods are offered at rock-bottom prices.

At the weekend the city seems deserted, which is ideal for us to cycle to the 40-metre-high waterfalls on the Paraná river. Ciudad del Este is very central. The Brazilian border, the "Saltos del Monday" waterfalls and the Itaipú power station are all within 10 kilometres. The lively driving style in the city centre, however, needs strong nerves and a constant readiness to brake!

The largest hydroelectric power station in the world!
On a chassis on wheels that calls itself the "Hernandarias" regional bus, we head for the Itaipú mega power station, 10 kilometres away. In the auditorium there is an information film (available in 3 languages), followed by a tour of the site in a luxury coach. Seeing this brilliant pioneering achievement is an absolute "must", and, believe it or not, it's free!

The Itaipú power station was opened in May 1991 as a "monument to solidarity, cooperation and integration". The agreement of 1966 laid the foundation stone for this binational venture between Brazil and Paraguay. The Paraná river was to be used equally by both for generating energy. The contract went to an international consortium of IECO (USA) and ELC (Italy). Building this gigantic project took 16 years (1975 -1991) and reportedly cost 22 billion dollars.

Figures:
The 1.2 million construction plans, drawings and materials lists, stacked on top of each other, would be as high as a 50-storey building. The 12.3 million cubic metres of concrete would be enough to build 210 football stadiums. With the iron and structural steel used, you could build 380 Eiffel Towers. The flood spillway, at 62.2 million cubic metres, carries 40 times the flow of the Iguazú Falls and reaches a speed of 120 km/h. The reservoir covers 1,350 square kilometres and stretches for 170 km, making it 2.3 times bigger than Lake Geneva. 20 Francis turbines (10 for Brazil, 10 for Paraguay) reach a total output of 14 million megawatts. One turbine can supply a city of 1.5 million people. At its highest point the dam is 196 m high.

On the way back to Ciudad del Este, "El Museo de la Tierra Guaraní" and its zoo are not to be missed. They show the culture of the Guaraní people and the wildlife of the continent, preserved in display cases and alive in enclosures. We were told several times that wild mountain lions, jaguars and panthers live in Paraguay (in the Chaco), so it's dangerous to cross this region. These animals wouldn't leave cyclists off the menu either.

For us Paraguay was a "transit country" on the way to the Iguazú Falls (Brazil) and on to Argentina. Apart from the Itaipú hydroelectric power station and the Saltos del Monday waterfalls, which were the "saving" highlights for us, Paraguay didn't offer us much more.

After 380 kilometres we leave Paraguay with these memories:

Slums in the middle of Asunción's city centre

Dangerous tigers, panthers and jaguars in the Chaco

A trip on the Río Paraguay

Our odyssey to Porto Esperança, Brazil

The Saltos del Monday waterfalls

Itaipú, the largest hydroelectric power station in the world

For us a transit country, comparable to Panama (each with one gigantic structure)

Biker info for the route

-
Active (5 days of riding)
380 kilometres
-
Transfer to Asunción (bus)
450 kilometres
-
Total climbing
450 m
-
Average speed
18.1 km/h
-
Riding time in motion
21 hours

/berichte/peru.title: Peru
/berichte/peru.html:
Peru
24 March - 9 May 2009

Macará to Trujillo
The border crossing at Macará was free of charge, free of red tape and free of crowds. After 92 not entirely flat kilometres, in 38 degrees of heat, we reach the town of "Tambo Grande". Our arrival in this small town of 20,000 people is dominated by a 20-metre-wide passage under a barrel and an abrupt change from asphalt to fine dust centimetres deep. Several kilometres before the town we had already noticed the many three-wheeled "tuk-tuks". They dominate the streets, making up 90% of all passenger and goods vehicles. On these converted 125 - 200 cc motorbikes, with seats and room for loads, everything gets transported: families of five, schoolchildren, pigs and goats, and whatever else fits on the back.

And somewhere for us to sleep? We ask: "¿Dónde hay un hotel?" The answer: "Este es un hotel – es el mejor de la ciudad" (this is a hotel – the best in town). Great! First we carry all our luggage and the bikes up 60 steps to the 2nd floor. The room: a missing window pane, a door with a generous hole in the wall beside it for ventilation, damp, hot, mouldy….. and the fan on its wobbly legs had to be repaired first, so we could sleep at all.

Without breakfast (chicken with rice 3 times a day is too much for us), we leave Tambo Grande heading for Chulucanas. It turns into one of the most adventurous short stretches ever, just 38 kilometres. Yesterday's dusty roads have turned into mud tracks overnight. The choice on offer was 3 days on asphalt or 1 day on a dirt road. We decide on the short route. After 2 kilometres of bumpy track, dotted with countless mud puddles, nothing moves any more. Wheels, drivetrain and brakes all jam. A sticky mixture of water and sand has built up between the mudguards and the tyres, and it keeps getting harder. We wait at the roadside for a lift and soon find room on a pickup where 4 people are already sitting.

All sorted? Far too easy!

After 16 kilometres our ride comes to an end. The driver apologises: this river can't be crossed by car, he will try to call his brother on the other side. Shortly afterwards, a tractor rattles through the water. Load everything on and change banks. The front wheels sink, the alternator scoops up water…. if only this goes well! On the other bank there is no stop; instead we are driven another 300 metres behind a house. Only here are we unloaded, and being told to disappear as quickly as possible makes it clear to us that the situation here could be "dicey" for us. This crossing cost us 10 soles (3 USD), which we handed over to the farmer with relief. At the next "washing facility", a puddle in the road, we remove the mud baked hard by the blazing sun and ride on.

No! After 3 kilometres another river has to be crossed. Instead of a tractor, mules with two-wheeled carts are now used. The crossing is supposed to cost 2 soles per mule (about 80 centimes). Once on the other bank, we pay. It soon turns out that we gave the money to the "wrong" driver, and the "mule owner" now wants to be paid. Cost: 6 soles – what the heck! Our stomachs are rumbling; let's quickly get the remaining kilometres behind us so we can eat soon.

This can't be true! There are 2 more rivers to cross. Not as deep or as fast-flowing, but still: shoes off, and carry the panniers and bikes piece by piece across the water. Although the brown road soup is gradually firming up, we still ride through mud holes as deep as our rims. Slowly we get closer to civilisation again. By now it is already 16:00. Have we arrived? By chance we notice the word "Chulucanas" on a rubbish bin standing by the road. The hotel is just around the corner, and we move into our room. Shower, change, our first steps outside the hotel, and what…..? An interview with us? A reporter from the local radio asks us for a chat, holding out his voice recorder. We are happy to agree and tell him about our journey….. and to top it all, our departure in 2 days is to be documented and filmed by the television.

What a day! Our well-earned sleep doesn't last long. Several crickets that have fallen through the wide-meshed ventilation grille get on our nerves with their chirping. Without further ado, we change rooms. A big mistake: the street noise at night in the room next door is unbearable. In the end we prefer to put up with the crickets and move back, because there is nothing better. At 23:00 this day finally comes to an end.

There is nothing special to report about the stretch Chulucanas – Olmos – Chiclayo. The next 3 days are all about pedalling as many kilometres as possible. Up to Motupe everything is green and farmed; after that we see a sudden change to drought and dry, hard-baked ground. The temperature is between 35 – 39 degrees, and the closer we get to the Pacific coast, the stronger the headwind. There is a constant south-westerly wind, which slows us down to 13 km/h for the last 40 kilometres and takes an enormous amount of effort.

In Chiclayo we take a "day off" to prepare the rest of the route.

From Chiclayo to Trujillo there are 220 kilometres to cover through desert. The Pan-American Highway, with only a few changes of direction, takes us between dunes and the odd rocky outcrop, and above all through vast expanses of sand without any vegetation. Between the settlements there are usually 50 kilometres of uninhabited land with nowhere to buy anything. Relieved by the "bad" weather, we get to cross this otherwise scorching wasteland under cloud, without a headwind, and with the odd cooling shower. After 108 kilometres we reach the town of Pacasmayo on the Pacific. A place we can recommend! With excellent food and a cosy hotel right on the beach, we enjoy the rest of the afternoon. The remaining 112 kilometres to Trujillo are largely unspectacular, apart from a few rice and sugar cane fields where irrigation is possible.

Trujillo, with its tempting reputation as the city of "eternal spring", is Peru's third-largest city (1.5 million inhabitants). As in most larger cities, the traffic here is "Wild West". Very few traffic lights control the traffic. Honking and pushing decide who goes first. Anyone who doesn't "play along" gets left behind and arrives late. It seems as if the little ones are given a horn in their cradle before they can even walk. With whistles we get the attention we need and fight our way successfully through the chaos.

For once without stress, we prefer to spend a day of archaeology and culture on the back seat of a taxi (30 USD). We visit the Huaca de la Luna (Temple of the Moon), the Museo de Sitio, the Palacio Tschudi, the Huaca del Dragón or Templo Arco Iris (Rainbow Temple), and Chan Chan. The Huaca del Sol (Temple of the Sun), the largest pyramid ruin, is not yet open to the public. A "huaca" is a burial site or a pyramid-like sanctuary, usually dedicated to the moon. The smaller Temple of the Moon, with an English-speaking guide, brought us closer to the culture of the Moche, who lived around 200 AD, and we liked it best. The Moche built the highest adobe pyramids in South America. Even today, houses are still built with mud blocks (adobe bricks), usually combined with fired bricks. The ruins of Chan Chan, of the "Chimú" who lived around 1000 AD, are surely fascinating for archaeologists, but for us they were rather weathered, washed-out remains of an old coastal kingdom.

We end the 4-hour tour in Huanchaco, 10 kilometres north-west of Trujillo. Here on the beach you can watch the reed boats (caballitos de totora), which look a bit like standing stones and are hired out as a tourist attraction. They share the breaking Pacific waves with the modern boards of the surfers. A tip: enjoy some fish specialities in a nearby restaurant.

The die is cast, and we have made our decision:

The Lima – Huancayo railway is a technical marvel built by the Chinese (1870 – 1893). With a length of only 160 kilometres, it has the highest railway station, at 4,781 metres above sea level. Our research into the reopening of this railway confirms two tourist trips a month. Getting the sought-after tickets is not easy, and for us they can only be booked in Lima. So we decide to take the bus (8 hours) straight to Lima to reserve 2 seats in time. From the terminus in Huancayo we will "carry on cycling" over 4 passes and 637 kilometres to Abancay.

Lima
In the comfortable coach of "LINEA", we reach Lima after 8 hours, mostly through uninhabited desert. The "Nacional 1" runs right through the "pueblos jóvenes" (slums) and the most troubled districts of Lima. Choosing the bus, with the bikes in the luggage hold, spares us the stress of riding into this sprawling city of 7 million people.

The districts that are safe for tourists (at least during the day) are Miraflores, with hotels, restaurants and elegant shops. There is also good accommodation in San Isidro. The centre, the "Ciudad Histórica", with most of the sights, appealed to us most, and here you can also find accommodation (not only backpacker hostels) for every budget.

A walking tour of the old town takes about 6 hours and gives you an illuminating impression of colonial and present-day Lima. On Sundays, when most of the city's people are at the beach, the centre seems deserted, which is when you get the best photos. A good starting point is the newly restored and most beautiful square in the city, the Plaza Mayor. This is also where the processions and military parades take place, with the historic buildings as a backdrop.

No other South American city offers a greater variety of museums and exhibitions than Lima.

We especially recommend:
The National Museum, which presents the different cultures of ancient Peru from the beginnings up to the Inca period.
The "Museo del Oro" is considered the richest in South America after the Gold Museum in Bogotá. It displays the magnificent gold treasures of the Chimú and Inca cultures.
The church of San Francisco, built in 1546, and the Franciscan monastery attached to it (a UNESCO World Heritage Site) are among the most beautiful and largest colonial buildings in Lima. The monastery is famous for its many tiled murals, its stucco ceilings, its historic writings and above all its catacombs. In 1951, underground passages were discovered that lead to catacombs more than 300 years old. Until 1808, more than 70,000 dead were buried in them. A guided tour (unfortunately photos are not allowed) shows us neatly sorted and stacked skulls and bones.

The rural exodus from the highlands to Lima is an acute problem in Peru. The districts "Cono Sur, Cono Norte and Cono Este" surround the city and stretch far into the desert hills. It is a dreary picture of reed and tin shacks and unfinished stone buildings. About a third of Lima's inhabitants live here, in the shimmering hot desert sand. There is not enough running water, and the electricity supply is poor. The "newcomers" hope for better living conditions in Lima. They are wrong! Many hire themselves out as labourers, scrap collectors, porters or street vendors on the streets of Lima.

The absolute top favourite is a ride on the "Tren". The Lima – Huancayo railway is a technical marvel, planned by Henry Meiggs and built by the Chinese between 1870 and 1893. It is the highest railway line, with the highest station, "Galera", at 4,781 metres above sea level. Before Galera is the longest tunnel on the 160-kilometre line, at 1,117 metres. Up to Huancayo the train crosses 45 bridges and goes through 67 tunnels and over 1,000 curves and switchbacks. Many of the steep climbs are tackled by reversing (zigzagging). Until 1992 a passenger train left Lima station every day and reached Huancayo after a 12-hour journey. Since 1998 there have again been occasional tourist excursion trains, now twice a month.

Unfortunately we had no chance of getting two of the sought-after tickets. The train had already been fully booked for 2 weeks. So we leave Lima heading south, through the hectic streets and suburbs, making for Paracas and the Islas Ballestas.

Tip: always show your passport with your entry papers. That way you get the room at the net price without having to pay the 19% VAT. Taxis are cheap and always better than public transport.

More information about Lima can be found at: www.munlima.gob.pe

Important information for getting "Tren tickets":
WONG market or METRO market in Lima
or directly at www.fcca.com.pe , email: reservas@fcca.com,pe , tel: 226 63 63 222

Bus travel in Peru: www.adonde.com/turismo/buses.php

Islas Ballestas, the Huacachina oasis and the Nazca Lines
As a "substitute" for the Galápagos Islands, which we didn't visit, we decide to go on a wildlife-watching tour by boat. This much cheaper option was a great experience and gave us a relaxing day out. The Paracas Peninsula and the Islas Ballestas, with a total area of 335,000 hectares, form the Paracas National Reserve. There you find plenty of sea lions, blue-footed boobies, pelicans, penguins and other marine mammals. On the peninsula there is also a large geoglyph, the "Candelabro de Paracas", which is similar to the Nazca Lines. The candelabra of Paracas probably served as a landmark for seafarers to navigate by.

Pisco: on 15 August 2007, an earthquake destroyed 85% of this picturesque little colonial town. In this magnitude 8.0 earthquake, which lasted an unusually long 2 minutes, more than 500 people died and 1,500 were injured. In the town's largest church, San Clemente, alone, over 90 people died. All that remained of the church were two stone columns and the dome. The archaeological treasures and cultural monuments of the Ica region were badly affected. In the museums of Ica and Paracas, walls collapsed and display cases were destroyed. Valuable archaeological objects, including mummies from early Peru, suffered irreparable damage. The bizarre rock formations in the Paracas nature reserve were badly damaged, and one of the most famous, the "Cathedral", has disappeared. To this day, Pisco still consists of many fields of rubble, and the damage has still not been fully cleared up.

The Huacachina oasis
Just 5 kilometres west of Ica lies the Huacachina oasis, said to be known for its healing waters. For us, this little desert resort is a chance to "hang out" a bit and watch the sandboarders. The many dune buggies, carrying up to 20 passengers, can't be missed with their deafening noise. Huacachina offers plenty of accommodation from 3 – 200 US dollars in a surprisingly small area.

Huacachina - Palpa (100 km)
After the first 15 kilometres, at Santiago, there is the last "sure" chance to stock up before the 60-kilometre desert crossing. After 50 kilometres (half the day's distance) 2 radio masts come into view, and there are 2 "kiosks" there with drinks and limited food. Whether these huts will still be standing in future is questionable. What is certain, though, is that we need 0.75 litres of fluid per hour per person. The 60-kilometre desert crossing, almost all of it dead straight, with no shade and 43 degrees of heat, took us 3 hours. Ideally, you set off at sunrise, at 6 o'clock. In total we needed 5 hours from Huacachina to Palpa. The route includes 3 climbs with a total of 500 metres of ascent, a 200-metre tunnel, and a bumpy track down the mountain, dropping 250 metres, to Río Grande. At the Hospedaje Foursbi in Palpa we spend a sleepless night to the sound of disco music (every Saturday), and only find out at breakfast that there are other places to stay in town.

The Nazca Lines
On the way to Nazca (25 kilometres after Palpa) we visit the Maria Reiche Museum. Maria Reiche (1903 – 1998) is known for uncovering the Nazca Lines. The museum, her former home, seems a little run-down to us, and the exhibition rather thin. For the next 30 kilometres we ride right over these scratched images without noticing a thing. A viewing platform gives us the chance to photograph 2 of these mysterious glyphs. In Nazca, countless travel agencies offer sightseeing flights in "Cessnas". An experience of 35 – 60 minutes (60 – 90 US dollars) that needs careful thought. People with sensitive stomachs or a fear of flying are strongly advised against this adventure. As compensation, we recommend a visit to the "Museo Regional de Ica", where the model of the Nazca Lines gives a better overview than from the air. Postcards replace the photos that couldn't be "shot" because of nausea.

Nazca to Cusco
Now we have to cross the "Cordillera Occidental". Several passes up to 4,300 metres high and altiplanos at 4,500 metres lie ahead of us. A brutally tough undertaking over 455 kilometres from Nazca to Abancay. The 155-kilometre stretch from Nazca to Puquio, with 2,600 metres of climbing, a road with countless hairpin bends, is considered extremely difficult and dangerous. Lorries and buses, which have to cut the corners for lack of space, labour up the mountain and leave a cyclist no room at all. What's more, according to the locals the top of the pass is at 5,000 metres, so altitude sickness is another danger for us. So we decide to take a taxi, a minibus, and get ourselves some "soroche pills" to survive the rapidly rising altitude and the Abra Condorcenca without problems. With every metre we gain in height, it gets greener, and the picture of "grey elephant backs" gradually changes into lush pasture and dense vegetation. Unique, and a completely new experience for us. After 3½ hours we reach Puquio at 3,214 metres. 2 days of acclimatisation, buying supplies, getting advice from the locals and drawing up an elevation profile are what we need to get to Abancay.

Everything's ready, off we go. After 2 hours, grey clouds roll in; the almost daily afternoon rain will soon start, so we pitch our camp for the night at 3,700 metres. Tasty spaghetti is on the menu. Cooking at this altitude turns the pasta into a sticky lump. The sauce doesn't help much either, because by mistake we bought pizza sauce instead of tomato sauce. By now it has become bitterly cold, and at 18:00 we crawl into our sleeping bags. The first signs of altitude sickness don't let us rest. The hours until dawn seem endless.

The higher you go, the longer everything takes; breathing becomes laboured, and headaches are an unpleasant side effect. To ease these symptoms we chew coca leaves, ride on, and conquer the highest point at 4,500 metres. At this altitude you can't think straight any more, and you only take in the landscape in passing. Completely drained, and by now also suffering from nausea and nosebleeds, we get a small van to take us to the next village further down. It's too late to carry on at this time of day; dusk has already fallen.

At the only hospedaje in Pampamarca (4,000 metres) we get soup with something in it, biscuits for dessert, coca tea and a place to sleep. A room with no water, candlelight (electricity is too expensive) and a long-drop toilet behind the house: that's our bed for the night. Still, we are relieved to have found somewhere to stay, and we fall exhausted onto 2 sagging mattresses on an indefinable base. The department of Apurímac is considered the least developed region of Peru.

Altitude sickness didn't spare us either. Even the best preparation, with elevation profiles, distances and time planning, is no guarantee for cycle tourists of crossing these high plateaus without risk. To reach a lower region, we would have had to climb another 500 metres. The coach in the early morning hours comes in very handy. In a comfortable reclining seat in first class, with the bikes stowed in the luggage hold, we reach Chalhuanca at 2,900 metres. Free of symptoms, we now let our bikes roll 100 kilometres downhill without any effort. Only now can we enjoy the landscape again. A liberating feeling, and a reward for all the hardships we've been through. After a final climb of 400 metres (nothing comes for free) we reach Abancay at 2,360 metres. We are looking forward to a shower, a "proper bed" and above all some peace and quiet. A wedding party, in a makeshift marquee in the hotel car park, with a 10-piece band, celebrates until 3 in the morning. Better a live band than distorted disco music: we celebrate when there's a party.

Route description Abancay - Cusco
From the centre of Abancay there is a steep climb of 400 metres. After 25 kilometres, at 3,400 m above sea level, you can get food (drinks) at a hamlet. Only after another 5 kilometres, at 3,600 m, is camping possible. Abancay (2,400 m) to Abra Sorccacasa (4,000 m), 39 kilometres, takes 5 – 6 hours of riding. The weather can change at any time. You have to expect fog, rain and cold almost every day. At night the thermometer can drop to a bitter 5 degrees. From the top of the pass it's 34 kilometres down to Curahuasi and another 19 kilometres to the bridge over the "Río Apurímac" (1,900 m)! Then comes a climb of 700 metres over 27 kilometres to Limatambo (2,600 m). Camping in the gorge is not possible for 10 kilometres after the bridge because of falling rocks and "sandfly attacks". Accommodation is only available in Curahuasi and Limatambo, which are 46 kilometres apart. From Limatambo there is a steady climb to Abra Huillque (3,600 m). This is followed by a moderate descent to Cusco (3,430 m), with one more short climb of 300 m before the city. This stretch (Limatambo – Cusco) of 85 kilometres takes about 8 hours of riding. There are hotels in Cusco in every price range.

Many thanks to our friends:

To Christian for the „lift“ and the invitation for dinner at the Hotel Eco Inn

To Dr. Eduardo for the medicine and the information about cycling in the highlands

To Ty, a friendly biker, met at Ulrikes Cafe, thank's for postage, the excellent food and the „Cicling-Brownie-Bar

To Yerald Candia, Teambike, Bicycleshop in Cusco for the perfect service and repair of our two KOGA'S

Cusco and the Sacred Valley

Cusco, officially called Qosqo (centre), lies at 3,430 m above sea level and, because of its historical importance, is surely the most interesting city in South America. Once the "navel of the world" and the heart of the Inca empire, Cusco was just as rich and powerful as Rome. Cusco's charming townscape is shaped by colonial buildings and Inca walls. In the earthquake of 1650, only the foundation walls from the Inca period survived.

Cusco, firmly in the hands of tourism (1 million visitors a year), is something you have to experience for yourself. You should plan 1 – 2 days for a tour of the city (not counting the rest day for acclimatisation!). Anyone who buys the 10-day "Boleto Turístico del Cusco" (40 USD) to visit 6 museums and the 10 surrounding ruins should plan another day on top.

Trekking the 80 or 90-kilometre Inca Trail to Machu Picchu takes 3 – 4 days. A visit to the Inca city of Machu Picchu can be done in one day by train from Cusco to Aguas Calientes, followed by a bus ride. But this day's programme is very stressful, because the train alone takes 8 hours there and back. So we recommend staying in Cusco for at least 6 days.

We put together a special "Machu Picchu programme" for ourselves, which can also be a great experience without a bike, by taxi, train and bus.

Equipped with the "Boleto Turístico", we leave Cusco on one of the main roads towards the Valle Sagrado (Sacred Valley). Here begins one of the most beautiful bike tours in South America, and along the way you get to know the most important Inca remains. About 200 metres of climbing, on cobblestones and in places so steep that pushing is the way to go, and we are at our first ruin, "Saqsaywaman". As at all accessible historic Inca sites, you should take your own photos before the tourist coaches roll in. Otherwise these unique buildings are hidden behind the bright colours of the latest "trekking fashion".

Over the next 20 kilometres come the ruins of Q'enqo, Puka Pukara and Tambomachay. All these Inca buildings are close to the road, and entry is included in the "Boleto Turístico".

After the following 25-kilometre descent, we are in Pisac, at only 3,050 m. At first this place seems a little run-down and neglected to us, so we decide to ride on through. About 2 kilometres outside Pisac, towards Urubamba, we notice the beautiful, well-kept hotel "Inti Wasi". On the spur of the moment we decide to stay here. We take a taxi to the ruins of Pisac. In our view, these remains are just as worth seeing as Machu Picchu, but much cheaper, because entry is included in the Boleto Turístico. You should on no account miss the ruins of Pisac. We recommend allowing about 3-4 hours to visit the ruins and walk back down to Pisac afterwards. Make sure you are driven to the entrance by taxi (7 USD) before 14:00, because the walk back to the village takes at least 1½ hours. The afternoon sun is just right for photos, and the remaining warmth is enough to enjoy the walk down the valley without an "alpaca fur". This walk, with only a few tourists, was a real pleasure for us.

The next 60 kilometres to Ollantaytambo, the starting point for the train to Aguas Calientes, also called Machu Picchu Pueblo, went by quickly with a tailwind. The train ride from Ollantaytambo (2,850) to Aguas Calientes (2,040) takes 1½ hours.

Tip
If you have 3 nights (2 days) available, book 1 night in Ollantaytambo, one night in Aguas Calientes and one more night in Ollantaytambo. Leaving luggage at the hotels is no problem.

We recommend a "backpacker ticket"; check the departure times in the timetable.

If you can "get hold of" a student card, don't leave it at home, because there are discounts in many places.

What Machu Picchu costs
Train Ollantaytambo – Aguas Calientes (return) 70 USD per person.

Bus Aguas Calientes – Machu Picchu (return) 14 USD per person.

Entry to Machu Picchu 40 USD per person.

Important: take enough water and food with you, as it is hugely overpriced on site!

We don't want to say much about this UNESCO-protected wonder of the world, www.machupicchu.perucultural.org.pe. A visit to this very well-preserved Inca ruin is a "must" on any trip to Peru. For those who are still fit, with good footwear, no problems with altitude and absolutely no fear of heights, there is also the free climb up Wayna Picchu (2,667 m above sea level), 2½ hours there and back. Only 400 people are admitted each day, and they have to sign in and out. For us, this climb was the highlight of the day. For the rest of Machu Picchu, we "secretly" tagged along with a guided group of tourists. We skipped the taxi ride down and walked back for 1½ hours on the Inca path to Aguas Calientes, to take the train back to Ollantaytambo.

The next day we cycle back to Urubamba (2,900 m) to tackle the winding road over a pass at 3,800 m to Chinchero. The remaining ruins of Moray and Chinchero, Moray especially, are a bit too far off our route, so we let them "rest in peace". Besides, by now we are a little saturated with Inca architecture. After 190 kilometres from Cusco and 6 days through the Sacred Valley, we are warmly welcomed back and given a room at the Hotel Eco Inn. The bikes go in for a service, Claudia to the doctor because of an infection, and Alexandre for his final treatment at the dentist. We will spend our "rest day" writing the travel report and preparing the next stage, 345 km to Puno on Lake Titicaca.

Note: In our opinion, Machu Picchu is hugely overcrowded. Everyone wants to visit these ruins. An alternative is a 5-day/4-night trek to the ruins of Choquequirao, discovered in 1834 (only bookable in Cusco). The price is about 650 USD, all inclusive, and even 5 kg of your own luggage is carried by porters. We have experienced and seen "the must", Machu Picchu. If only we had had the courage, the cash and the right footwear, we would have chosen the trek to the ruins of Choquequirao. An outdoor experience in a small group, with reliable guides, closer to nature, and the experience of walking in the footsteps of the Incas would surely have been just as good. Next time this will definitely be our top excursion.

Cusco to Puno
Ahead of us lies a very beautiful stretch with a varied landscape. The Pan-American Highway runs alongside the railway line with a moderate gradient over the "Abra La Raya" (4,338 m above sea level). A short descent of about 300 metres brings us onto the altiplano, which stretches for 150 kilometres. The road winds without climbs at 3,900 metres through several side valleys, surrounded by snow-capped peaks of 5,000 – 6,000 metres. At these altitudes, the mountain ranges seem close enough to touch.

The highland farmers still work their meagre fields mostly with hook ploughs and digging spades. Herds of llamas, sheep and cattle are usually led through the pastures by Peruvian women and kept together by dogs. On this stretch, Cusco – Juliaca, the Indigenous people unfortunately don't "take kindly" to tourism and tend to greet us with dislike and incomprehension. This may be due to their isolation, illiteracy and lack of education. Just before Santa Rosa we spot some flamingos at a shallow lagoon. Amazing that these animals have found a home at 4,000 metres. Late in the evening, after 145 kilometres, we reach the town of Puno (3,830 m above sea level) on Lake Titicaca, with a little over 100,000 inhabitants.

Lake Titicaca, covering 8,000 km², is the highest navigable lake in the world. We visit the 33-metre-long "Yavari". This steel ship, completed in 1870 and once steam-powered, now lies at anchor as a museum near Puno for the foreseeable future. The first renovation has been completed; what's still missing is a new diesel engine costing 250,000 USD. When the Yavari will carry passengers across Lake Titicaca again is uncertain.

Interesting fact:
In 1862 the parts of the ship were shipped from London round Cape Horn to "Arica", to be carried on by rail from the Pacific to "Tacna" (550 m above sea level). Between there and Puno, where the ship was to be completed, lay the Andes, with heights of up to 4,850 metres, which had to be crossed. The ship, taken apart into 2,766 pieces, was carried by mules over 6 years to Lake Titicaca, at 3,250 metres. More at www.yavari.org

For the rest of the day we take a taxi to the nearby tourist attractions. The Condor, Inca and Puma viewpoints give us excellent views over the town and out to the reed islands. Another attraction is the Uros islands. A half-hour boat ride takes us, between countless reed beds, to the "floating" Uros islands. Always floating, the islands rise by 1 – 2 metres from December to March during the rainy season. The group is made up of 80 individual islands, tied by ropes to the dry zone, and there is even a school island among them. Each island is home to 8 – 9 families and is represented by a president, and all the islands together are governed by one president. The islanders live mainly from fishing. The food they don't have, such as potatoes and fruit, they get by trading fish. An Uros islander explains to us how an island is "built". First, 4 peat-like blocks are tied together. Several thousand blocks together form the load-bearing part of the island and reach up to 1 metre deep into the water. This base is covered with another metre of reeds. And the "land" is finished. A lookout, houses of woven reeds and a cooking place are built on top. The bundles of reeds on the islands have to be repaired every six months, a necessary task which the younger generation unfortunately neglects all too often, which is why even larger reed islands regularly sink in the lake. The individual islands can reach each other by "totora boats".

After 2 days we leave Puno heading for Bolivia. There are only 150 kilometres left to the border, along Lake Titicaca.

Between Cusco and Puno we meet more cycling globetrotters:

Dorothee & Sven; South America to Alaska: www.auf-radreise.de

Japanese Tandem Bikers, travelling around the world:www.h2.dion.ne.jp/~fumiya

    The cyclists coming from Alaska cross paths here in Peru with those coming from Patagonia. There's a good chance of meeting here, and it makes for a helpful exchange of experiences about the latest state of the routes.

After 2,000 kilometres we leave Peru with these memories:

Crossing rivers by tractor and donkey cart near Tambo Grande.

Idyllic Pacasmayo on the Pacific.

The Islas Ballestas nature reserve (a little Galápagos) with seals, penguins and loads of birds.

The Huaca del Sol and Chan Chan near Trujillo.

The capital, Lima: the Ciudad Histórica with churches, cathedrals and catacombs.

The Huacachina oasis: sand dunes and lots of tourism in a tiny space near the city of Ica.

The Nazca Lines on both sides of the Pan-American Highway after three days of riding through the desert.

Our camp at 3,800 m above sea level, and altitude sickness on the altiplano at 4,500 m.

Cusco, built on the remains of the Inca walls, and the starting point for the Sacred Valley.

A carnival and artesanía parade lasting several days.

The ruins of Pisac, followed by a 1½-hour walk down the valley to the village.

The "must" (?) Machu Picchu, with the climb up Wayna Picchu and the walk back to Aguas Calientes. Overrun by tourists! An alternative is the 5-day Choquequirao trek.

The most beautiful "Peru cycling route", from Cusco to Puno, with the Abra La Raya pass and the 150 km of altiplano that follow.

Sadly we didn't see any condors, but we did spot our first flamingos, at 4,000 m above sea level.

The boat trip from Puno to the floating "Uros islands", 80 raft-like "plots of land" built of reeds.

Lake Titicaca (60% Peru, 40% Bolivia), 13 times larger than Lake Constance, and at 3,850 m above sea level the highest navigable lake in the world.

Unfortunately:
The attractive Cusco – Puno route is in places (in 2009, 100 kilometres) a bumpy track of countless patches and potholes. We found this section extremely dangerous. The highland people meet tourism with hostility: children throw stones at bicycles, the adults "greet" us with loud swearing, and vehicles harassed us with reckless overtaking.

Biker info for the route Macará - Kasani

- Active (26 days of riding) 2,012 kilometres
- Transfer (bus, car) 1,070 kilometres
- Total climbing 14,270 m
- Average speed 15.7 km/h
- Riding time in motion 128 hours

/berichte/singapur.title: Singapore
/berichte/singapur.html:
Singapore
13 - 21 January 2013

We have reached our planned destination! How time flies!

Our "destination port", the huge metropolis of Singapore, at the end of the Malay Peninsula. Since the start in Istanbul 9 months ago, we have covered 12,000 kilometres and 113,000 metres of climbing in 794 hours of riding.

The border crossing from Johor Bahru confused us. Which way to Singapore? Are the "Woodlands" already in the north of the island city? The maps we have loaded can't do "routing" – the GPS can't show us the way. We follow the sign "Motosikal", and after just 100 metres we were at the Malaysian "check-out". Now just over the bridge of the "Johor-Singapore Causeway" to Singapore immigration, followed by 30 kilometres on the perfectly built highway to Marina Bay in the south.

Our bikes stay in the garage for a week. We are staying with Pat and Brö, cycling globetrotters www.somewhereonearth.org. Their home is ideally placed for reaching most of the sights quickly and easily on the well-developed transport system (MRT). As well as updating our website, we have plenty of time to visit the following attractions:

The Merlion is the emblem of the South-East Asian metropolis of Singapore. There are two of them: a 37-metre-high statue on the leisure island of Sentosa and a smaller one on the Singapore River. The name Merlion is a made-up word combining "mermaid" and "lion". A legendary creature with a lion's head and a fish's body, symbolising strength and a bond with the sea.

Sentosa Island was an important British military base before 1945; today it is a five-square-kilometre tourist pleasure island. From "VivoCity" we took the Sentosa Express, a monorail, to reach the attractions on Sentosa in just a few minutes. Lots of restaurants, bars and three beaches make for plenty of "chilling". Every year Siloso Beach hosts "ZoukOut", where around 20,000 party-goers from all over the world party through the night. We strolled back on foot along the Sentosa Boardwalk to HarbourFront, past architectural masterpieces and with a magnificent view of the Singapore River.

Underwater World opened in 1991 and is the largest walk-through tropical oceanarium in the world. It is on Sentosa Island and is mostly underground. It lets you marvel at the wonders of the sea from a fish's point of view. An underwater tunnel shows visitors more than 6,000 sea creatures from every part of the world.

Little India, Arab Street, Chinatown and Orchard Road
A "must"! Everyone talks about these districts. We expected more than what we got to see. We often wondered whether we were in the wrong district. We are convinced you can discover more attractive streets and corners than the ones suggested in the "to do and to see" brochures.

When we arrived in the Little India district, we felt as if we had been catapulted into another world. This district is packed with shops, souvenir stalls and gold dealers. It also wasn't as clean as other parts of the city.

After a walk of just 1.3 km from "Little India" we reached Arab Street. It stands out for its unique architecture. The Arabs were the first traders to settle here in Singapore. More and more immigrants of Arab Muslim origin followed. Soon this district was named after Arab Street. A big bazaar with shop after shop. For little money you can buy basketware and leather goods, brass, jewellery, perfume and textiles from all over Asia. Customs such as the call of the muezzin and veiled women are all part of life around "Arab Street".

Singapore's unique Chinatown should be enjoyed by day as well as by night. Many of the historic buildings have survived here to this day. A place where old traditions are still kept alive. Old and new meet, and so new ideas for the future are developed here. Hindu temples and mosques stand close together.

Orchard Road is a 2.2 km shopping street with all the well-known brands and high-end shops. With our friends we enjoy an excellent Korean dinner. To feast, you go to one of the gigantic "shopping malls".

The Marina Bay Sands Hotel was built in 2010 for around 4.6 billion euros. Because of its extraordinary architecture, it has become Singapore's trademark. The 3 hotel towers, each with 55 floors, are linked by a rooftop platform. At a height of 191 metres, next to a 146-metre-long "infinity pool", is the largest publicly accessible cantilevered platform in the world. The ticket for the lift can be bought at the ticket office (by the escalator) outside Tower 3. The 20 SGD is worth it. The public area of the platform gives you a view over an impressive skyline.
"Another way to do it" tip:
In the Tower 3 building, at the exit opposite the "Sweet Spot", look out for the "SkyPark" sign. At the security desk you get a free lift pass to the terrace bar, to have a drink there.

The rainforest zoo in Singapore was a highlight for us that we didn't want to miss. What makes it special is that its more than 3,000 animals live and move as if in the wild. This modern zoo houses about 300 different species in open enclosures on 28 hectares. The operators place great value on keeping the animals as naturally as possible.

Check-in Singapore: Before 1819 the island was home to only 20 Malay fishing families and was a refuge for pirates. Today this city-state has five million inhabitants. Singapore is known as the cleanest city in the world and the smallest country in South-East Asia. Public transport is excellently developed, and because the island is so compact, you can reach any destination in no time. Singapore is also a shopping paradise!

Singapore is a fine city! This saying refers to the enormous fines ("fine" meaning a penalty or fee) imposed in Singapore. You should find out about the most important prohibitions before you arrive. A seemingly harmless offence is punished here with draconian penalties. Carelessly throwing away chewing gum or a cigarette costs the equivalent of 300 euros. You may not bring in more than 17 cigarettes; anything more becomes very expensive. Anyone caught with more than 15 grams of heroin, 28 grams of morphine or 500 grams of cannabis faces the death penalty. (Information from 2013)

Other sights:
The cable car from Sentosa to Mount Faber, with a 360° view over Singapore.
Universal Studios on Sentosa.
The Singapore Flyer, at 165 metres high, the largest Ferris wheel in the world
The Botanic Gardens
Night Safari in the rainforest zoo

Supposedly the bridge, and so the customs post, in the west of Singapore that links Tuas with Gelang Patah is closed to bicycles (you will be turned back).

Singapore: things worth knowing and interesting facts
In the east of the city-state is Singapore Changi Airport, one of the most important airports in South-East Asia. It is served by 64 international airlines. However, a large share of civil flights is transit traffic that only stops over in Singapore, especially on the Europe–Australia route. Singapore is of great importance as an international financial centre and in the trade in goods. The Port of Singapore is one of the busiest in the world and the most important container hub worldwide. This is due, among other things and especially in terms of its historical development, to its favourable location on the sea route from China and Japan to Europe. Singapore has a dense, high-frequency and relatively cheap public transport system that is being systematically expanded. The underground network, called the MRT (Mass Rapid Transit), is well developed. Singapore is an island city-state and, by area, the smallest country in South-East Asia.

Because of its British colonial past, traffic drives on the left. There are two land links with Malaysia. The Johor–Singapore Causeway in the north connects Woodlands (Singapore) with Johor Bahru (Malaysia) for road vehicles and rail. It is also the main link for Singapore's water supply. A second bridge lies in the west of Singapore. It connects Tuas (Singapore) with Gelang Patah (Malaysia). Imported motor vehicles are taxed at rates of over 200% in some cases, but cars are very important as a status symbol. A licence to buy a car is granted by the state. This licence is auctioned; at present the purchase price is around 100,000 SGD. On top of that, the vehicle itself "has" to be bought. Traffic in the city centre is also subject to high charges through an electronic road-pricing system.

While in many countries it is often hard to imagine institutions of different religions right next to each other, in Singapore this is nothing unusual because of its limited space. Hindu temples and Islamic mosques stand side by side or directly opposite each other, just like Buddhist temples and churches. There are no disputes because of the lack of space. What looks like easily achieved harmony is the result of years of effort, equal rights and a guarantee of mutual respect. For example, the canteens of all state schools follow halal rules – the halal crockery is kept separate from the rest. The pupils or students eat together, however; they just take their crockery back to different places after eating. This is only one of many approaches in Singapore to allow close interaction between people of different religions while guaranteeing everyone the freedom to practise their own. The Sri Mariamman Temple in the middle of Chinatown is another example of the unusual way people live together in Singapore. Great importance is placed on all ethnic groups living together in harmony. In part this is laid down by the state, for example in public housing (HDB – Housing Development Board) through so-called ethnic group quotas. So only a certain percentage of the flats in a block may be sold to Chinese, Malays and Indians.

Singapore is a parliamentary republic based on the Westminster system (similar to the United Kingdom). The head of state is the president, who has veto rights in some key areas and appoints the most senior judges. Since 1993 the president has, in theory, been elected directly by the people every six years. In 1993 Ong Teng Cheong was elected president. Since then the elections of 1999 and 2006 did not take place, because only one candidate – Sellapan Ramanathan – was accepted by the election commission. Only after 18 years, in 2011, was there another election, which Dr Tony Tan won.

Vandalism and graffiti can result in fines and caning. The sale of chewing gum was banned from 1992 until May 2004. Heavy fines and community service are imposed on people who carelessly throw rubbish and cigarette ends onto the street. Eating, drinking, smoking and carrying dangerous goods on public transport are subject to heavy penalties. There is a general ban on smoking in public buildings, on public transport and in restaurants, and in groups of more than five people, for example in queues.

Singapore is the only country in the world where cigarettes may not be imported duty-free. The fine for importing a carton of cigarettes is ten times the price inside Singapore, currently around 550 euros.

Lying, if it can be proven, is punished with heavy penalties similar to fraud (1,000 to 5,000 euros). In addition, the offence can also be punished with 3–8 strokes of the cane.

Sexual practices that the government considers "unnatural" are illegal. This includes any form of homosexual sex. Only in October 2007 were oral and anal sex legalised for heterosexual people aged 16 and over. Between 1990 and 2005 around 420 people were hanged, mainly for drug trafficking, possession and smuggling. Among them were some Western foreigners. Scaled up to the population of Germany, around 8,000 people would have been executed in the same period. The last execution took place in 2010. The rules on narcotics are very strict. Anyone caught with more than 15 grams of heroin, 28 grams of morphine or 500 grams of cannabis faces the death penalty.

There is no press freedom in Singapore: the media are subject to strict state censorship. The reporting rules for foreign correspondents include a ban on criticising government policy. Private ownership of satellite dishes is forbidden. Cable gives access to selected international channels such as Deutsche Welle, BBC and CNN. In the world ranking of the Press Freedom Index, Singapore was placed 135th out of 179. Pornography is banned; the depiction of sex and nudity is restricted. So Playboy and other "adult magazines", such as Cosmopolitan, are banned in Singapore.

Key figures: year 2008
The people of Singapore are among the wealthiest in the world: GDP 132 billion euros – GDP per head 49,714 euros. Industry 26%. Services 69%. Agriculture hardly exists. Unemployment only 3.4%

According to Singapore's statistics office, the total population in June 2009 was 4.8 million people. The citizens and "permanent residents" belong to different ethnic groups: 77% are Chinese, 13% Malay, 8% Indian and 2% others. According to the Department of Statistics, there are about 1.2 million foreign workers and foreigners in Singapore.

As of 2011: Singapore has a fertility rate of 1.2 children per woman. 17% of the population are under 15, and 9% are over 64. Life expectancy at birth was 79 years for men and 84 years for women.

The main religions in Singapore are: Buddhism 42% of the total population, Islam 15%, Christianity 15%, Taoism 8%, Hinduism 5%, no religion 15%. The activities of Jehovah's Witnesses and the Unification Church are banned in Singapore. (Source: Census 2000)
