/berichte/tadschikistan.title: Tajikistan
/berichte/tadschikistan.html:
Tajikistan
9 July - 4 August 2012

Getting through Uzbek customs took strong nerves, with endless queuing. At the border police all our bags were rummaged through! Just before 10:00 everything has finally been checked, and we get our exit stamp. The Tajik entry formalities are done quickly, and so half an hour later we are already in our fifth country since the start of the journey.

The road to Dushanbe was so bad and took so much time that we only reach the capital late in the evening. As usual, finding suitable accommodation wasn't easy. The streets are signposted with Russian names and unfamiliar letters, and, to make things even harder, we don't speak any of the common local languages. Despite giving the street and house number, we are sent left and right. After a long search, as it's already getting dark, we finally find it. At Marian's Guesthouse we get a room and are spoilt with a generous breakfast the next morning.

So as not to wait several days at a border again, we decide to extend our Kyrgyz visa by 2 weeks. In Dushanbe the consulate is not far from the guesthouse. 2 photos + 40 USD per person, and an hour later we have another visa, starting on 31 July. That means from that date until 22 August we can enter Kyrgyzstan at any time.

Now we still need the Pamir "GBAO permit". Without this permit you are not allowed to travel through the autonomous regions. By handing over our passports and paying 180 somoni at the "Visa Center", Pushkin Street 46, we receive the necessary paper and are ready to continue.

Because there won't be much food available along our route, we decide to stock up here in Dushanbe. Two roads lead to Khorog, the starting point for the "Roof of the World": the northern route M41 and the southern route via Kulob. Both roads join at Kalaikhum. Maintenance of both roads has been completely neglected in recent years, so their condition doesn't bode well. We were recommended the southern route, supposedly better but 50 kilometres longer. So the next 630 kilometres via Kulob were decided. During our three days in Dushanbe, we have already fallen for the comforts of a big city again. Restaurants run to European standards surprise us with rich menus and the best "cappuccino". In the capital, Dushanbe, with its wide green spaces, avenues, parks and countless fountains, we felt as if we had been "catapulted" back to Europe. Tajikistan surprises us with a completely different picture from what you would expect. With the paperwork for the visa and GBAO done, the bikes serviced and our supplies topped up, we leave Dushanbe after 3 days, with noticeably heavier bikes, heading for Khorog.

Here in the lowlands, temperatures above 40 degrees are nothing unusual. On the very first day we are challenged by a pass that isn't shown on the map (1,571 m). Then comes a fast descent and, as usual, another exhausting climb. The recently built, lit and ventilated Shar-Shar tunnel, 2,223 metres long, saves us another pass (1,650 m). We are allowed to ride through with our bikes, which have front and rear lights, and at the end of the "tube" we are given 2 bottles of mineral water for the next climb. After 190 kilometres of "up and down", we reach Kulob after two days, where dusk has already fallen at 19:30. Once again our search for a suitable place to camp was unsuccessful, and we spend the remaining hours until dawn on the grounds of a petrol station.

Now things really get going. From 400 m above sea level, by four in the afternoon we reach the next pass, at 1,966 m. Another night in the tent lies ahead. "Benjamin", a shepherd of sheep and goats, shows us the "most beautiful" place to camp, with a view into the valley and the surrounding mountains. His mother gives us bread, yoghurt and apricots for breakfast. Snow-capped 4,000-metre peaks come into view.

We had imagined the descent from the pass differently. The road, with washed-out scree covered by up to 10 centimetres of dust, got worse and worse. Half a day was needed to get down into the valley 1,500 metres below, too long to reach a bed in time! At the Turkish road construction camp, which has been commissioned to build this new road, we are given a place to sleep, allowed to use the shower and given food. The workers tell us that the road will be finished in 2 years (2014) and covered with smooth asphalt. Ahead of us are another 90 kilometres (to "Zigar") of unrenovated road full of potholes. Bad luck, we're too early!

The 5,000-metre peaks come closer, the valley gets narrower, and 100 metres separate the Tajik border from the Afghan one. We can call "hello" to each other. The road ahead is exhausting and full of stretches where we have to push. 160 kilometres take 3 days!

The bed of the "Panj" river gets narrower; only 50 metres lie between us and the Afghan border. Soon you could almost shake hands. In Kalaikhum, Claudia falls ill with a stomach bug. With fever and stomach pains, cycling is impossible for now. After 2 days of tea and rice we try to carry on. On the way Claudia gets visibly worse, so we look for a "homestay" again. The next morning, after 10 kilometres, it's clear that Claudia won't make it to Khorog in her condition. In the next village, Alexandre organises a suitable car with a driver to take Claudia safely to Khorog.

Badly shaken about, Claudia reaches the town of Khorog after 5 hours and can now recover from the virus for a few days. Alexandre covers the remaining 195 kilometres alone and reaches the agreed meeting point just a day later. Within two days Claudia has recovered and built up new strength. The preparations for the "Pamir Highway" have now been completed, when events come thick and fast.

Conflict in Khorog
At 03:30 in the morning, shots ring out and a crowd of shouting men passes the guesthouse. The exchange of fire gets heavier and heavier. We are long since out of our beds, lying on the floor of the bathroom, which seems safe. We spend the next 4 hours in the steel-protected bathtub, while bullets pierce the walls of the house. To get onto the roof of our guesthouse, the front door is shot up all round the lock. Luckily for us, this bent the door frame and the door could no longer be opened. The bathroom, safe at first, now faces the rebels' side and becomes unsafe. We leave this room and crawl into a room whose outside wall faces away from the shooting.

Meanwhile tanks have rolled up! The guesthouse is barely 20 metres from the strategically important, and therefore fiercely contested, bridge. The machine-gun bursts, pistol shots and heavy shells fired by the army right next to the house seem to be getting out of control. In between we hear the screams of soldiers who have been wounded or who are calling for retreat. We have already been lying on the floor for 12 hours. Spending another night in the combat zone is becoming more and more dangerous. We decide to leave the house by 17:00 at the latest, while it's still light. Alexandre asks the army several times for help to get us out of the danger zone. We are told to stay in the house! During a pause in the shooting, probably a ceasefire, the moment is right for us to escape. Because the front door won't open for us either, the only way out is through a window. We hastily knot two bed sheets together to get from the 1st floor down to the street. We were able to take our passports and cash with us; the rest of our equipment and the bikes had to stay behind. Crouching, we run to the Delhi Darbar Hotel, where other tourists and cyclists have gathered.

Since the fighting began, the electricity supply has been cut in large parts of the town. Mobile phones, internet, landlines and TV are all down. A guided cycling group has a satellite phone, with which they were able to reach the US embassy in Dushanbe. The details of everyone present, including those who are not US citizens, are reported, and the possibility of an evacuation is looked into. We are relieved, because the Swiss embassy and the "FDFA" will now be informed of where we are. Together with others affected, we feel much safer here in the hotel than before. The tension of the last 15 hours eases. For now the rebels have won the fight and, cheering, drive the army out of the town. The conflict seems to be resolved for the time being, so the people of Khorog venture back onto the streets.

The night stays quiet. A ceasefire has been agreed until 14:00 the next day. During this time we fetch the luggage and bikes we left behind from the badly damaged guesthouse. Despite the ceasefire, the odd shot is still fired. The negotiations in Dushanbe come to nothing. The roads are still blocked by felled trees, barbed wire and lorries.

Good news from a "Pamiri": on orders from Dushanbe, the army will withdraw on 25 July and the conflict is resolved. Unfortunately a mistake, as will turn out later.

On 26 July we notice the tension on the streets of Khorog again. Another cycling group tells us that a second ultimatum runs out at 12:00 and that further fighting is then to be expected. We decide to leave the town as quickly as possible.

At 12:30, with the access roads already closed, we are on our bikes and leave the town by a roundabout route. The "Pamir Highway", a main road that runs through Khorog, seems completely deserted. Apart from a few taxis and us, we see no other vehicles. What if the roadblocks are extended? How can we continue our journey? An oppressive feeling!

Press reports:
Tages Anzeiger
Welt-online
NZZ
Wallstreet

By now we are 30 kilometres from Khorog. Riding through villages, we are stopped several times to explain the situation to the unsuspecting people. A family whose relatives live in the combat zone invited us to dinner and to sleep. Our thoughts remain in Khorog, because the rumble of the artillery echoing through the mountains was impossible to miss.

Within just 4½ days we reached Murghab. Behind us now lay a safe distance of 300 kilometres and 3 passes, each over 4,000 metres. Because of the turmoil of war, the mobile network was no longer available, and landlines and internet don't exist in these remote mountain regions. So we couldn't let anyone know about our successful "escape". Our goal now was to get over the "Pamir" to China quickly, to get back in touch with the people at home.

What the locals knew about events in Khorog couldn't have been more varied. The roadblocks and the mobile network outage left room only for guesswork. There was talk of anything from the war being over to heavy artillery and combat helicopters. This uncertainty accompanied us throughout the whole ride over the "Roof of the World".

The cause of these events happened while we were on our way to Khorog. A high-ranking officer was murdered, which led the government to hunt down those responsible. Nobody could have guessed that it would lead to such a massive military operation. This event showed us how quickly a situation can escalate.

Within 25 days we covered 1,242 kilometres and crossed 8 passes. The "Ak-Baital Pass" (4,655 m) was the highest, the "Uy-Buloq Pass", with a hurricane-force headwind and temperatures below freezing, the coldest, and the "Kyzyl-Art Pass" made us flee into the tent in a shower of sleet.

13:00: for 4 hours we have been "working" our way up to the top of the pass. A hurricane-force headwind and the cold mean we make very slow progress. The short but steep climbs up to the Tajik passport control (4,220 m) turn into exhausting stretches of pushing. Short of breath, we reach the first barrier of the Tajik border. The exit formalities are straightforward and quickly done.

By bike on the "Roof of the World"
Once again we were fascinated by the turquoise lakes, the high plateaus and the snow-capped summits of the 5,000-metre peaks against a blue sky. The "Pamir Highway", unique as it is, enjoys an international reputation among many cycling enthusiasts. Anyone who doesn't always want to ride on asphalt, and wants to enjoy nature in all its facets, is in exactly the right place here.

An anecdote from Alexandre:
On the way to Khorog, a car honks wildly beside me and the passenger shouts something to me. A few metres further on, the jeep stops. After the usual standard questions, "where are you from, where are you going, are you married, do you have children", the driver explains that he is Russian and thinks it's fantastic to meet "bicyclers" who cover this route with their luggage under their own muscle power. He says he is on the "Pamir Highway" right now especially because of these "bicyclers", to support everyone he meets with money, bread, water and fruit.

No, not a dream or a made-up story. Reality: the driver pulls out his wallet and hands me a few notes, 2 litres of water, apricots and a plastic bag of bread. In the meantime, drivers have come up from in front and behind, honking impatiently to claim their right of way. The Russian puts them in their place with a few words and calmly carries on our conversation.

After a few minutes the Russian gets back into his car, assures me once more of his enthusiasm for "globetrotters" like me, and drives on in his jeep. I can hardly believe it, and yet...... it's real.

Info on the "Pamir Highway" route:
Section 1: Dushanbe - Kalaikhum, 385 km, 6,650 m of climbing
Dushanbe - Vahdat - "Shar-Shar Pass": at 1,200 m, a well-built, 2,200 m long tunnel, lit and ventilated. Danghara - Kulob - up to the top of the pass (1,966 m) about 10 km before Anjirob, a steady climb on asphalt. CAUTION: dry region! Carry enough to drink! Camping at the top of the pass; to Zigar (90 km) partly unpaved, disastrous road conditions (2 days!), stretches of pushing! (Widening + renovation to be finished by 2014.) From Zigar to Yoged (38 km) excellent; Yoged to Kalaikhum (27 km) unpaved, bone-shaking track.

Section 2: Kalaikhum - Khorog (Pamir M41), 250 km, 3,500 m of climbing
From Kalaikhum, 10 km of good road, then getting worse and worse, down to very bad, with steep climbs. From "Shipad" the road improves, and from "Rushan" it rolls well to Khorog. Few places to camp (rock on the left, river on the right), but good "homestays" (look out for the signs), and some water taps.

Section 3: Khorog - Murghab (Pamir M41)
"Koitezek" Pass 4,280 m
From Khorog (2,070 m), 150 km to the last house/construction machinery/last water tap (3,950 m).
7 km of riding (good), partly pushing (fine), to the "Koitezek" Pass, 4,280 m; 19 km of gravel (bone-shaking track) across the high plateau, then 3 km of pushing to the "Tagarkaty" Pass, 4,176 m; then a 5 km descent, then 32 km to Alichur, 3,890 m. 53 km of asphalt to the "Neizatash" Pass, 4,137 m, 2 steep climbs, then 51 km of asphalt to Murghab.
Note on Alichur: 2 homestays, 2 small kiosks, no bottled water! After 4 km clean water again; a yurt stay each at 8 km and 10 km from Alichur.

Section 4: Murghab (Tajikistan) - Sary-Tash (Kyrgyzstan)
"Ak-Baital" Pass 4,655 m
61 km from Murghab, 3,620 m, to the end of the asphalt at 4,270 m, then 15 km to the top of the pass, 4,655 m (partly pushing, broken asphalt with potholes; we needed 2.5 hours for 385 metres of climbing). From the top of the pass, 4,655 m: a very good 5 km descent (clean water again) – then 17 km of very bad gravel, followed by 38 km to Karakul, 3,930 m.
"Kyzyl-Art" Pass 4,290 m
From Karakul, 45 km of asphalt, then 9 km of gravel to the Tajik border post, 4,220 m (exit), then 2 km of gravel to the top of the "Kyzyl-Art" Pass, 4,290 m. A 22 km descent on gravel to the Kyrgyz border post, 3,495 m (entry). 25 km of asphalt (collapsed road + bridge) to Sary-Tash, 3,150 m.

/berichte/thailand.title: Thailand
/berichte/thailand.html:
Thailand
23 November 2012 - 2 January 2013

The biggest change of all now was driving on the left. There was no sign when we entered to tell us "which way to go". Although the customs building was on the left side of the road, we carried on riding on the right as usual. The Thais are very considerate drivers. No honking or head-shaking: they simply let us ride wherever we thought was right. It took more and more oncoming traffic before we realised that something had changed.

In a few moves, the rear-view mirrors were switched from left to right so we could get used to the new situation as quickly as possible. And yet, it isn't that easy. Our old habits keep catching us out: crossing the road, turning right, changing lanes and making unfamiliar "U-turns". Driving on the left now calls for extra care.

Are we back in the West already? The change of country from Cambodia to Thailand felt like being back at our start in Istanbul. On the smooth asphalt the bikes roll almost by themselves, and the kilometres soon add up.

On the multi-lane expressways, with hills no higher than 15 metres, we reach Bangkok after just 2 days. Vehicles of every kind, from rusty bicycles to oversized coaches, tolerate each other so that everyone gets ahead. Criss-crossing every which way, it works amazingly well. By now we have got used to driving on the left and quickly find our way into the centre of this metropolis of 8 million people. Putting up the tent, unpacking the stove and washing in a cold mountain stream: that now definitely belongs to the past. We are adaptable! With so many hotels, finding a place to stay shouldn't be a problem. How wrong we were! After 3 hours of circling blocks and hearing the familiar answer "fully booked", the only help left is McDonald's, Starbucks and all the rest. In an internet café we use "ebookers and booking.com" to find somewhere to stay within our budget. Searching the websites took two coffees with cake, patience and a bit of luck. At 18:00 we "check in" to a 5-star hotel at a bargain price. In our sweaty cycling clothes, with vehicles that look like anything but luxury limousines, we are given a friendly welcome. The bikes find a safe spot in the hotel lobby, and we find ours in a "deluxe room" on the 26th floor.

For breakfast an 8 x 3 metre buffet awaits us, with French croissants, sushi, eggs in every variation and everything your heart desires. A treat for the taste buds that unfortunately also goes straight to the hips, and we aren't spared either. The white bathrobes stay in the room; we prefer to visit the "fitness park" in our usual outfit. On the 14th floor: a swimming pool, wicker chairs and loungers, an air-conditioned gym with floor-to-ceiling glass, and the whole area bathed in "chill-out" music. Oh yes, we almost forgot: plus a magnificent 180-degree view over the "skyline" of Bangkok. Through the hotel's own passage you reach the elevated "Skytrain" in a few steps. Our bikes stay safely in the care of reception for 4 days.

Our "sightseeing tour": 
The Royal Palace, or Grand Palace, is the most spectacular sight in Bangkok and an absolute highlight. From far away you can already see the high white walls and huge gates. The complex consists of more than 100 buildings and covers an area of 200,000 square metres.

The Wat Phra Kaew temple, the holiest shrine in the country, lies in the north-eastern part of the palace grounds. Wat Phra Kaew is a cluster of buildings decorated with gold leaf, coloured tiles and mirror mosaics. Golden statues of mythological beings (kinnari), and statues of nature spirits and gods (yaksha), all guard the treasures in the temple buildings.

At Wat Pho we meet the legendary reclining Buddha. At 15 metres high and a full 43 metres long, it is the largest Buddha in Bangkok. The huge grounds hold countless statues and temples.

The Emerald Buddha is the most important religious symbol in the country. It is said to have magical powers that bring prosperity to its owner. To this day, Thailand's king changes the Emerald Buddha's robes in a solemn ceremony. They are adapted to the seasons, so there is a separate robe for the cool season, the hot season and the rainy season.

The Chao Phraya River is the largest and most important river in Thailand. Ferries, also called the "river boats of the Venice of the East", link the piers along the river. Apart from the Skytrain, this is the most pleasant way to get around and explore the city and its main attractions. A trip on the Chao Phraya, with its peaceful atmosphere in the middle of a modern city, was a "highlight" for us.

The Floating Market is one of Thailand's biggest attractions. This tourist magnet is not in Bangkok, but in Damnoen Saduak, 110 kilometres away. Every day from 9:00 to 13:00, huge crowds of tourists visit the floating market. This kind of sight seems overrun to us, and it has turned into a souvenir shop. We do without the old flair of Siam and cycle on towards Chumphon.

Now it's time to cover as many kilometres as possible again. There isn't much exciting to see on the hard shoulder and along the crash barrier. For a change and some relaxation, in Hua Hin and Prachuap Khiri Khan there are unobstructed views of the "Gulf of Thailand" and a dip in the cool water.

We still have the best memories of Laos and Cambodia. We had imagined Thailand differently. Where are the lonely white beaches with the turquoise sea? The shady palms with coconuts lying around? The thatched bungalow with the roaring surf?

We reach Bang Boet, a completely unspectacular place by the sea, 15 kilometres from the main road. Here we hope for a few days of beach life. The road leads through a fishing village and disappoints us with the stinking smell of rotting fish carcasses. The beach is covered with rubbish, and the water is cloudy brown. The fishing boats look as if they will soon be making their last trip to the scrapyard. This can't be it! An inconspicuous path, climbing steeply and winding round a rocky outcrop, catches our interest. Our curiosity paid off. By chance we come across a "bungalow resort". Three barking dogs greet us, the doors and windows of the main building are open, there's no vehicle in the car park, and the place seems completely forgotten.

After a short exploration, this deserted place turns out to be an "oasis" and exactly what we had dreamed of. This is where we want to spend the next few days. No welcome? No reception? Nobody there? So one of the empty bungalows was ours to use. Settled comfortably in a deckchair on the veranda, we wait for the "hotel manager". A moped pulls up: the gardener is the owner. He gratefully accepted our suggestion of a daily rate of 500 baht. We get the keys and a few extra tips on using the whole beach complex. The first-class resort next door gives us free access to its restaurant, swimming pool, beach showers and Wi-Fi. What more could you want?

We leave Bang Boet heading for Chumphon, our starting point for the planned island hopping. The minor road runs along the coast through pine forests and oil palm and pineapple plantations. A welcome change for us from the hard shoulder of the main road.

Looking for:
bungalows, palms and white sand
the pearls of the "Gulf of Thailand"
idyll on lonely beaches

Koh Tao (Turtle Island)
Just after 12:00 we reach the town of Chumphon. The ferry piers for Koh Tao are 20 kilometres away in an outlying district. With no idea of the departure times, we cycle to the port area. At the ticket office we learn that the pier is another 20 kilometres away, that the "Lomprayah catamaran" has already left, and that it doesn't carry bicycles anyway. There are no more ferries today. A night in Chumphon was unavoidable. A local tour guide advises us to load the bikes onto the island supply boat and have them taken over overnight. The next morning we will be picked up at the hotel and taken to the "Lomprayah speedboat", which leaves at 13:00 and reaches Koh Tao 2 hours later. As an extra offer he suggests an idyllically located bungalow with a private beach. A look at a few photos, accommodation booked, tickets bought: tomorrow we'll be able to enjoy "paradise on earth".

On Koh Tao, the owner of the bungalow we booked is already waiting for us. On an unpaved, washed-out track, past steep slopes, he took us in his 4WD pickup to his resort on "Lang Khaai Bay". Great! We are the only guests. Another "Bang Boet"?

After a sleepless night we left this exotic spot. What had looked like a Robinson Crusoe idyll in the brochure turned out to be a massive mosquito infestation, bedbugs in the bedding, and barking dogs. The white sandy beach had been washed away by the breaking waves, making room for sharp-edged banks of shells. This idyll wasn't what we had imagined, so we have ourselves taken back to civilisation. A little closer to the pulse of Koh Tao, we spend 3 days at the "Sairee Beach Grand Coral Resort".

Koh Phangan
It doesn't always have to be the last corner at the end of the world! With the "Seatran Ferry", island hopping became much easier. The loaded bikes could easily be pushed up the "gangway" onto the deck and covered with a tarpaulin. Because of heavy rain showers, storms and high waves, we had a very uncomfortable crossing. As the faces of some passengers turned a pale white, little blue paper bags were handed out. Spared from seasickness, after two hours of rocking and rolling, we left the ferry in "Thong Sala".

Koh Phangan is famous for its Full Moon Parties and was a mecca for tourists in the 90s. A small island with only 13,000 inhabitants, it has more than 5,000 hotel rooms, more than 100 bars and a lively nightlife. The first party goes back to 1987. By now the event has grown into wild festivals and Half Moon Parties twice a month. A recommendation from the local tour guide: party on the beach, then enjoy some sleep in a bay "behind the mountain".

Koh Samui
With an area of 247 square kilometres, Koh Samui is, after Koh Phuket and Koh Chang, the third-largest island in Thailand in the "Gulf of Thailand". After an hour's crossing we go ashore in Nathon. On Koh Samui the Christmas and year-end tourist rush has already begun. Some beaches are already overcrowded. Relaxed sunbathing is now only restful on the surrounding islands. Guests are taken to the island beaches in longtail boats. While the sun-hungry wander around with snorkelling gear, food bags, sunshades and unsuitable footwear, we stay behind and "relax" on the roof of the excursion boat.

Krabi - Ao Nang Beach
Still searching for the romantic, idyllic white sandy beach, we decide to switch from the east coast to the west coast. From Surat Thani to Krabi there are small rises, called mountains in Thailand, to get over. In Krabi Town and at "Ao Nang Beach", 20 kilometres away, we want to spend Christmas in a holiday paradise. The public minibus, with variable seating, standing and running-board places, carries people and anything that fits somehow on 4 wheels. We choose to ride on the running board.

Where's the lonely beach with turquoise water? Over the road here, down the steps, was the driver's answer. We hadn't expected that. A crowd like at a fairground. On the beach we count up to 35 "longtail boats", which run to the offshore islands like buses. Noise and blue fumes pour out of the unsilenced exhaust pipes. Often the exposed four-cylinder car engines aren't switched off, because without a battery they can no longer be started. There are no sun loungers. Plastic chairs lined up in rows save space. Each seat has a number. The front row may, or must, enjoy the sun, while the back rows have the luck, or bad luck, of sitting in the shade. We found the quiet corner at the end of the beach, near the bar with a visibly stressed barman who was still clearing away the empty bottles from the night before.

Ao Nang wasn't what we had imagined. No hasty prejudices! Together with other tourists, shopping bags, Heineken six-packs, flippers and snorkels, we sit down in a "longtail boat". We wait patiently until all 30 seats are taken and the boat can put to sea. The destination of our afternoon: Poda Island, Tup Island and Chicken Island.

Already as we pass the small islands, we realise that we had the wrong expectations of this trip. Once we've run aground and got off the boat, we're immediately asked to pay the national park fee. We are released into a crowd of people moving from left to right along the sandbank. 2½ hours to hold out until the return trip. A few "water rats" wear swimming costumes and stand up to their hips in the water. The reef, rocks and broken coral limit the fun of swimming and bathing. Astonished, we watch what's going on, sitting in 40 cm of water in the scorching sun. This isn't how we had imagined it.

Buddhists and Muslims
1,300 kilometres to Singapore still lie ahead of us. Undecided about which coast to take, the monsoon, the beaches and places to stay, we decide to cross over to the east coast once more. On the way to "Hat Yai" we noticed the first mosques and headscarves. In Songkhla we realise that the southern part of Thailand, 5 districts in all, is mainly populated by Muslims. Between Songkhla and Pattani we pass more and more checkpoints, guarded by heavily armed soldiers.

After the hotel manager in Pattani has explained the conflict between religion and government to us, we face another decision. Back to the west coast, heavily used by tourists, or carry on through the disputed area? At the breakfast table we discuss what to do next, while armoured vehicles drive the hotel owner to a Buddhist ceremony. An uneasy feeling!

A word with the "District Senator" confirms that it is safe for foreigners to stay, and that the checkpoints keep the roads secure. A hotel employee, a member of the "Cyclist Association Pattani", had a brilliant idea. The 90-kilometre route to Narathiwat is split into three sections. Club members of Buddhist and Islamic faith are to accompany us. Despite the heavy rain showers and the holidays, 18 cyclists from various cycling clubs followed us. With shouts of "hello" and clapping, the bicycle convoy, led by two Swiss, rode through villages and along the market stalls.

For once the monsoon rain was kind to us. We were able to cover the remaining 42 kilometres to the Thai border without the annoying business of putting our rain capes on and taking them off. Because the big ferry was out of action with engine damage, there was only limited customs processing for pedestrians. That sounds familiar: ferry out of action for weeks! We already know the solution: we need a boat! Negotiate the price, load the gear, soaking wet shoes, a rocking crossing, unload again, empty the shoes and dry our feet. A private "longtail boat" for passengers brought us and the bikes to the Malaysian bank opposite.

We had the wrong expectations of Thailand. Lots of kilometres covered to visit Bangkok and the Royal Palace and to spend a few days on "Bang Boet beach". What we will never forget are the friendly, helpful Thais and the "Cycling Association Pattani".

/berichte/tuerkei.html:
Turkey
1 April - 15 May 2012

The somewhat unusual travel report, part 1
After a short flight with Pegasus Airlines, we land in Istanbul in stormy winds and heavy rain. Someone is waiting for us at the airport, and after a 45-minute drive we reach the Hotel Blue Tuana, booked in advance, not far from the Blue Mosque.
The rooms are extremely small, and right outside the window the railway rattles past, impossible to ignore, from early morning until late at night. To get the bikes ready to ride and to escape the railway noise, we will look for new accommodation. But first comes the "visa odyssey":

Day 1
To get the Uzbekistan visa, we take a taxi to İstinye. The drive takes about 40 minutes. We are let in, and the official present immediately informs us that we have to come with a completed visa application. We sort that out at the internet café down by the Sea of Marmara. At a brisk pace we go back to the embassy and hand in the application. We are told to come back in a week. We ask for express processing and collection on Friday. Possibly yes, says the consul, irritated. We don't want to bother him with any more questions and hope for his "goodwill". We had already been told about the "visa odyssey" in advance by former fellow sufferers. Still, stressed by all the running around and the preparations for the journey, we fall into bed exhausted and let the railway noise "force" us to sleep.

Day 2
The next day we set off for the Kyrgyz consulate. We search and search, and finally... we find it in an inconspicuous house. We have brought the wrong form and have to fill in an almost identical one again. The nice lady wants us to go straight to the bank just 100 metres away, pay 80 USD per person, and then bring her the receipt. After walking round the block and crossing Taksim Square 3 times, we go back and have the way explained to us again. Now, you would think, we should find the bank straight away... but easier said than done.... finally! The right bank. First take a ticket from the machine, followed by half an hour's wait until our number lights up and, no surprise.......... we are not at the right branch. The transfer costs a fee, the bank clerk says; we should go to the branch that holds the account, where it's free of charge.
After more searching and wandering about, we reach the right bank 2 minutes before 12. We are served as the last customers and hope that the embassy is open in the afternoon so we can show the receipt. At 14:00 we are standing in front of the door of the Kyrgyz consulate: "Closed in the afternoon". Someone who lives in the building lets us into the embassy through a back door. The lady who was so nice in the morning, now a little irritable, goes to ask the consul whether we may take our passports back. All fine, as long as we bring them back on Friday morning by 11:00 at the latest and only come to collect them again in the afternoon. That puts us under time pressure. On Friday morning we are supposed to collect our hoped-for visas at the Uzbek embassy. Somehow it will work out, possibly, maybe, if possible, if the consul is there.

Day 3
Today we move 100 m further on to another hotel, lugging 2 bike boxes of 30 kg each and 12 panniers. In the spacious room of the Obelisk Hotel we will put our bikes together. Our first free day to recover lies ahead.

Day 4
Today it's "sightseeing". With the modern tram we go to the districts of Karaköy and Galata, where life is buzzing, and stroll along the promenade "İstiklal Caddesi". The nostalgic, spruced-up tram reminds us of San Francisco, and the Galata Bridge with its floating bazaar marks the beginning of oriental culture.

Day 5
The plan for the day: taxi to İstinye to collect the visa at the Uzbek embassy. In our frantic rush to get the visas quickly, we realise too late that the taxi driver has cheated us. An "exchange rate difference" has boosted his day's earnings by 75 euros! At 10:00, right on opening time, the queuing in front of the embassy gate begins. After an hour we are called in to the consul. The visa hasn't been issued yet. Please come back at 12:00. Now we are visibly annoyed. At 12:00, queuing again. Half an hour later we are put off until 13:00. Finally, the consul has had a good lunch, and in exchange for 220 USD we receive the visas, issued in a great hurry. We jump straight into the next taxi to Taksim Square to collect the Kyrgyz visa. 15:00, both visas in the bag, back to the hotel, load the bikes we had got ready, and off to the ferry, which leaves for Mudanya at 17:30. On the way we eat a tasty bread roll with a fried fish fillet inside. At 19:00 we reach the other shore at Mudanya and look for a hotel. The staff speak fluent Turkish, and Turkish as their second language. Using body language, we get a room with breakfast for 143 Turkish lira. At the nearby MIGROS we stock up on the supplies we need to start the first stage towards Singapore.

From the 1st to the 2nd travel report
Route: Mudanya - Söloz - Çerçiler - Soğuksu - Geyve - Ankara
8 o'clock! After breakfast we set off on our first cycling stage. The ride starts hilly. Truly a tough start to our life as cycling nomads. At "İznik Gölü" we camp for the first time among the olive trees. Everything set up and ready for bed, dried porcini mushrooms soaking in cold water, stove lit. "Firstly things turn out differently, and secondly not the way you think": promptly the owner of the olive grove sends us off his field. Everything hastily packed up and tucked under our arms, he takes us to the shore of Lake İznik. To the croaking of frogs in the mating season, we spend our first night in the tent.

The ride to Ankara is packed with climbing, and our legs get heavier and heavier. The weather isn't kind to us either. It rains again and again. With 320 km already behind us, we reach Ankara, the capital of Turkey, in Central Anatolia. From the suburbs to the city centre, after a heavy thunderstorm, the expressway is full of ankle-deep puddles. Again and again, feet up, and don't stray too far from the kerb. The "rush hour" lasts 24 hours. Two lanes turn into three, or, nothing unusual, into four. Whoever honks first wins, greets, gets right of way, or is annoyed because things aren't moving.

The "Atatürk Bulvarı", a roaring north-south traffic artery, is unavoidable for us to get to modern "Yenişehir" (the new town). In the swarm of traffic we haven't yet seen a single bicycle. You might think that muscle-powered bikes are completely unknown here. To our surprise, the motorists are considerate, give us right of way and leave us gaps to change lanes. Splattered with dirt from the road, we look as if we have been in a mud fight. Not so easy to find accommodation with a generous bathroom in this outfit. The shower has to be big enough to clean us, our clothes and our equipment. After a day like this you really appreciate a clean bed.

The somewhat unusual travel report, part 2
We are not spared the hunt for the remaining visas. We still need Turkmenistan and Tajikistan. To apply for the Turkmen transit visa, you must already have the Uzbek and Iranian visas of the neighbouring countries. The problem: independent tourists with bicycles, without a letter of invitation, aren't very welcome here either. We can't afford to make a single mistake on the visa applications.

According to various travel reports, the Tajik visa can be obtained within a day. By taxi we get to "Panora Mall", an ultra-modern shopping centre for designer brands, for well-off Turks. Without any preconceptions we head for the hill opposite, where many embassies are. In a well-kept house, the Tajik vice-consul receives us, checks our passports, and wants to keep them straight away, to hand them back to us in the afternoon with the much-coveted sticker.

Wrong assumption! That won't work! We try politely to explain to the consul that without our passports we won't get the Turkmen visa. With our passports back, we go to "Panora Shopping Mall" and spend 2 hours there without buying a Rolex. Instead we eat a döner with chips. Then we go back to the Turkmen consulate at the other end of the city.

Already knowing that this 5-day transit visa will be the most unpleasant and time-consuming one, we try to stay calm. Here is a brief summary of the rest of the day:

Waiting outside the gates of the Turkmen embassy
Passport check. Followed by a long, drawn-out wait in the anteroom
Instead of the application form, a letter of explanation is required.

Crossing the country as an independent tourist by bicycle: impossible! Must NOT be mentioned!
Copies of the first page of the passport and of the visas for the neighbouring countries, plus a photo
Find a photocopier (there isn't one at the consulate!). Once again time is pressing! At the nearby MIGROS, where we almost feel at home by now, the copies are made for us.
Back to the embassy, all the papers, with the letter of explanation, handed to the consul.
The visa will be handed to us in 10 days. Great! Wait? Ride on?

After a long and exhausting discussion: the express solution (for a fee).
A confirmation in the form of an email is to be sent to us soon. With this letter we would get the 5-day transit visa at the border (with Iran) in Sarakhs. In only 5 days we have to reach Farab on the border with Uzbekistan, 410 kilometres away. 100 km a day, with a reserve built in for headwinds! The processing fee has to be paid at the border in US dollars. We agree to this uncertain "deal", at the risk of getting stuck between 2 countries. If we are refused transit between Iran and Turkmenistan and our Iranian visa has run out in the meantime: for that case we have no solution.

We are still in Ankara:

Now back to the Tajik embassy to get hold of the last remaining visa. Miscalculated again! Our nerves are in shreds! Contrary to what the third secretary promised, the "sticker" that is supposedly so easy to get may only be issued on Friday. So our passports stay at the embassy until tomorrow at the earliest.

Friday at 10:00, our phone call. Annoyed by the unreliability, we have to accept that the visa hasn't been issued yet. Then the usual: waiting, possibly, maybe, perhaps we'll be able to celebrate success on Monday. Let's wait and see.

As we finish this travel report, we still don't know whether we'll be able to collect the visa on Monday so we can start our journey on 17 April with nothing hanging over us.

On 29 April the email "Letter of Invitation" from the Turkmen ministry was sent to us. With this document we are entitled to collect the transit visa at the Turkmen border. So it does work after all! We are relieved.

Route: Ankara - Sungurlu (bus) - Boğazkale - Yozgat - Kalaba - Göreme - Zelve - Kayseri - Bünyan - Pazarsuyu - Malatya (bus)

To gain some time, we decide on our first bus transfer, from Ankara to Sungurlu, where we arrive at 15:00. Faced with the unfamiliar road layout and not knowing the language, we have by now expanded our Turkish vocabulary. The signpost most important for us, "Şehir Merkezi", meaning centre or town centre, now makes sense to us.

Since our start in Istanbul, here in Malatya we have covered 760 km and 9,700 metres of climbing. Ahead of us are another 840 km to the Iranian border, which we must reach not before 15 May, but not later either. From Van to the border crossing at Kapıköy there will then be 100 Turkish kilometres left.

The weather hasn't settled down yet. From Sungurlu to Yozgat we get lots of rain showers and headwinds with violent gusts, accompanied by hail. Temperatures of 7° mean gloves for the first time. Worn out by the weather, we reach the "tourist trap" of Boğazkale and took the first place to stay. When the bill arrives it confirms our suspicions: we can't recommend the Hotel and Restaurant Aşıkoğlu or the Hittite House. It would have been better to ride on up the last "ramp" of 500 metres and choose the Hotel/Motel Demir-Başkent Camping instead.

The next morning we cycle on an ancient cobbled road, 300 metres of climbing and 10 kilometres, through Hattusa, the capital of the Hittite empire on the Anatolian plateau. Added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1986, this excavation site is said to be one of the oldest settlements in the world.

On the way to Yozgat we notice lots of new housing developments springing up like mushrooms. Roads are being widened and resurfaced. We suspect this building boom is being driven by the economic upturn and the need for new housing. On this stretch our trip computer shows our biggest climb so far: 1,444 metres. Claudia has caught a stubborn cold, which means 2 rest days and a course of antibiotics.

Surprising for us! The roads are well built and have only a few potholes. Again and again, at least every 30 kilometres, there is a petrol station with a shop attached. Here we can always top up our supplies. 5-6 litres of water are enough for our daily needs. When we pitch the tent, another 5 litres are needed for cooking and washing. Along the way we get countless shouts of hello, invitations to tea, or are offered lunch.

The ride on from Yozgat to Göreme is unspectacular, but this is what we have been waiting for: the weather improves! And yet another climb to conquer. The sudden rise in temperature takes it out of us. Then a lorry is standing at the roadside, blocking our way. The driver gets out and offers to take us further on his articulated lorry. In English, of which he surely understood nothing, we gladly accept the offer and are carried 65 kilometres over the mountains. As a result (that's the price of comfort), the bikes need a thorough wash to get rid of red brick dust.

We reach Cappadocia, another "highlight" of our journey. Cappadocia means "land of beautiful horses", because the Persians bought all their horses here. The region is made up of the provinces of Nevşehir, Niğde, Aksaray, Kırşehir and Kayseri in Central Anatolia.

Göreme, with its cave churches carved out of the soft tuff, is considered the centre of Cappadocia. The rock formations and a large number of underground cities were declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1985. Striking is the snow-covered Erciyes, 3,995 metres above sea level, which accompanies us as a "signpost" for quite a long time.

Göreme is like a magnet for countless coaches full of tourists. The viewpoints and car parks are bursting at the seams, but with our touring bikes we always find somewhere to stop. We ask around and are told that the Göreme campsite is closed, so we end up at the Panorama campsite, which we can't recommend. With the tent already up and furnished, a strong wind with gusts sets in. In no time our home had been sandblasted. Even inside the inner tent and the bags, fine sand dust settled. You have to be lucky: the owner of the Göreme campsite opens his gates for us. Determined to flee the "Panoramic" site, we order a taxi, stuff everything in and have our gear taken to a well-kept, sheltered lawn.

After a thorough clean-up, a 13 km "loop" to Zelve makes up for it. By bike along narrow bridleways and through small villages, and with a walk through a long-abandoned civilisation, we can relax.

In contrast: the Göreme National Park, massively overcrowded with tourists. Waiting times of up to an hour at every attraction make visitors impatient and aggressive. It's a crush. Anyone who doesn't want to be first at the entrance should spare themselves this ordeal and go to Zelve instead.

Our recommendation: the "Green - Ihlara day tour", which you can book with Hiro Tour Travel Agency. For just TL 160 (CHF 80), an excellent round trip with the following attractions:

The Göreme panorama, with an impressive view of inactive volcanoes and dwellings carved into the sandstone, shaped by wind and rain.
Derinkuyu, a 4,000-year-old underground city with 9 kilometres of tunnels. Its 13 underground floors gave 4,000 inhabitants safety from attacks from the "upper world".
A walk through the "Ihlara Valley", with an excellent lunch in Belisırma.
The "Selime Rock Monastery" with its caravanserai. On the Silk Road there was a caravanserai every 30 kilometres, because camels could only cover 30 kilometres a day.
Uçhisar, the village pressed against the mountain.
The "Pigeon Valley", where birds were bred because the white eggshells were used to make paint for rock paintings, the droppings were spread on the fields as fertiliser, and they carried the mail.
Before the drive back, there is a look inside an onyx-cutting factory. In this region the stone is mined from 100-200 metres below ground.

We leave Göreme and reach Kayseri. A city of 1,000,000 inhabitants, nothing special, very industrial and business-like. In Kayseri the first bike service is also due. The best "master" in town, Ramazan Usta, and his workshop assistant do this job for us, including replacing the broken bottom bracket. Perfect work, which for 2 hours costs only 50 TL (CHF 25).

We decide to visit the "Seljuk caravanserai of Sultanhanı", 10 kilometres off our route. This detour was worth it. We are the only visitors. The gate is opened just for us, and the gatekeeper kindly points out the small details of the building. From the tower you get a view that, in good weather, reaches as far as the next caravanserai. In the stables, the cloister and the nave, countless pigeons flutter about and "decorate" the floors. Over Turkish coffee, which by now already seems like a ritual to us, we say goodbye to our host.

It's already 16:00, and we have to hurry to reach Bünyan before the approaching heat thunderstorm (they mostly come in the afternoon). In this village of 20,000 souls we looked in vain for a hotel or any other accommodation. On the guarded, fenced-in grounds of the police station, we are given a patch of grass for the tent, access to a toilet and shower, and of course çay.

Pınarbaşı: in a restaurant we linger over Turkish coffee and plan the next part of our journey. Our Turkish vocabulary is growing visibly: what does it cost? "Bunun fiyatı ne kadar?" To which we get the answer in German: "Nothing, you are our guests". Many Turks speak our language because they used to work in Germany.

Another heat thunderstorm is brewing. To escape the rain, we look for a lift. The number plate should start with a "44" – that could be our direction, to Malatya. After 2 hours of waiting in vain for the right lorry, without red brick sand on the loading platform, we decide on the scheduled bus. We hope there is enough room for the bikes in the hold, otherwise we'll be "left behind". Lucky us: everything fits in the hold. After more than 3 hours on the road, we reach Malatya at 20:15.

Route: Malatya - Sürgü - Adıyaman - Kâhta - Diyarbakır - Tatvan - Gevaş - Van - Muradiye - Doğubayazıt - Iranian border

A magnificent ride through countless apricot orchards awaits us. Many trees are in blossom, everything is turning green, a landscape full of variety. The world's best apricots come from the Malatya region. We could have set off without breakfast, because we are offered dried fruit as a snack again and again. All untreated, without additives, "pure nature", free of charge! Several times we are asked to stop and answer the question "where are you from". You simply can't ride past – the Turks are outgoing and curious, and always want to invite us to something. We get the best tips at stops like these. That's how we reach "Ali Dayı", a fish restaurant. Thousands of trout of every size swim about in ponds of various sizes, until they....... are grilled over charcoal, then finished off in an earthenware dish and served to the guest with salad. A delicious change from the huge amounts of apricots we have eaten.

Well fed, we find the right place for our camp at a farmer's. Now! We really only wanted a spot for the tent. Unbelievable! Straight away a blanket with cushions is laid out for us and, what else, tea is served. No! Not enough. The son is called, a TV and a table are carried out onto the field, the satellite dish connected – it works – Turkish television. They actively help us put up the tent, and quickly make a call on the mobile. Surprise! A few friends have been invited, and what gets delivered? Trout, of course, and "EFES", the Turkish beer. Hospitality! We spend an unforgettable evening and have made friends. It works! We don't speak Turkish and the Turks don't speak English. Tired, we withdraw, the others considerately carry on talking quietly, and "Thomas" the guard dog keeps watch over the surroundings.

Up at 06:00 – at 08:00 we carry on over the mountains, 80 kilometres to Adıyaman. Just before Adıyaman we visit "Perrhe". This relic in the district of "Örenli" was once an ancient city in the kingdom of "Commagene". In Kâhta we are surprised by a tour agent with an attractive offer: "Nemrut Dağı at sunset". His package deal: storage for the bikes in his office, a hot shower before the tour, and a night in his hotel after we get back. We soon agree; the price is right, and at 13:00 we're off. On the way we were shown more sights:

- Karakuş Tumulus (burial mound of the royal family of Commagene)
- Cendere Bridge
- The ruins of Arsameia

The highlight: "Nemrut Dağı" (2,300 metres above sea level), shrouded in fog and heavy rain showers. In the mountain hut people drank tea and waited for the weather to improve. Yes, now, a few rays of sunshine: walk quickly to the summit in 15 minutes and take the usual photos. With moderate success! Once again no view, rain, and on the way down, extreme hail. Trickles turned into torrents along the footpath. Soaked to the skin, shoes full of water, we get back to the hut. By now the hut was packed with people "fleeing the mountain", so we fled to our minibus in our underpants. So much for the sunset! Back in Kâhta: wash our clothes, and while we wait, eat a döner between the spinning drums. Back at the hotel: sort out our gear, pack, and get everything ready for the next morning.

Diyarbakır: apart from the restored city walls, this town of 650,460 inhabitants doesn't have much to offer. Claudia is still suffering from the flu. The cold, wet weather made a visit to the doctor at the regional hospital necessary. The medicines she had already been given hadn't had the desired effect. An injection in the backside was now supposed to do the trick. We are drawn further into eastern Turkey, into Kurdish country, where the feared PKK is supposed to be active.

On the way from Diyarbakır to Tatvan there was nowhere acceptable to camp. It's already late afternoon, so we take it easy and "hop" onto the next lorry. No, not just any lorry! By now we have learned to tell the well-kept cabs from the smoky ones. The number plates, which show the direction, tell us whether it will stop. The legally required rest break makes the driver stop along the way. From the little kitchen between the trailer axles, we are handed Turkish coffee and chocolate bars. Conversation in "Turkish versus English", with hands and feet; the driver is happy about the change. Food and transport free of charge, of course. Arrival in Tatvan, another unspectacular traffic junction.

Our next destination: along the shore of "Van Gölü" to Gevaş, to take a ferry from there to the island of Akdamar. The usual: sunny from early morning until 11:00, then thunderstorms. The weather changes very quickly. Usually there's only just time to put on our rain gear. Cycling in waterproof overclothes is demotivating and exhausting. Because you sweat, you soon end up almost as wet on your skin as without them. Yes, you can guess what's coming: once again we pedal up the mountain in the rain and headwind. Help arrives as if we had called for it; so far we have always been lucky! A construction crew in a crew bus throws open the doors, all the workers help, and within 2 minutes we and our gear are loaded. In the dry, with Turkish "background singing", we go 5 km further to the canteen hut. We are given lunch and can warm up over tea. There is usually someone who speaks English, which makes it easier to tell them about our adventure and to swap email addresses. At the end of the lunch break we cycle on towards Gevaş, well aware that it will soon be pouring again.

"The unexpected often happens": long stretches of the road are under construction, not yet paved, or torn up by heavy machinery. The whole pass road is being widened to 4 lanes, reinforced or rebuilt with tunnels. We need an enormous amount of time to reach the top of the pass at 2,230 metres in time. It's already part of our daily ritual: at around 1,800 metres we are caught by another thunderstorm. Far and wide, no shelter, no house and no petrol station nearby. Pitch the tent in this weather? No! Keep pedalling, there's bound to be a solution. After about 2 kilometres we reach a heavy-goods lorry that also can't continue because of the storm. The driver, a Kurd, gets out and offers us his heated cab to warm up. From a little English and his gestures, we understand that he would let us have his sleeping bunk for the night. A little later: one of his long-distance trucker friends notices our bikes "parked" at the roadside. He stops, and we change vehicles. Relieved not to have to spend the night in a nicotine-soaked cab, we let his friend take us over the pass to Gevaş.

On the shore of Lake Van there are lots of campsites and picnic spots, restaurants and beaches for swimming. A Turkish "holiday strip" like on the Riviera. The season hasn't started yet, and all the businesses and hotels are still closed. Looking for a place to sleep, we come across a fish farm with a lokanta (restaurant) attached. The owner welcomes us and opens his kitchen for us; we are his first guests today and get two fried trout, salad, tea, and a bed for the night between the tables and chairs. The day, so demotivating at first, has had a happy ending after all.

For the next day we had planned to take the ferry from Gevaş to Akdamar. We wanted to take our gear with us and spend a night on the island. A boatman's statement that he would only set off after a tour group arrived at 13:00 was too risky for us, so we decide to cycle on to Van.

Thousands of years ago, Lake Van was just a river. A volcanic eruption dammed the natural watercourse, and a lake of 3,740 km² was formed (7 times as big as Lake Constance). Minerals are constantly washed into the lake from the mountains. Because there is no outflow and the water evaporates, a soapy alkaline solution forms. You get into the lake with dirty clothes and come out with clean ones.

On 19 October 2011 the city was shaken by an earthquake. 2,300 houses were destroyed or made uninhabitable because they were in danger of collapsing. Many inhabitants did not survive the disaster. The survivors now live in container settlements and are waiting for their houses to be rebuilt. In Turkey there is no law on building permits, building regulations or building inspections. People build as they like, as profitably as possible, with the help of acquaintances and friends. Anyone can be an architect. Unprofessionally built houses sink into the sandy ground or collapse. That makes another earthquake correspondingly dangerous.

The comforts of a hotel put us in touch with a tour group from the USA. Our bikes, parked in the lobby, were soon noticed and aroused interest in the "Zentralbikers". The tour leader invites us to join the full-day excursion to Akdamar and Van Fortress. A free day's round trip awaits us, in a first-class coach with plenty of legroom, a reserved ferry and an excellent lunch.

The island has a ferry landing, a staircase up to the monastery, and of course a souvenir shop with a cafeteria. At the highest point, among lots of almond trees, stands the Armenian Orthodox church. This sight, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, was an autonomous Armenian territory until the First World War, and so also part of Kurdish culture. Here there was a physical border between Persia, Africa and Europe. The "old" Armenians had their own architecture, alphabet and language, and were known among the Turks as trustworthy partners.

Recommendation:
 Because there's no road, there are steps and there's nowhere to camp, it's best to leave your bike on the mainland

6 kilometres after Muradiye (a campsite by the waterfall), our night's rest was badly disturbed. Contrary to the restaurant owner's advice to put the tent up in the middle of the brightly lit football pitch, we prefer the "safe" woods. We aren't the only ones who like it better in the dark. Several times during the night, our sleep is interrupted by the barking of wild dogs. They fight all around the tent and get their paws caught in the guy ropes. The campsite owner's Dobermann, armed with a spiked collar, comes to our rescue and drives the troublemakers away.

We cycle within a hair's breadth of the Iranian border. The border posts and their fortifications are clearly visible. Over the Tendürek Geçidi, officially 2,644 m high, at a 9% gradient, we reach the top of the pass. More than 5 hours have passed since we set off in the morning. We were looking forward to a fast descent, but once again we are caught by rain showers and a strong wind that means we have to pedal even going downhill. And so we reach the town of Doğubayazıt. Without the sight of "İshak Paşa" you would leave this town again as fast as possible. To finish off, after 85 kilometres and over 1,100 metres of climbing, comes "dessert". On cobblestones we push our fully loaded bikes for 7 kilometres at a 10% gradient up to Murat Camping. An effort that isn't worth it (but there is no alternative). This campsite is the starting point for expeditions to Mount Ararat (5,134 m), the highest mountain in Turkey. Noah's Ark is supposed to have run aground on this rock. According to one account, an American now wants to dig up the ark, which has supposedly already been "located". Seek and you shall find (maybe).

The end of Turkey is near; the Iranian border, 40 kilometres away, is getting closer! No more free choice of clothes, and so the start of the legally required covering of bare skin. Apart from the hands and face, uncovered skin is forbidden in Iran. Women in particular are punished for disobedience. Claudia already bought a headscarf in Van, and a long-sleeved top reaching below the hips. More about how comfortable these are for cycling in temperatures above 50 degrees follows in the Iran travel report.

There are many reasons for conflict.
Yes, Kurdistan is in conflict with the government and the "Jandarma". A dangerous PKK, robberies, terrorist attacks, kidnappings of tourists and roadblocks – we noticed none of that. Contrary to all the "well-meant" warnings, we only had good encounters with Kurds. Our experience of Kurdistan paints a completely different picture:

Interesting facts:
Proud Kurds are friendly and helpful.
A patriotic Kurdish construction crew rescues us from the thunderstorm. In the canteen hut we are given tea and lunch and can warm up.
A hospitable Kurd offers us dinner for three and a bed for the night in his lokanta.
Considerate Kurdish drivers honk, not to push us off the road, but to show how happy they are that we are there.
At the police "checkpoints" only the tachographs and the papers of the lorry drivers are checked, as is usual in other countries too.
Turkey, with its area of 814,578 km², is 19 times bigger than Switzerland.
3% of the country is on European soil – the rest on Asian soil.
Istanbul, with 15 million inhabitants, is the only city in the world that stretches across 2 continents.
Of its 75 million inhabitants, 99% are Muslim.
Ararat (5,137 metres) is the highest mountain in Turkey.
Turkey is now one of the 20 largest economies in the world.
40% of industrial companies, with 2/5 of the country's jobs, are in Istanbul.
With more than 500,000 soldiers, the army is one of the largest armed forces in the world.

/berichte/turkmenistan.title: Turkmenistan
/berichte/turkmenistan.html:
Turkmenistan
12 - 15 June 2012

At 10:00 we are standing at the Iran-Turkmenistan customs. Although there is a ramp for processing, we have to carry the bikes and luggage up 5 steps into the building. A sign directs tourists on foot to this entrance, and no exception is made for us either. The usual procedure: wait, wait, wait, and watch our passports being passed from office to office, "organisation professionnelle". Changing rial into manat in the customs area came to nothing. The man in charge of the exchange sends us back out to the street to do our business. Contrary to expectations, the Iranian export check goes quickly. After a spot check of our panniers, we walk through the barbed-wire gate towards the Turkmen border post. For about 500 metres you are in the no-man's-land corridor until the first checkpoint, where our passports are examined. "No entry, you don't have a visa", whereupon we hand over our "letter of invitation" issued by the Turkmen embassy. "There is no stamp." Now we start to get a little uneasy. The consequences of not getting the transit visa would be disastrous. After some lengthy explanations, we are asked to see the immigration officer in the border building 200 metres away. But the bureaucracy! By now it's 12:00, lunchtime; never mind that we've already been waiting 2 hours, protesting is no use. At 13:00 the team reappears. 65 dollars per person lighter, and with another coloured sticker in our passports, we move on to the X-ray machine. To our horror, the luggage of an Uzbek family is being completely taken apart. Every bag, suitcase and purse is emptied and spread out on a table. No! Even the children's toys are X-rayed one by one and opened where possible. The contents of the thermos flask are poured out and the tea bags squeezed. If this happens to us, laying out and checking our equipment will take another 2 - 3 hours.

No, that seems too much trouble for the officer after all. A quick question about which electronic devices are in our luggage, a spot check of the handlebar bag, and that's it. The declaration form is decorated by three more officials with various stamps and signatures, and the procedure is over. After a total of 4 hours in the border area, we are allowed to enter Turkmen territory with our 5-day transit visa. By now the temperatures have climbed to their highest, and the wind has become our strongest "opponent".

We battle forward for two hours at a maximum of 10 km/h and need huge amounts of water. It's grinding us down! It can't go on like this. 410 kilometres to Turkmenabat in 5 days? We can't keep to that target like this. The penalty for arriving late could cut our budget by several hundred dollars. The solution: once again, wait for a lift on a lorry. It doesn't take long, and we are moving on several axles towards the nearest town.

The road is in a disastrous state. The heat makes the asphalt melt, creating countless ruts and ridges. Riddled with countless potholes, the road becomes a uniquely bone-shaking track. The whole vehicle is shaken about, and our bikes bounce on the loading platform. Visibly relieved, we reach "Tejen" at 17:00. We've had enough of the wind, the heat and the bad roads, and decide to take the night train to Turkmenabat.

In a great hurry we change a few dollars into manat to pay for the ticket and dinner. Time seems to have stood still here. It looks like Russia, and people drive old Ladas. Some Turkmen are sly foxes and keep trying to rip us off. By now we know how to deal with this bad habit and negotiate the prices. The ticket for us and our "baggage" costs a ridiculous 10 US dollars. With a handwritten, stamped and punched piece of cardboard, we board the "express train" to Turkmenabat.

Apart from ugly Soviet buildings, an oversized main street and only a handful of hotels, Turkmenabat offers nothing out of the ordinary. Only the bazaar is worth a visit, to have our Iran trousers shortened to a length that works on a bike.

We use the 2-day wait until our Uzbek visa starts to give our bikes an overhaul. First a thorough clean, followed by a check of the mechanical parts for wear. After 1,000 kilometres the chain is changed, and the old one cleaned and got ready for the next change. Fixing a flat tyre for the 4th time. An almost invisible steel wire, which we couldn't find at first, had bored into the tyre and kept piercing new holes in the tube. All the equipment has been checked, fuel and supplies topped up, clothes washed and the crew rested. After only 4 days in Turkmenistan we leave the country, hoping for less headwind and better roads.

/berichte/uruguay.title: Uruguay
/berichte/uruguay.html:
Uruguay
3 - 14 July 2009

We will cross Uruguay "easily" and soon reach our destination, Montevideo. Wrong! One day after crossing the border at Bella Unión, we are surprised by a strong headwind from the south, which at times only lets the speedometer show single figures. We struggle painfully against a force of nature that really "grates" on our nerves and our panniers. At least the road surface doesn't "grate" on our tyres as well, so we roll along nicely. The roads are perfectly paved and well built. They remind us once again of the Argentinian "corrugated" profile of ranges of hills lying across the road, rising to 500 metres above sea level. A seemingly endless up and down.

The difference from Argentina is striking: the traffic has dropped noticeably, and now in Uruguay we enjoy stress-free cycling. What stands out are the vintage cars, lorries and cars of American origin. Often, however, these vehicles are in a worrying state, and many have no liability insurance. You wonder how many years ago their last service was. We prefer being overtaken by old bangers with a friendly wave to being pushed off the road with "non-stop honking" by angry drivers, as in Argentina. Although there is a give-way-to-the-right rule, the law of the stronger or faster tends to apply. By now we have got used to this and understand "other countries, other customs".

Cycling through Uruguay …. Because the country is so thinly populated, the towns are often more than 50 kilometres apart. The flora offers no shade from the intense sun, and the small patches of woodland are often far from the road. For cycle tourists, these conditions make for real "lean stretches". Few places to stay or buy supplies means camping often, so a tent and a stove are essential. Far and wide there is nothing but prickly, coarse grassland and water (20% of Uruguay's 177,000 km² is water). Nobody would mind a tent, wild camping is no problem – or so you'd think. No, all the farms have fenced off their land with posts and wire fences you can't get over. The water "pumps" are not at the roadside, or the water is only drinkable with a Katadyn filter and chlorine tablets. The farms, with their striking wind-powered towers for pumping groundwater, give us the feeling that we haven't been completely abandoned by civilisation. Most of the time these "estancias" give us a place to spend the night. Sometimes we were even invited to shower in the workers' house and warm up by the fire.

The most beautiful thermal baths in Uruguay are on the Río Arapey (90 km north-east of Salto). Don't miss this "must"! That's the well-meant advice of a local. So off we go; we have enough time to add the place, 19 kilometres off our route, to our "timetable". Into a headwind, with countless potholes in the asphalt, we reach the "Termas del Arapey" after 2 hours. This resort, heavily "marked" by tourism, feels more like a holiday complex and didn't convince us of its supposed attractions. The same day we cycle the 19 kilometres back to Ruta 3, to find an "estancia" to camp at before dark. By now the southern polar wind has picked up alarmingly, and big black thunderclouds are approaching. Just 1 hour later, with no farm in sight yet, we are caught by a hurricane-like thunderstorm. A "bus stop shelter" gives us a little protection from the rain, but only standing on the bench, where the roof has stayed watertight.

Only 470 kilometres to go! A week has already passed since we crossed the border into Uruguay. Mostly into the cold headwind from the South Pole, we are steadily getting closer to our destination, Montevideo. If only it weren't for these cold nights that freeze the water in our bottles. It's winter here! Nothing happens before 8 in the morning. The outside of the tent is covered with frost, and the inside is wet with condensation. Every day we wait for the morning sun to dry our "house". It's usually no warmer than 7 degrees.

Only 200 kilometres to go! It will get even colder, a farmer predicts. You soon find yourself wishing for the summer warmth of the northern hemisphere again. The corrugated profile, caused by the ranges of hills lying across the road, has by now stretched out a little. Our road runs dead straight towards Montevideo, and tomorrow we will already be able to read our………

10,000th kilometre since the start of our journey in San Francisco on the counter. 125 kilometres before Montevideo, the milestone by the road tells us: "now you've left the 10,000th behind you". Quickly capture the moment on camera, a sandwich between the teeth, a handful of biscuits in the pocket, and on we go.

Only 100 kilometres to go! Tomorrow we could already reach Montevideo. Do the laundry (which is urgently needed), sleep in a bed with fresh sheets again, and not eat out of one "feeding bowl" with two spoons. Have we missed the comforts of everyday life? Yes, no, maybe, a little?

The "Antel Tower" (Uruguay's telecommunications giant) is Montevideo's landmark and shows us the way to the city centre. We don't need the road map any more. We reach the shore of the "Río de la Plata", where the Río Paraná and the Río Uruguay meet. The opposite shore (Argentina) is 100 kilometres away. Interesting: these gigantic masses of water flow into the South Atlantic Ocean, and the direction of the wind decides whether the water is salty or fresh.

Montevideo seems calm to us, with no traffic chaos. It was surprisingly easy to find our way into the centre of this big city by bike. The capital of Uruguay, with 1.5 million inhabitants, seems easy to find your way around and well kept, even if the unsightly "ANCAP refinery" for petroleum production at first makes you think it's an industrial city.

We've made it! Montevideo!
Now we want to rest first, plan the journey home, enjoy a sightseeing tour of Montevideo and forget about the bikes for a few days, before we take the coach from Montevideo to Colonia del Sacramento and the ferry across the "Río de la Plata" to Buenos Aires (Argentina).

The country and its people:
Uruguay has 3.3 million inhabitants, 40% of whom live in the capital, Montevideo, 50% in the other large towns, and 10% in the countryside (farmland). Salto, the country's second-largest city, with "only" 100,000 inhabitants, seems almost "provincial" compared with the capital.
Uruguay borders Argentina, Brazil and the Atlantic Ocean, and is the smallest Spanish-speaking country in South America.

The wide grasslands of the pampas are used by large herds of up to 5,000 cattle per "estancia" (farm). Only 5% of Uruguay's total area is forested. Uruguay is also the first country in the world to have the right to water guaranteed in its constitution.

The bus companies have modern, air-conditioned vehicles for long-distance travel, which makes the bus the country's main means of transport.

2,000 km of railway, 9,000 km of roads, 1,600 km of navigable waterways, 9 ports, 64 airfields, 14 of them with paved runways

The main port of South America is in Montevideo, not far from the city boundary, and handles more than 1 million containers a year. According to statistics, Montevideo is the second-safest city in the world after Tokyo.

The name Montevideo is made up of:

Monte = hill,
vi (Roman VI) = 6
d (de) = of
e (este) = east
o (oeste) = west

Alligators are only found on the upper reaches of the "Río Uruguay". After Alaska, Uruguay has the 2nd-largest colony of seals and sea lions, which live on the "Isla de Lobos" near Punta del Este.

Uruguay is one of the few countries where school and higher education are free. Although the level of education is one of the highest in South America, over 20% of people live below the poverty line.

After 750 kilometres we leave Uruguay with these memories:

Our 10,000th kilometre, reached at milestone "125" before Montevideo

An extreme southern polar wind that only lets the speedometer show single figures

Cold: hat, gloves, windstopper

The outer tent coated with ice, the water in our bottles frozen

Temperatures: -2 degrees at night, +2 degrees in the tent, +7 degrees from 08:00 in the morning

Lots of camping at petrol stations, farms and the roadside

Little traffic: vintage cars, horse-drawn carts, new cars and rusty old bangers

Corrugated terrain across the whole country, with ranges of hills lying across the road

From sea level up to max. 500 metres above sea level, up and down like in Argentina

Huge farmland, fauna, flora and huge herds of cattle

Our water filter lets us get drinking water from the marshes

A sightseeing tour of Montevideo
