/berichte/usbekistan.title: Uzbekistan
/berichte/usbekistan.html:
Uzbekistan
15 June - 9 July 2012

30 kilometres after the border we look for a suitable place to sleep. This doesn't seem to be so easy here, because large areas are used for farming. Seen from the road, a few places to pitch the tent look suitable. Looked at a little more closely, it's a completely different picture. The "idyllic" finds are often full of thorns, ploughs have turned the farmland into corrugated iron, and cooking on cowpats or soaking wet ground isn't easy. During heavy rain, trickles become unpredictable streams, and streams become raging rivers. Fields flooded by small watercourses shouldn't be underestimated either. You never know exactly when and where the farmers will open the valves or sluices of the irrigation system. Water bubbles under the tent floor are "only" an unpleasant surprise – hastily moving the tent in the dark at night is the real nuisance. If you can sleep lying flat at all, it's almost a "stroke of luck".

After more than an hour we give up and try our luck in the farmers' gardens instead. With success. A family offers us a place to sleep in their living room, or on the 3 x 3 metre outdoor daybed. There's no need to put up the tent, and on top of that we are spoilt with dinner. Because the temperature doesn't drop below 30 degrees even at night, we prefer to sleep outside, so we can fall asleep before midnight. We wanted to set off early at sunrise. Claudia's bike has a flat for the third time in 24 hours. So: find the hole, patch it, breakfast, and then on we go. Our route leads to Bukhara and gives us the hottest day so far. In the sun, at 55 degrees, cycling becomes almost unbearable. Our lunch breaks are stretched to 3 hours with a "nap" in the shade. That way we can also make up for our lack of sleep.

Bukhara surprises us with magnificently restored caravanserais, madrasas and mausoleums. Here we meet Axel and Sylvia again, whom we already know well from the Silk Road Hotel (Iran). We are happy to speak German with like-minded people again. Together we look for a friendly place to stay for the next 2 nights at an acceptable tourist price. Here in Bukhara we finally get to enjoy an excellent coffee with little treats again, something unusual in these countries. Axel and Sylvia travel on towards Tashkent, and we to Samarkand.

Alexandre is suffering from stomach ache and diarrhoea, so the ride to Samarkand becomes an ordeal. Samarkand, an almost over-restored city with lots of tourists, does offer plenty of chances to recover, though. From a New Zealander who has already visited 175 countries, we learn that the Panjakent border crossing is closed. Because of the conflict between Uzbekistan and Tajikistan in April 2012, this main route to Dushanbe was closed. The surprising news forces us to use the border crossing further south, which means a 300-kilometre detour via Boysun to Denov.

Over passes of up to 1,650 metres, through pastures, steppe and cornfields, we come across varied vegetation full of variety. Passing the foothills of the 4,200-metre "Hisor" mountains, we feel a little better again. After 4 days of cycling in more bearable temperatures, we reach the overheated lowlands of Denov. 300 kilometres on gravel and unpaved roads were a "treat" compared with 45 degrees of heat.

While preparing our visa applications, we "miscalculated". Tashkent wasn't part of our travel plan, so 20 days in Uzbekistan instead of 30 would have been enough. Assuming we could have our visas brought forward at the Tajik border, we look forward to crossing it. Unfortunately, wrong. The Uzbek officials would let us through, but the Tajik ones would turn us back. As a result, since we don't have a "double entry" for Uzbekistan, we would have to "camp" between the borders.

There is no exception, so we are advised to go back to Tashkent, 820 kilometres away, to make a new application at the Tajik embassy. For cyclists, an absurd suggestion! At 80 kilometres a day, we would need 20 days there and back. Not counting the unpredictable wait for the visas. So we decide to "while away" the 10 days in Denov, 40 kilometres away. We broke off the detour to Termez after 20 kilometres because of the extreme temperatures and Alexandre's digestive problems, which hadn't healed yet. A request to bring forward our entry date is still pending at the Tajik embassy. At the Hotel EURASIA near the border, we spend the remaining time preparing for our "Pamir Highway adventure".

/berichte.title: Reports
/berichte.html:
America
Amerige, the land of Americus: we want to discover it too, not by ship but by bicycle. For one year we cycle from San Francisco through the double continent of North America (with Central America) and South America, and after 10,000 kilometres in the saddle we finally reach our goal in Montevideo, Uruguay.

Asia
The Silk Road, a network of roads linking the Mediterranean with East Asia. Over the Pamir Highway to Kashgar, where merchants once carried silk, gunpowder and paper from China to Europe. Where caravans once dragged themselves through the dust, we travel by bicycle, right across South-East Asia to Singapore.

Oceania
La Paz, at an altitude of 3,200 to 4,100 m, is the highest seat of government in the world. The Salar de Uyuni, at more than 10,000 square kilometres, is the largest salt flat on earth. Chile, 4,300 kilometres long and cut off like an island by the peaks of the Andes, and Patagonia, with Tierra del Fuego at the stormy end of the world. New Zealand, the green island at the other end of the world, which has a lot to offer, from kiwis and the Maori to volcanic glaciers.

/claudia.title: Claudia
/claudia.html:
As a keen mountain biker, she sees riding her bike to work in any weather as training. So her idea of a trekking adventure across another continent came as no surprise. Her stamina, her solution-oriented way of thinking and her motto "try, experiment and test" have proved their worth many times.

Easy-going as she is, she does not give up even in difficult situations, and she fights her way through. Her perseverance and her enthusiasm are good qualities for this adventure. Her reliability and her willingness to compromise give me the feeling of security I need to cope with the unexpected.

Alexandre

/.title: Home
/.html:
Idea – Decision – Planning

The greatest sight of all is the world itself.

What you have seen, experienced and touched yourself stays in your memory far better than things you have only read about. In our times, everything can be calculated and planned much more easily. Perhaps authentic travel lies precisely in the gap between the plan and reality.

The stories of other world travellers give us a hint of where an unfamiliar road might lead. Travelling is not only about choosing a destination, but much more about the joyful anticipation of opening ourselves up to the unknown. Recording our encounters, impressions and feelings is also part of our travel experience.

We often ask ourselves: is it wanderlust that needs to be satisfied, or a longing for the extraordinary? Is it the fantasy of places and people, or saying goodbye to the old and meeting the new?


Even though the age of the great conquerors and explorers is long gone, a little explorer still slumbers inside us, one who wants to see what it does not yet know.

And so we want to feel life, and give up the familiar in order to discover the unfamiliar.

Footprints fade, memories last forever.

/info/fluege.title: Flights
/info/fluege.html:
Flight rules, America

1 September 2008 / 08:10: Zurich - London BA709
1 September 2008 / 09:05: London - San Francisco BA285
Return flight reserved: Buenos Aires Ezeiza - London BA246
Connecting flight: London - Zurich BA712

Taking a bicycle on a plane used to be a complicated and frustrating business, but by now the airlines are used to bike travellers……

Provided that:
1. You book early
2. You check your open-jaw ticket, flight connections and connecting flights precisely
3. You get written confirmation of the transport of your trekking bike, tandem or yak for both the outward and return flights

At this point, at the latest, the exhausting back-and-forth with the airlines begins about how the extra luggage can be transported. At first, it was impossible to get binding information about the free baggage allowance:

Is sports luggage carried free of charge?
Is it transported as part of the free baggage allowance?
Overseas: 2 pieces of luggage of 32 kg or 22.7 kg each?
Weight concept or piece concept?
Bike packed in a cardboard box or in a plastic bag?
Size of the bike box: L 160 x H 92 x W 30?
Maximum weight of hand luggage 5 kg or 10 kg?

And the small print:
"All information without guarantee – subject to change"

Transporting windsurfing equipment (300 x 60 x 50 cm / no weight limit given) for 25 euros per item each way is much easier!

Without written confirmation from the airline, taking a bike (because of the limit on the number of pieces) can cause unexpected problems. Anything can happen: unpacking and repacking at the airport, paying for excess weight at a price per kilo set at the airline's discretion, or in the end having to leave your gear behind.

The travel agency Globetrotter Luzern stood up for us and managed to get written confirmation from the airline allowing us the following free allowance for checked luggage:

2 pieces of luggage per person of max. 23 kg each
1 additional piece of sports equipment per person of max. 23 kg in a cardboard box

Note from the airline:
"The limit of 158 cm per piece of luggage is more of a guideline; it is no longer measured at the airport. What matters is that the bikes are registered with the correct dimensions and confirmed by us, which means we also have the possibility of loading them onto the right aircraft. On www.ba.com there are exact instructions on how the bikes must be packed, and you can also read the rules for hand luggage there. We strongly recommend taking out luggage insurance, as the cover is usually not enough in the event of damage."

And so we would like to thank British Airways and Globetrotter for their support.

/info/impfung.title: Vaccinations
/info/impfung.html:
Vaccination requirements
Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil, Uruguay, Laos, Cambodia, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore

Yellow fever
Proof of yellow fever vaccination is required for all travellers arriving from yellow fever areas. Yellow fever endemic areas are the areas of yellow fever transmission designated by the WHO.

Recommended vaccinations
Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, Turkey, Iran, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, China, Laos, Cambodia, Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Chile, New Zealand, Australia

Diphtheria
Everyone should be vaccinated (booster every 10 years).
Hepatitis A
All travellers to countries where hepatitis A is common.
Hepatitis B
Travellers to areas where hepatitis B is common, when there is an increased risk of infection, and for longer stays (> 1 month). It is advisable to consider a hepatitis B vaccination. In Germany, the vaccination is routinely recommended for children and teenagers.
Malaria
In risk areas there is a risk all year round (carry emergency medication).
Tetanus
Everyone should be vaccinated (booster every 10 years).
Rabies
Vaccination. Keep away from free-roaming and stray animals.
Typhoid
Travel to countries with poor hygiene and poor drinking water supplies.

Health risks
Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, Costa Rica, Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Paraguay, Argentina, Laos, Cambodia, Thailand, Malaysia, Australia

Chagas disease
When sleeping outdoors: protect yourself from the carrier, the so-called kissing bug, which lives mainly in mud huts and is active at night.
Cholera
Careful food and drinking water hygiene.
Dengue fever
Protect yourself from mosquitoes with clothing that covers the skin. Use insect repellent, mosquito coils, mosquito nets, etc.
Intestinal infections
Careful food and drinking water hygiene.
Leishmaniasis
Protect yourself from mosquitoes with clothing that covers the skin. Use insect repellent and fine-mesh mosquito nets.
Filariasis
Protect yourself from insects and mosquitoes with clothing that covers the skin. Use insect repellent, mosquito coils and mosquito nets.
Kala-azar
Protect yourself from mosquitoes with clothing that covers the skin. Use insect repellent and fine-mesh mosquito nets.
Typhus
Protect yourself from body lice through regular, thorough hygiene. Vaccination is only recommended in rare cases!
Plague (Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Brazil)
Protect yourself from rats and fleas (a safe place to sleep and frequent, hygienic changes of clothes). Travellers should keep away from people with plague. After exposure, antibiotics can be taken as a precaution.
Bilharzia (Brazil)
Avoid skin contact with fresh water.
Meningococcus, meningitis (Brazil)
Vaccination. Avoid large crowds (cramped living conditions, overcrowded transport).
Japanese encephalitis
Vaccination is recommended in special situations. There is no specific treatment. You can prevent the disease by protecting yourself from mosquito bites (air-conditioned rooms, using a mosquito net, wearing long-sleeved clothing at dusk and at night, using insect repellent sprays, etc.).
Ross River fever (Australia)
Protect yourself from mosquitoes with clothing that covers the skin. Use insect repellent and fine-mesh mosquito nets. The symptoms are high fever, headaches and joint pain, which can last for several months.
Chikungunya (North, Central and South America)
Protect yourself from mosquitoes with clothing that covers the skin. Use insect repellent and fine-mesh mosquito nets. Chikungunya is usually harmless and shows itself as fever and joint pain in the knees, ankles and the small joints of the hands and feet.

/info/visa.title: Visas
/info/visa.html:
For a maximum stay of 90 days, no visa is required in North, Central and South America! These rules are a snapshot in time and should definitely be checked again before you travel.

Entry requirements:

USA
Passport and a tourist card (handed out on the plane). You may stay 3 months without a visa (you may have to show a return ticket).
Mexico
Passport and a tourist card (handed out at the border). You can usually stay 90 days. If you enter overland (so also as a cyclist coming from the USA), you pay an entry tax of 20 USD the first time you enter.
Guatemala
Passport valid for at least another 6 months. If you enter or leave overland, expect to pay fees of between 10 and 20 quetzales at the border. You are usually given a residence permit for 90 days.
Honduras
Passport valid for at least another 6 months. Swiss citizens are given a visa on entry for a stay of 30 to 90 days. A return or onward ticket, or enough money, is required (you are asked about the money when entering overland).
Nicaragua
Passport valid for at least another 6 months. You can usually stay 90 days.
Costa Rica
Passport valid for at least another 6 months.
Panama
Passport valid for at least another 6 months.
Colombia
Passport valid for at least another 6 months.
Ecuador
Passport valid for at least another 6 months.
Peru
Passport valid for at least another 6 months. You can usually stay 183 days. Entry and customs cards are handed out at the border crossings.
Bolivia
Passport valid for at least another 6 months. You can usually stay 30 days.
Paraguay
Passport valid for at least another 3 months. You can usually stay 90 days.
Argentina
Passport valid for at least another 3 months. You can usually stay 90 days (the stay can be extended by 3 months). You may be given a tourist card at the border.
Uruguay
Passport valid for at least another 3 months. You can usually stay 90 days (the stay can be extended by 3 months).
Chile
Passport valid for at least another 6 months. You can usually stay 90 days (the stay can be extended once by 90 days). You are given a tourist card.

Travelling through Asia or Oceania is a different story. Practically every country requires a visa! The individual entry requirements are listed below.

Turkey
Swiss citizens need an identity card or a passport valid for at least 6 months beyond their return date (no visa required).
Iran
To enter, Swiss citizens need a passport with a visa, valid for at least 6 months beyond their return date.
Turkmenistan
To enter, Swiss citizens need a passport with a visa, valid for at least 6 months beyond their return date.
Uzbekistan
To enter, Swiss citizens need a passport with a visa, valid for at least 6 months beyond their return date.
Tajikistan
To enter, Swiss citizens need a passport with a visa, valid for at least 6 months beyond their return date.
Kyrgyzstan
Swiss citizens need a passport valid for at least six months beyond their return date (no visa required).
China
To enter, Swiss citizens need a passport with a visa, valid for at least 6 months beyond their return date.
Laos
For stays of up to 15 days, Swiss citizens need a Swiss passport valid for at least 6 months after the end of their stay, without a tourist visa.
Anyone staying longer than 15 days in Laos can, as before, get a so-called "visa on arrival" for about 35 US dollars directly at one of the official border crossings or at the airports of Vientiane, Luang Prabang and Pakse. It allows a stay of up to 30 days and can be extended.
Cambodia
To enter, Swiss citizens need a passport with a visa, valid for at least 6 months beyond their return date.
Tourist and business visas are issued to citizens of all nationalities on arrival at the international airports of Pochentong (Phnom Penh) and Siem Reap. Visas on arrival are also available at the border crossings of Poipet/Aranyaprathet, Hat Lek/Cham Yeam and Koh Kong (Thailand), and Bavet/Moc Bai and Kaom Samnor (Vietnam).
Thailand
For stays of up to 30 days, Swiss citizens need a Swiss passport valid for at least 6 months after the end of their stay, without a visa. For longer stays, ask at the country's diplomatic missions.
Malaysia
Swiss citizens need an identity card or a passport valid for at least 6 months beyond their return date (no visa required).
Singapore
For stays of up to 1 month (14 days when entering overland), Swiss citizens need a Swiss passport valid for at least 6 months after arrival, without a visa (a "Social Visit Pass" is issued on arrival at the airport).
Extending your stay
The Social Visit Pass can be extended in Singapore to a maximum of 90 days. Information is available from the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority under "Visitors".
New Zealand
Passport valid for at least another 3 months. You can usually stay 90 days. A visa is required for stays of more than 3 months.
Australia
To enter, Swiss citizens need a passport with a visa, valid for at least 6 months beyond their return date.

/ueber-uns.title: About us
/ueber-uns.html:
Alexandre
Claudia


As keen mountain bikers, hardly any "mountain" is safe from us. Again and again we discover new routes that take us up to the summits of our home mountains in Central Switzerland.

Our favourite stage is the Four Lakes Tour, which leads from Lucerne to Melchsee-Frutt, over the Joch Pass to Engelberg and back to Lucerne. On longer tours with long stretches of carrying our bikes, such as over the "Surenen Pass", we spend the night at the "Stäfeli Hut" on the way up to the top of the pass. We also love riding the Rigi, the Bürgenstock and the Stanserhorn.

Now and then we also take part in bike marathons. The Swiss Bike Masters in the Prättigau, where we wait for the starting gun together with more than 3,000 other riders, is always a special experience. In 2007 we were thrilled by the Engadin Bike Marathon in the Grisons (138 km and 4,000 m of climbing) and its unique landscape. Smaller events like the "Brittnauer", where there is no timing and afterwards we talk shop with other cyclists over a plate of spaghetti, are always welcome to us as a chance to make new friends.

We love experiencing nature on two wheels and feeling that high of having once again "pedalled off" a few more kilometres.

To balance out our bike training, we spend our holidays windsurfing in Egypt.
